title: [IDEA-WIZARD] Swarm-scale responsiveness and resource-governor program
description:
## Background
Phase 2/3 idea-wizard outcome for the saturated ready queue: make Pi compelling for massive agent swarms on 64+ CPU / 256GB+ RAM hosts by turning runtime responsiveness, resource governance, RCH evidence integrity, and degraded coordination behavior into measurable, replayable product surfaces. This epic deliberately avoids duplicating the closed coverage-traceability lane bd-8t27h and leaves the active full-suite stabilization bead bd-kniej to its current owner.

## Scope
Coordinate a set of implementation and testing beads that make swarm readiness observable, replayable, and fail-closed. The work should improve operator confidence without adding release-facing performance claims unless existing claim-integrity gates are satisfied.

## Success Criteria
- At least one child bead produces deterministic non-mock swarm replay evidence.
- Resource and headroom diagnostics cover cgroup/NUMA/tmpfs/RCH concerns with machine-readable output.
- RCH artifact sync requirements are checked before artifact-dependent gates.
- Degraded Agent Mail behavior has a productive Beads fallback path.
- New reports are schema/freshness checked and do not bypass drop-in or performance claim gates.
notes: Refinement pass: parent epic lowered to P4 container so ready-work selection points at concrete child beads. Do not claim this parent until child tasks are complete; use bd-07cku.1/.2/.3 as the highest-priority starting lanes.
close_reason: All swarm-scale child beads completed with replay evidence, resource/RCH diagnostics, degraded-mail fallback, and schema/freshness-checked diagnostic runpack

title: [IDEA-WIZARD] Build swarm flight-recorder replay harness
description:
## Background
Large agent swarms need a way to replay real runtime behavior instead of relying on anecdotal traces. Existing reports cover individual surfaces, but not one deterministic multi-agent flight recorder across Pi entrypoints and runtime components.

## Scope
Create a deterministic multi-agent flight-recorder harness that captures redacted events across RPC/interactive entrypoints, tool execution, extension hostcalls, session persistence, and external coordination markers into a replayable JSONL bundle.

## Acceptance Criteria
- A non-mock E2E scenario launches multiple Pi sessions against isolated temp workspaces.
- The bundle records turn/tool/session/extension timing with correlation IDs and redaction summaries.
- Replay works without live provider credentials.
- The report identifies dominant latency components and coordination failures.
- JSONL schema validation and operator docs are included.
- Heavy validation runs through rch when Cargo is involved.
close_reason: Completed

title: [IDEA-WIZARD] Add cgroup and NUMA aware swarm resource preflight
description:
## Background
Swarm operators need preflight guidance that reflects the host they actually have: cgroup CPU quota, cpuset limits, NUMA topology, memory, tmpfs headroom, and expected concurrent-agent pressure.

## Scope
Extend the swarm/operator preflight path so Pi can report host topology and recommended concurrency budgets before large swarms or heavy validation runs.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Text and JSON output include cgroup CPU quota, cpuset size, NUMA topology, memory limits, tmpfs/headroom, and recommended concurrency budgets.
- Missing critical headroom fails closed with actionable diagnostics.
- Unit tests cover cgroup and NUMA parser edge cases.
- E2E or fixture tests cover constrained-container and high-capacity-host profiles.
- Docs explain how operators should interpret the budgets.
close_reason: Completed cgroup and NUMA aware swarm resource preflight

title: [IDEA-WIZARD] Verify RCH mirror completeness before artifact-dependent gates
description:
## Background
Recent RCH validation was blocked because nested test artifacts were accidentally excluded from worker sync. Artifact-dependent gates need a preflight that proves required files will reach the worker before the expensive run starts.

## Scope
Add a preflight that verifies required generated/artifact paths are included in the RCH sync set before remote tests or report generation consume them.

## Acceptance Criteria
- The check detects unsynced nested artifact directories.
- Diagnostics name the exact ignore or sync rule at fault.
- Dry-run JSON output lists required paths, matched rules, and pass/fail state.
- Regression coverage uses a miniature fixture where root artifact excludes must not hide test-owned artifacts.
- The check is documented for RCH-backed cargo/test/report workflows.

title: [IDEA-WIZARD] Add Agent Mail degraded-mode Beads fallback diagnostics
description:
## Background
Agent Mail can be semantically corrupt while Beads remains usable. Agents should get crisp diagnostics and a productive fallback instead of getting stuck retrying mailbox operations.

## Scope
Make swarm diagnostics useful when Agent Mail schema health, ack, send, or registration paths fail but Beads is still available.

## Acceptance Criteria
- A doctor or swarm diagnostics path identifies missing mail schema and ack/send failures.
- When reads still work, active agent names and recent activity are listed.
- Output recommends Beads comments/status as the soft lock without blocking useful work.
- A machine-readable degraded-mode artifact is emitted.
- Tests simulate red/read-only mail health and prove actionable fallback guidance.

title: [IDEA-WIZARD] Stress extension hostcall admission under 64-core swarm profiles
description:
## Background
The extension hostcall dispatcher has fast lanes, compatibility lanes, backpressure, fairness, and rollback metrics. Swarm-scale confidence requires high-contention profiles that stress those controls under many concurrent agents.

## Scope
Add a high-contention extension hostcall benchmark/replay profile that models simultaneous agents on large hosts and records admission-control behavior.

## Acceptance Criteria
- The harness exercises fast-lane and compatibility-lane hostcalls with bounded queues.
- Metrics include fairness, backpressure, rollback, starvation, and tail latency.
- Sequential, batched, and adaptive scheduling modes are compared where supported.
- The report has deterministic thresholds that fail closed on tail latency or starvation regressions.
- Heavy runs use rch-backed Cargo commands and isolated target/temp dirs.
close_reason: Completed deterministic 64-agent hostcall admission replay with fail-closed fairness, backpressure, rollback, starvation, and tail-latency thresholds

title: [IDEA-WIZARD] Add large-session store v2 recovery stress gate
description:
## Background
Session Store V2 and SQLite indexing are core to responsiveness with huge histories. Swarm workloads need recovery evidence for large sessions, concurrent readers, and crash-adjacent writes.

## Scope
Create a focused long-history session stress gate for Session Store V2 and SQLite indexing under swarm-like concurrency.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Fixtures cover large token-class histories, checkpoint rebuild, stale sidecar fallback, truncated trailing frame recovery, and concurrent index reads/writes.
- Crash-resilient save behavior is asserted with deterministic temp dirs.
- JSONL timing and recovery evidence is emitted.
- Heavy variants run through rch with isolated target/temp dirs.
- Failure output includes enough context for a future agent to reproduce the bad segment or index state.
close_reason: Added large Session Store V2 recovery/concurrency stress gate with JSONL evidence

title: [IDEA-WIZARD] Add non-mock concurrent RPC swarm E2E
description:
## Background
Pi should prove concurrent RPC behavior with real filesystem/session side effects, not only unit mocks. This is central for IDE integrations and multi-agent operators.

## Scope
Add an E2E test that starts multiple RPC-mode Pi sessions in one project with isolated session dirs and real filesystem tools, then drives prompt, follow-up, abort, and get-state flows concurrently.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Filesystem and session behavior are non-mock and use temp workspaces.
- Structured logs include session IDs, queue state, command IDs, and redaction summaries.
- Assertions prove session-index locking remains healthy under concurrent sessions.
- Provider calls are avoided through a documented replay/keyless path without weakening runtime coverage.
- The test is stable under default parallel test execution.

title: Workspace trust-on-first-use gate for project-local .pi config (GH #151)
description: Implements the standard TOFU fix for GitHub #151: project-local .pi/settings.json packages and .pi/extensions execute code at startup with no trust decision. New src/workspace_trust.rs: content digest (sha256 manifest over .pi/settings.json + every file under .pi/extensions), persistent store at global_dir/workspace-trust.json keyed workspace path + digest, establish() decision flow. Interactive first launch prompts once (lists packages + extension entries) and persists trusted/untrusted; content change re-prompts; non-interactive launches fail closed with warning, nothing persisted. Automation: --trust flag (persists), PI_WORKSPACE_TRUST env (one-shot, wins over flag), global-settings trustAllWorkspaces. Untrusted runs skip the project settings merge (Config::load_with_project_trust) and all project-local resolution (PackageManager::with_project_trust -> ResolveRoots.project_settings_enabled). Explicit -e/--skill CLI paths stay ungated (user consent); explicit package subcommands stay trusted; PI_CONFIG_PATH override skips the gate (project resolution already disabled).

title: Keybindings: parse key strings + normalize to KeyId
description:
# Goal
Implement parsing for legacy keybinding strings (e.g. `ctrl+shift+p`, `pageUp`, `alt+enter`) into a canonical `KeyId` representation used by interactive mode.

# Scope / Deliverables
- Parse `modifier+key` strings where modifiers are any combination of: `ctrl`, `shift`, `alt`.
- Support canonical key names and legacy synonyms:
  - `esc`/`escape`
  - `return`/`enter`
  - `pageUp`/`pageDown` (case-insensitive parsing)
  - `backspace`, `delete`, `insert`, `home`, `end`, `tab`, `space`
  - arrows: `up`, `down`, `left`, `right`
  - function keys: `f1`-`f12`
  - symbols listed in legacy docs (including punctuation and shifted variants)

- Normalize to a canonical string form (for display and stable matching).
- Ensure case-insensitivity for parsing, but stable output casing.

# Edge Cases / Correctness
- Reject impossible combos (e.g., empty key, unknown modifier).
- Reject duplicate modifiers (`ctrl+ctrl+x`).
- Ensure that `shift` is treated as a modifier *in addition* to the underlying key code.

# Tests
- Table-driven tests for valid/invalid parsing.
- Normalization snapshot tests for representative keys.

# Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All key strings in `legacy .../docs/keybindings.md` parse successfully.
- [ ] Invalid user config produces diagnostics but does not crash.

title: Feature: Extension Event Hook Dispatch
description:
# Feature: Extension Event Hook Dispatch

## Overview

This feature enables the agent to call INTO extensions at lifecycle events. Extensions register handlers via pi.on(eventName, handler), and the agent dispatches events at appropriate points.

## Distinction from Events Hostcall

- **Events Hostcall (pi.events)**: Extension-initiated, asks runtime about events
- **Event Hook Dispatch**: Agent-initiated, calls extension handlers at lifecycle points

## Event Types (from EXISTING_PI_STRUCTURE.md §12.7)

### Agent Lifecycle Events

| Event | When | Handler Can |
|-------|------|-------------|
| startup | Agent initialized | Access session, configure |
| agent_start | Before first API call | Modify system prompt |
| agent_end | After agent loop ends | Log, cleanup |

### Turn Lifecycle Events

| Event | When | Handler Can |
|-------|------|-------------|
| turn_start | Before provider.stream() | Modify context |
| turn_end | After response processed | Log, analyze |

### Tool Events

| Event | When | Handler Can |
|-------|------|-------------|
| tool_call | Before tool execution | Block, modify |
| tool_result | After tool execution | Modify result |

### Session Events

| Event | When | Handler Can |
|-------|------|-------------|
| session_before_switch | Before session switch | Cancel switch |
| session_before_fork | Before session fork | Cancel fork |

### Input Events

| Event | When | Handler Can |
|-------|------|-------------|
| input | Before processing user message | Transform, block |

## Event Handler Return Values

Different events allow different return values:

```typescript
// tool_call: Can block execution
interface ToolCallEventResult {
    block?: boolean;
    reason?: string;
}

// tool_result: Can modify the result
interface ToolResultEventResult {
    content?: ContentBlock[];
    details?: unknown;
}

// session events: Return false to cancel
type SessionEventResult = boolean;
```

## Implementation Architecture

```
Agent Loop (src/agent.rs)
    │
    ├─── dispatch_event("turn_start", context)
    │           │
    │           ▼
    │    PiJsRuntime.__pi_dispatch_extension_event()
    │           │
    │           ▼
    │    [Extension handlers called in sequence]
    │           │
    │           ▼
    │    Results aggregated and returned
    │
    └─── [Continue with turn]
```

## Success Criteria

- [ ] All documented events dispatch at correct points
- [ ] Blocking events (tool_call) can prevent execution
- [ ] Modifying events (tool_result) can change data
- [ ] Cancellable events (session_*) return boolean
- [ ] Handler errors don't crash agent
- [ ] Extension context passed correctly to handlers
close_reason: All 7 sub-tasks complete: EventDispatcher created (bd-tg4w), agent lifecycle events (bd-13gm), turn lifecycle events (bd-5yyc), tool_call dispatch (bd-35hz), tool_result dispatch (bd-318h), input event (bd-s1hx), session events (bd-3avm). All event types dispatch at correct lifecycle points with fail-open error handling.

title: PiWasm: Spec WebAssembly JS subset + glue patterns
description:
# Goal
Lock the *minimum sufficient* WebAssembly JS API surface for PiWasm (WebAssembly-in-JS) to support the pinned extension corpus without Node/Bun.

# Why
- QuickJS does not ship WebAssembly; the bridge must be explicit, deterministic, capability-gated, and testable.
- A crisp spec prevents accidental Node/Bun scope creep.

# Deliverables
- Supported API list (MVP): WebAssembly.instantiate(bytes, imports), WebAssembly.compile(bytes) (optional), WebAssembly.Module/Instance (if needed), WebAssembly.Memory (required).
- Explicitly unsupported APIs (with required error shapes + diagnostics).
- Glue compatibility matrix: common JS+WASM bundle patterns (Emscripten-style) we intend to support and their required semantics.
- Determinism + security invariants: budgets, import gating, no ambient OS.

# Acceptance
- Spec is detailed enough to implement without consulting external notes.
- Includes example call shapes + expected failure mapping.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## PiWasm JS API Spec (Final)

### Supported APIs (MVP)

#### WebAssembly.compile(bufferSource) → Promise<Module>
- Accepts: Uint8Array, ArrayBuffer, or array of bytes
- Returns: A compiled Module handle
- Errors: WebAssembly.CompileError on invalid bytes

#### WebAssembly.instantiate(bufferSource, importObject?) → Promise<{module, instance}>
- Accepts: WASM bytes + optional import object
- Import object: { module_name: { func_name: func, ... }, ... }
- Returns: { module: Module, instance: Instance }
- Overload: instantiate(Module, importObject?) → Promise<Instance>
- Errors: WebAssembly.LinkError on import mismatch

#### WebAssembly.Instance
- instance.exports → object with exported funcs + memory

#### WebAssembly.Memory
- new Memory({initial, maximum?}) → standalone memory
- memory.buffer → ArrayBuffer (snapshot of linear memory)
- memory.grow(delta) → previous page count (or -1 on failure)

#### WebAssembly.RuntimeError / CompileError / LinkError
- Standard error constructors for WASM trap/compile/link failures

### Explicitly Unsupported (MVP)
- instantiateStreaming/compileStreaming → NotSupportedError
- Table, Global, validate → not yet supported error
- Shared memory / atomics → not supported

### Memory Sync Protocol
1. After instantiate: copy wasmtime memory → JS ArrayBuffer
2. Before export call: copy JS ArrayBuffer → wasmtime memory
3. After export call: copy wasmtime memory → JS ArrayBuffer
4. On grow: create new larger ArrayBuffer, old reference stale

### Import Handling (MVP - core polyfill only)
- Module imports satisfied by generic Rust stubs (return 0/no-op)
- Full JS callback imports deferred to bd-ltk7
- WASI/Emscripten-specific stubs in bd-ltk7

### Security Invariants
- Memory limited to max_memory_pages from policy
- Structured tracing logs for compile/instantiate
- No raw OS access from WASM execution
- All operations capability-gated

# Implement provider streaming tests using VCR cassettes

## Goal
Write comprehensive provider streaming tests using recorded VCR cassettes (no live network).

## Runtime + Determinism
- Do not introduce new tokio-only tests.
- Prefer `#[asupersync::test]` or an explicit `Runtime::new().block_on(...)` wrapper to match the active runtime.
- Force `VCR_MODE=playback` + `VCR_CASSETTE_DIR` for all tests.
- Set `PI_CONFIG_PATH` and `PI_SESSIONS_DIR` to temp dirs; assert zero live HTTP calls.

## Logging Requirements
- Use TestLogger (bd-3ml) to log cassette name/path, request summary, event timeline, and diffs.
- On failure, dump expected vs actual event sequences + stop reasons.

## Test File Structure
```rust
// tests/provider_streaming.rs

mod vcr;
use vcr::VcrRecorder;

mod anthropic {
    use super::*;

    #[asupersync::test]
    async fn test_simple_text_response() {
        let vcr = VcrRecorder::new("anthropic_simple_text");
        let provider = AnthropicProvider::new_with_client(vcr.client());

        let stream = provider.stream(&context, &options).await.unwrap();
        let events: Vec<_> = stream.collect().await;

        assert!(matches!(events[0], StreamEvent::Start { .. }));
        assert!(matches!(events[1], StreamEvent::TextStart { .. }));
        // ... verify all events
        let final_msg = events.last().unwrap();
        assert_eq!(final_msg.stop_reason, StopReason::Stop);
    }
}
```

## Test Categories

### Streaming Event Sequence Tests
Verify correct event ordering:
- Start → TextStart → TextDelta* → TextEnd → Done
- Start → ThinkingStart → ThinkingDelta* → ThinkingEnd → TextStart → ... → Done
- Start → ToolCallStart → ToolCallDelta* → ToolCallEnd → Done(ToolUse)

### Content Parsing Tests
Verify content is parsed correctly:
- Text content extraction
- Thinking content extraction
- Tool call argument parsing (JSON)
- Multiple content blocks

### Usage Tracking Tests
Verify token counting:
- Input tokens
- Output tokens
- Cache read/write tokens
- Cost calculation

### Error Handling Tests

- Rate limit with retry-after
- Auth failure message
- Bad request details
- Server error handling

2. OpenAI (after Anthropic pattern established)

title: Spec: PiJS runtime contract + event loop semantics
description:
# Goal
Define the **authoritative PiJS runtime contract** for running JS/TS extensions **without Node/Bun**, with a **deterministic, testable event loop** and an explicit, capability-gated hostcall surface.

This spec is the reference for:
- bd-8mm (scheduler), bd-2ke (QuickJS promise/job bridge), bd-1f5 (JS runtime), bd-320/bd-xgo (pipeline), and all test harness work.

# Assumptions / Constraints
- **Assume QuickJS has no WebAssembly**: any JS bundle expecting `globalThis.WebAssembly` must use the PiWasm bridge (bd-1ry) or Tier A WASM components.
- No ambient OS APIs: all side effects must flow through the connector dispatcher (bd-h04) and therefore capability checks + structured logs.

# Definitions (terms)
- **Microtasks**: the QuickJS job queue (Promise reactions, queueMicrotask).
- **Macrotasks**: host-driven tasks (timers, inbound extension events, hostcall completions).
- **Tick**: one deterministic scheduling step that runs at most one macrotask plus a full microtask drain.
- **Hostcall**: a side-effecting request from JS to the host, enforced by capability policy, represented in protocol terms as `host_call`/`host_result` (bd-37z).

# 1) Module / Artifact Loader Contract
## 1.1 Artifact inputs
PiJS executes artifacts produced by extc (bd-xgo) from pinned sources (sample set in `docs/extension-sample.json`).

Extc output must be:
- deterministic (byte-for-byte stable under identical inputs)
- ESM-resolvable inside PiJS
- sourcemap-correct (runtime errors map to original TS/JS)

## 1.2 Allowed specifiers and resolution
The PiJS module resolver MUST:
- resolve relative specifiers (`./` and `../`) within the artifact
- resolve internal Pi-provided modules under a reserved namespace (recommended: `pi:*`)
- forbid network imports (`http:`/`https:`) and other ambient loaders

Recommended canonicalization performed by extc (bd-2ki): rewrite Node builtins to `pi:node/*` and inject any required polyfills deterministically.

## 1.3 Initialization contract
- The host loads the artifact entry module.
- The entry module must export a default function that receives the host-provided `pi` object (ExtensionAPI surface).
- Any thrown error during load/initialization is mapped to an extension error with sourcemapped location and emitted as structured log events.

# 2) The `pi` API Contract (JS-facing)
The `pi` object provided to extensions is the single ambient authority. It MUST be capability-gated internally.

## 2.1 Registration surface (protocol-facing)
At minimum (shape may follow the legacy API):
- `pi.registerTool(spec)`
- `pi.registerSlashCommand(spec)`
- `pi.on(event_name, handler)` for lifecycle/tool-call hooks
- provider registration APIs for provider extensions (if applicable in the sample)

Semantics:
- Registration MUST be idempotent per (extension_id, name).
- Invalid specs must fail fast with actionable errors.
- Registration affects what the host advertises/dispatches for that extension.

## 2.2 Connector surface (hostcall-facing)
At minimum:
- `pi.exec(cmd, args, options) -> Promise<{ stdout, stderr, exitCode }>`
- `pi.http(request) -> Promise<response>`
- `pi.session.*` accessors/mutations as defined by protocol
- `pi.ui.*` primitives (select/input/confirm/editor) that can be denied in non-interactive mode
- `pi.log(level, event, data)` for extension-authored logs

Rules:
- Every connector method maps to a `host_call` with a `call_id`, capability, method, params, timeout/cancel metadata.
- Every connector method MUST emit structured audit logs through bd-h04.
- Errors MUST map onto the hostcall error taxonomy (Denied/Timeout/IO/InvalidRequest/Internal).

## 2.3 Cancellation + timeouts
- Any async connector call MAY accept an AbortSignal; cancellation must map to hostcall cancel_token semantics.
- Timeouts must be enforced in the dispatcher; JS receives a deterministic Timeout error.

# 3) PiJS Event Loop: Formal State Machine
## 3.1 State
Define the runtime state as:

- `seq: u64` monotone counter (total-order tie-breaker)
- `Q_micro`: the QuickJS job queue (internal to engine; host can drain)
- `Q_macro`: FIFO queue of macrotasks, each tagged with an enqueue `seq`
- `Q_timer`: min-heap of timers keyed by `(deadline_ms, seq)`
- `Q_host`: conceptual source of hostcall completions (host must enqueue into `Q_macro` deterministically)
- `clock`: monotonic time source (injectable for tests)

Each macrotask is one of:
- `TimerFired(timer_id)`
- `HostcallComplete(call_id, outcome)`
- `InboundEvent(event_id, payload)` (tool_call, slash_command, lifecycle hook, ui response, etc.)

## 3.2 The `tick()` algorithm
`tick(state)` must be deterministic given the current state and the set of newly-arrived host completions.

Algorithm (normative):
1) **Ingest host completions**: any completed hostcalls since last tick are enqueued into `Q_macro` with a deterministic order key.
   - Recommended: assign each completion an enqueue `seq` in arrival order using the monotone counter.
2) **Move due timers**: while `Q_timer.min.deadline_ms <= clock.now_ms`, pop timers and enqueue `TimerFired` into `Q_macro` (preserving `(deadline_ms, seq)` order).
3) **Run one macrotask**:
   - If `Q_macro` non-empty: pop the lowest `seq` macrotask and execute it.
   - Else: idle (no-op).
4) **Drain microtasks to fixpoint**: repeatedly drain the QuickJS job queue until it is empty.
5) Return updated state.

## 3.3 Invariants (must hold)
- **I1 (single macrotask):** at most one macrotask executes per tick.
- **I2 (microtask fixpoint):** after any macrotask, microtasks are drained until empty.
- **I3 (stable timers):** timers with equal deadlines fire in increasing `seq` order.
- **I4 (no reentrancy):** hostcall completions do not synchronously re-enter JS; they enqueue macrotasks.
- **I5 (total order):** all externally observable scheduling is ordered by `seq` (deterministic tie-break).

## 3.4 Timers contract
- `setTimeout(fn, ms)` enqueues a timer with `(deadline_ms = clock.now_ms + ms, seq = next_seq())`.
- `clearTimeout(id)` removes it if pending.
- `setInterval` is optional unless required by the pinned sample; if implemented, it must be specified in terms of repeated `setTimeout` with stable ordering.

## 3.5 Hostcall completion contract
- Each hostcall has a stable `call_id` and (recommended) an issuance `seq`.
- Completion enqueuing must be deterministic:
  - In production: order by completion arrival, but *stabilize* with the monotone seq.
  - In tests: completion order can be controlled by recorded fixtures / deterministic runtime.

# 4) Determinism Contract (formal-ish)
## 4.1 What we promise
Given:
- identical artifact bytes + shim versions
- identical initial state
- identical sequence of inbound events (tool calls, lifecycle events, UI responses)
- identical sequence of hostcall results (including their enqueue order)
- identical clock behavior (or a deterministic clock)

Then:
- the sequence of executed macrotasks and the resulting observable outputs (tool results, logs, UI prompts) are identical.

## 4.2 Proof sketch (why)
- The scheduler is a pure function of `(state, arrivals)` with a total-order tie-breaker `seq`.
- Timer ordering is deterministic via `(deadline_ms, seq)`.
- Hostcall completion ordering is deterministic by construction (completion enqueue `seq`).
- Microtask draining to a fixpoint ensures no hidden interleavings.
- Therefore, by induction over ticks, the entire execution trace is deterministic under fixed inputs.

# 5) Observability / Trace Contract
- Every tick and every enqueue/dequeue event MAY be logged (debug-level) under `pi.ext.log.v1` with `trace_id`/`span_id` and correlation ids.
- Deterministic test runs must be able to compare traces for equality after normalization.

# Non-goals
- Full Node/Bun parity.
- Ambient OS access.
- Undefined behavior around timer ordering or microtask starvation.

title: [AUTH-TEST] Comprehensive tests for authentication parity features
description:
## Overview

Comprehensive test coverage for all AUTH track features with structured JSONL logging for debugging and CI artifact retention.

## Test Infrastructure

### JSONL Logging Helper
All tests use the log_test_event pattern for structured debugging:
```rust
fn log_test_event(test_name: &str, event: &str, data: &serde_json::Value) {
    let entry = serde_json::json\!({
        "schema": "pi.test.auth_event.v1",
        "test": test_name,
        "event": event,
        "timestamp_ms": std::time::SystemTime::now()
            .duration_since(std::time::UNIX_EPOCH).unwrap().as_millis(),
        "data": data,
    });
    eprintln\!("JSONL: {}", serde_json::to_string(&entry).unwrap());
}
```

Events captured per test:
- `test_start` — test name, scenario description
- `setup_complete` — fixture state (e.g., auth.json contents, mock server ready)
- `action` — what was triggered (e.g., OAuth URL generated, token exchange attempted)
- `assertion` — expected vs actual values
- `test_end` — pass/fail, duration_ms

---

## Unit Tests (src/auth.rs tests module)

### OpenAI OAuth/APIKey Flow
1. `test_openai_oauth_url_generation` — If OAuth supported: correct auth URL with PKCE challenge, scopes, redirect_uri. If API key mode: prompt for key stores correctly.
   - JSONL: `{"event":"url_generated","data":{"url":"...","has_pkce":true,"scopes":["openid"]}}`
2. `test_openai_token_exchange` — VCR-backed exchange: authorization_code -> access_token + refresh_token. Verify auth.json updated.
   - JSONL: `{"event":"token_exchanged","data":{"provider":"openai","has_refresh":true,"expires_in":3600}}`

### Google OAuth Flow
3. `test_google_oauth_url_generation` — Correct URL with access_type=offline, prompt=consent, generative-language scope
   - JSONL: `{"event":"url_generated","data":{"url":"...","access_type":"offline","prompt":"consent"}}`
4. `test_google_token_exchange` — VCR-backed exchange with refresh_token (Google returns refresh only on first consent)
   - JSONL: `{"event":"token_exchanged","data":{"provider":"google","has_refresh":true}}`

### Refresh Failure Recovery
5. `test_refresh_failure_produces_recovery_action` — RefreshFailure struct contains provider name, error type (auth vs network), and recovery action text ("/login {provider}")
   - JSONL: `{"event":"refresh_failed","data":{"provider":"anthropic","error_type":"invalid_grant","recovery":"/login anthropic"}}`
6. `test_refresh_failure_network_vs_auth_different_messages` — Network errors show "check connection", auth errors show "/login"
   - JSONL: `{"event":"error_classified","data":{"error_type":"network","message":"Check your network connection"}}`

### Provider Listing
7. `test_provider_listing_shows_all_providers` — List includes built-in (anthropic, openai, google) + any extension providers
8. `test_provider_listing_shows_expiry` — OAuth tokens show human-readable expiry ("expires in 23 hours")
9. `test_provider_listing_no_credentials` — Provider with no stored credentials shows "Not authenticated"

---

## TUI State Tests (tests/tui_state.rs)

10. `tui_login_no_args_shows_provider_table` — /login with no args renders table with all providers and their auth status
    - JSONL: `{"event":"provider_table_rendered","data":{"providers":["anthropic","openai","google"],"authenticated":["anthropic"]}}`
11. `tui_login_openai_starts_auth_flow` — /login openai triggers the appropriate auth flow (OAuth or API key prompt)
    - JSONL: `{"event":"auth_flow_started","data":{"provider":"openai","flow_type":"oauth|apikey"}}`
12. `tui_refresh_failure_shows_recovery_message` — RefreshFailure results in visible system message with actionable /login suggestion
    - JSONL: `{"event":"system_message_shown","data":{"message_contains":"/login anthropic"}}`
13. `tui_login_unknown_provider_shows_error` — /login unknown-provider shows clear error listing valid providers
14. `tui_login_gemini_aliases_to_google` — /login gemini internally routes to Google OAuth flow

---

## E2E Tests (tests/auth_oauth_refresh_vcr.rs)

### E2E Script 1: Full OAuth Dance
```bash
# Script: test_full_oauth_dance.sh
# Verifies: complete OAuth flow from /login to stored credentials
#
# 1. Start mock OAuth server (serves authorize + token endpoints)
# 2. Launch pi with --test-mode
# 3. Send /login openai
# 4. Verify auth URL opened (mock captures redirect)
# 5. Simulate callback with authorization_code
# 6. Verify auth.json contains access_token + refresh_token
# 7. Verify subsequent API call uses access_token in Authorization header

# {"event":"auth_url_captured","data":{"url":"...","provider":"openai"}}
# {"event":"callback_simulated","data":{"code":"test_auth_code"}}
# {"event":"token_stored","data":{"provider":"openai","auth_json_path":"..."}}
# {"event":"api_call_verified","data":{"auth_header":"Bearer ..."}}
```

### E2E Script 2: Token Refresh During Agent Run
```bash
# Script: test_refresh_during_agent_run.sh
# Verifies: transparent token refresh mid-conversation
#
# 1. Setup auth.json with token expiring in 5 minutes
# 2. Start mock provider that returns 401 on first call, 200 after refresh
# 3. Launch pi with prompt "hello"
# 4. Verify refresh triggered (mock sees token refresh request)
# 5. Verify agent completes successfully with new token
# 6. Verify auth.json updated with new expiry
#
# JSONL events:
# {"event":"token_near_expiry","data":{"expires_in_seconds":300}}
# {"event":"refresh_triggered","data":{"provider":"anthropic"}}
# {"event":"refresh_completed","data":{"new_expires_in":3600}}
# {"event":"agent_completed","data":{"response_received":true}}
```

### E2E Script 3: Refresh Failure Recovery Path
```bash
# Script: test_refresh_failure_recovery.sh
```

```bash
# Script: test_concurrent_refresh.sh
# Verifies: file lock prevents auth.json corruption

# 1. Setup auth.json with token expiring in 1 minute
# 2. Launch two pi processes simultaneously (RPC + interactive)

# {"event":"lock_waiting","data":{"process":"B","attempt":1}}
# {"event":"refresh_completed","data":{"process":"A"}}
```

title: Phase 7: Performance Conformance (load time and dispatch latency)
description:
# Phase 7: Performance Conformance (load time and dispatch latency)

## Purpose
Not just correctness -- we need competitive performance. The Rust runtime should be FASTER than the TypeScript runtime, or at worst within 2x.

## Metrics

### Extension Load Time
- Measure: time from loadExtension() call to Extension object available
- Target: Rust <= 2x TypeScript for any extension
- Stretch goal: Rust <= 1x TypeScript (faster than TS)
- Method: both harnesses report load_time_ms in their JSON output

### Event Dispatch Latency
- Measure: time from event fire to handler response received
- Target: Rust < 5ms p99 for all event types
- Method: fire 1000 events per type, measure each

### Memory Usage
- Measure: RSS increase from loading N extensions
- Target: Rust <= 1.5x TypeScript per extension
- Method: measure process RSS before/after loading

### Concurrent Extension Stress
- Load 10+ extensions simultaneously
- Fire events to all extensions concurrently
- Verify no deadlocks, no data races, no memory leaks
- Run for 1 hour continuously

## Implementation
- Load time: already captured by differential runner
- Event dispatch: add timing to event fire/response in both harnesses
- Memory: separate benchmark test with RSS monitoring
- Stress: dedicated stress test binary

## Acceptance Criteria
- Load time benchmarks for all 60 official extensions
- Event dispatch p99 < 5ms verified
- Memory growth < 10MB per extension loaded
- 1-hour stress test passes without degradation

title: Create deterministic test environment for both runtimes
description:
# Create deterministic test environment for both runtimes

## Context
For differential testing to work, BOTH runtimes must produce identical outputs for the same inputs. This requires eliminating all sources of non-determinism:
- Timestamps (Date.now(), new Date())
- Random values (Math.random())
- File paths (cwd, home directory)
- Process IDs, hostnames
- Network responses (must be mocked)
- Filesystem state (must be sandboxed)

## What To Do
1. For the TS runtime: create wrapper that patches Date, Math.random, process.cwd, etc.
2. For the Rust runtime: ensure QuickJS globals are patched similarly
3. Both runtimes must use identical mock values for:
   - Current time: fixed epoch (e.g., 1700000000000)
   - Random seed: fixed (e.g., always returns 0.5)
   - CWD: /tmp/ext-conformance-test
   - Home: /tmp/ext-conformance-home
4. Document all patched globals

## Why This Matters
Without deterministic environments, outputs will differ due to timestamps alone. Every comparison would be noisy with false positives. Determinism is a PREREQUISITE for meaningful differential testing.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Both runtimes produce byte-identical JSON for a simple extension that uses Date.now()
- Both runtimes produce byte-identical JSON for an extension that uses Math.random()
- CWD and home dir paths are normalized in both outputs
close_reason: Completed deterministic globals for TS+Rust harnesses and added deterministic diff test

title: Workstream: Session UX Parity (in-app /resume /new /tree /fork)
description:
# Goal
Match legacy interactive session UX:
- `/resume` opens a picker inside the running app (not “restart with flags”).
- Session picker supports interactive delete.
- `/new` starts a new session without restarting the process.
- `/tree` provides full tree navigation UI + optional branch summarization.
- `/fork` creates a new session file from the current branch.

# Legacy Spec (Source-of-Truth)
## `/resume` and deleting sessions
- `legacy_pi_mono_code/pi-mono/packages/coding-agent/docs/session.md`:
  - sessions can be deleted interactively from `/resume` via `Ctrl+D` then confirm.
  - when available, pi uses the `trash` CLI to avoid permanent deletion.

## `/tree`
- `legacy_pi_mono_code/pi-mono/packages/coding-agent/docs/tree.md` defines:
  - interactive tree UI (depth-first navigation)
  - filters toggled by Ctrl+U (user only) and Ctrl+O (show all)
  - selection behavior differs for user vs non-user nodes
  - optional branch summarization with 3 options (none / default / custom prompt)
  - summary stored as branch_summary entry

## `/fork`
- `/fork` creates a **new session file** from the current branch (vs `/tree` which changes leaf within same session).

# Current Rust State (Gap)
- `src/interactive.rs` `/resume` and `/new` are placeholders that tell users to restart with flags.
- `/tree` exists but is not the full interactive navigator described in legacy docs.
- `/fork` behavior does not match the legacy “new session file” semantics.

# Scope / Deliverables
1) In-app `/resume` → show session picker UI → load selected session.
2) Session picker: delete sessions with Ctrl+D + confirmation (use `trash` if present).
3) `/new`: create a new session object (and file if persistence enabled), reset UI + agent context.
4) `/tree`: implement interactive tree navigator per legacy docs (filters, selection rules, summary prompt choices).
5) `/fork`: implement new-session-file fork semantics, with UX comparable to legacy.

# Testing
- Integration/state tests for:
  - /resume selection loads correct session
  - delete uses trash when available (mock command runner)
  - /new resets conversation + session metadata
  - /tree selection semantics and summary entry creation
  - /fork creates a new session file and switches

# Dependencies
- Session index integration improves performance but should not be required for correctness.
- Keybindings workstream (`bd-3ip`) is needed for consistent picker and tree controls.

## Acceptance Criteria
[ ] /resume works in-app (no restart)
[ ] Session picker supports delete with trash fallback
[ ] /new creates a fresh session without restart
[ ] /tree matches legacy navigation semantics
[ ] /fork creates a new session file and switches
[ ] Double-escape behavior matches settings

title: Phase 4: Execute Conformance - Official Pi-Mono Extensions (60)
description:
# Phase 4: Execute Conformance - Official Pi-Mono Extensions (60)

## Purpose
Run all 60 official pi-mono example extensions through the differential test runner. These are the MOST important extensions because they define the expected API surface. If any of these fail, we have a runtime bug.

## The 60 Official Extensions (by tier)

### Tier 1 - Minimal (14 extensions)
Single capability, no external deps:
hello, pirate, session-name, custom-footer, custom-header, system-prompt-header, preset, titlebar-spinner, status-line, model-status, widget-placement, question, qna, send-user-message

### Tier 2 - Events Only (11 extensions)
Subscribe to events, no tool registration:
auto-commit-on-exit, bash-spawn-hook, confirm-destructive, dirty-repo-guard, file-trigger, git-checkpoint, input-transform, protected-paths, trigger-compact, timed-confirm, permission-gate

### Tier 3 - Tools (7 extensions)
Register LLM-callable tools:
tools, truncated-tool, tool-override, inline-bash, ssh, interactive-shell, summarize

### Tier 4 - Multi-Capability (12 extensions)
Multiple registrations (tools + events + commands):
bookmark, claude-rules, custom-compaction, event-bus, handoff, notify, todo, mac-system-theme, shutdown-command, dynamic-resources (multi-file), rpc-demo

### Tier 5 - Multi-File (9 extensions)
Require multiple source files and/or npm deps:
doom-overlay, plan-mode, subagent, sandbox, with-deps, custom-provider-anthropic, custom-provider-gitlab-duo, custom-provider-qwen-cli, dynamic-resources

### Tier 6 - UI Heavy (7 extensions)
Complex UI: overlays, editors, games:
overlay-test, overlay-qa-tests, modal-editor, rainbow-editor, message-renderer, snake, space-invaders

## Execution Order
Run tiers in order (1 through 6). Each tier builds confidence before moving to more complex extensions. Early tiers catch fundamental issues; later tiers catch edge cases.

## Acceptance Criteria
- All 60 extensions attempted
- 100% pass rate for Tiers 1-3 (32 extensions)
- 95%+ pass rate for Tiers 4-5 (21 extensions)
- 80%+ pass rate for Tier 6 (7 extensions) -- UI extensions may have known differences
- All failures documented with root cause analysis

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
EXECUTION STRATEGY: Run tiers in order. Tier 1 is the smoke test -- if hello.ts does not produce identical output in both runtimes, nothing else will work. Fix ALL Tier 1 failures before moving to Tier 2. Each tier exercises progressively more of the API surface, so failures at higher tiers likely indicate specific missing features rather than fundamental bugs.

TIER JUSTIFICATION:
- Tier 1 (14 exts): Basic loading, simple registrations. If these fail, the runtime is broken.
- Tier 2 (11 exts): Event system. Tests pi.on() and handler dispatch.
- Tier 3 (7 exts): Tool system. Tests registerTool() and execution.
- Tier 4 (12 exts): Multiple capabilities. Tests interaction between systems.
- Tier 5 (9 exts): Multi-file + deps. Tests module resolution and import handling.
- Tier 6 (7 exts): UI-heavy. Tests the most complex API surface (overlays, editors, games).

title: [SEC-3.2] Baseline modeling with robust statistics and Markov transition profiles

Extension behavior should be evaluated against mathematically grounded baselines, not brittle hardcoded thresholds.

## Scope

- Drift-detection primitives usable by online scorer.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Model handles sparse data with explicit fallback rules.
- [ ] Transition anomalies are explainable at rule/metric level.

title: PARITY-JSON.2: Emit compaction/retry events in JSON print mode event handler

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## PARITY-JSON.2: Emit Compaction/Retry Events in JSON Print Mode

### The Gap
Even after PARITY-JSON.1 adds the event variants, they need to be EMITTED at the right places in the agent loop and passed through to the JSON print mode event handler.

### Current Code Flow
In src/main.rs:1985, the print mode event handler receives AgentEvent and serializes to JSON:
```rust
let emit_json_events = mode == "json";
let make_event_handler = move || {
    move |event: AgentEvent| {
        if emit_json_events {
            if let Ok(serialized) = serde_json::to_string(&event) {
                println\!("{serialized}");
            }
        }
        ...
    }
};
```

The handler WILL automatically serialize the new variants (since it serializes all AgentEvent). The real work is in the agent loop: find where compaction and retry happen and emit the new events.

### Implementation Plan
1. Find compaction logic in src/agent.rs — search for "compact" or "compaction"
2. Before compaction starts: emit AgentEvent::AutoCompactionStart via the event callback
3. After compaction ends: emit AgentEvent::AutoCompactionEnd with summary
4. Find retry logic in src/agent.rs — search for "retry"
5. Before retry: emit AgentEvent::AutoRetryStart with error, attempt number, max attempts, delay
6. After retry: emit AgentEvent::AutoRetryEnd with success/failure

### Pi-Mono Reference for Emission Points
- Compaction: legacy_pi_mono_code/pi-mono/packages/coding-agent/src/core/agent-session.ts (search for onAutoCompactionStart/End)
- Retry: same file, search for onAutoRetryStart/End

### Important: RPC Mode Already Has These
Check if src/rpc.rs already emits compaction/retry events. If so, the RPC code can serve as a reference for WHAT to emit and WHERE, and the task becomes ensuring the agent loop emits these events generically (not just in RPC mode).

### Acceptance Criteria
- JSON mode output includes auto_compaction_start/end during compaction
- JSON mode output includes auto_retry_start/end during retries
- Events match pi-mono JSON schema
- Existing text mode behavior unchanged
- RPC mode still works correctly
- Tests verify events are emitted

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## Testing Requirements

### Unit Tests
1. **Compaction event emission**: Mock agent loop, trigger compaction threshold, verify AutoCompactionStart emitted before compaction and AutoCompactionEnd emitted after with summary
2. **Retry event emission**: Simulate API error + retry, verify AutoRetryStart emitted with correct error/attempt/maxAttempts/delayMs fields, AutoRetryEnd emitted with success=true on recovery
3. **Retry failure path**: Simulate max retries exhausted, verify AutoRetryEnd with success=false
4. **Event callback receives all events**: Register event callback, run scenario, verify callback receives compaction/retry events alongside regular events

### E2E Tests (tests/e2e_json_events.rs)
5. **Full JSON output pipeline**: Run pi binary with VCR cassette + `--mode json`, capture stdout, parse each line as JSON, verify auto_compaction_start/end and auto_retry_start/end present in output
6. **Text mode unaffected**: Same scenario with `--mode text`, verify no JSON pollution on stdout
7. **RPC mode parity**: If RPC already emits these events, verify JSON mode emits the same schema

### Structured Logging
- Each test logs: scenario name, events captured, events expected, diff
- VCR cassette name included in test output for reproducibility

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
Completed PARITY-JSON.2: Emit compaction/retry events in JSON print mode.

## Changes

### Compaction events (already working)
AutoCompactionStart/AutoCompactionEnd are already emitted in the agent loop (agent.rs:4124-4175) via the on_event callback. JSON print mode receives these automatically since it uses the same event handler.

### Retry events (newly added)
Added retry logic to run_print_mode() in main.rs, mirroring RPC mode's retry behaviour:

1. **run_print_prompt_with_retry()** - New async function wrapping each prompt call with automatic retry. On retryable errors (rate limit, server errors, etc.), emits AutoRetryStart event, sleeps with exponential backoff, then re-sends the same prompt. After retries complete, emits AutoRetryEnd with success/failure status.

2. **print_mode_retry_delay_ms()** - Exponential backoff delay calculator (same logic as rpc.rs).

3. **emit_json_event()** - Helper to serialize AgentEvent to JSON stdout.

4. **is_retryable_prompt_result()** - Checks if an AssistantMessage represents a retryable error.

5. **PromptInput enum** - Discriminated union for Text vs Content prompts, enabling the generic retry function.

### Config integration
- Added `config: &Config` parameter to run_print_mode()
- Uses config.retry_enabled(), config.retry_max_retries(), config.retry_base_delay_ms(), config.retry_max_delay_ms()

title: Perf: eliminate per-chunk allocations in SSE stream (SseStream)
description:
# Goal
Reduce CPU + allocation churn on provider streaming path by removing per-chunk String/Vec allocations in src/sse.rs (SseStream UTF-8 handling).

# Why
SSE streaming is on the hot path for all providers. Today SseStream copies bytes into utf8_buffer, then allocates an owned String for valid UTF-8, then copies again into SseParser\x27s buffer. It also allocates a new Vec for trailing bytes when UTF-8 is split across chunks.

# Approach (Extreme Optimization)
- Baseline: add a micro-bench covering SseStream parsing with realistic chunk sizes.
- Optimize: feed &str slices directly from utf8_buffer into SseParser (no intermediate String) and keep trailing bytes in-place (no to_vec).
- Prove: existing SSE unit tests + added chunked UTF-8 regression coverage.

# Acceptance
- [ ] No behavior change (all SSE tests pass)
- [ ] Micro-bench shows improved throughput for chunked inputs
- [ ] Quality gates pass
notes:
## Implementation
- `src/sse.rs`: add a fast-path in `SseStream::poll_next_event` to avoid copying the full incoming chunk into `utf8_buffer` when there is no pending UTF-8 tail.
- Keeps existing behavior for invalid UTF-8 (surface `InvalidData`) and for partial UTF-8 sequences (buffer remainder, continue parsing next chunk).

## Measurement (Criterion)
Command:
- `CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/pi_agent_rust_target_blackfalcon cargo bench --bench tools sse_stream -- --noplot`

Before:
- `sse_stream/parse/64`:   `[883.52 us 889.96 us 895.67 us]`
- `sse_stream/parse/1024`: `[688.67 us 693.27 us 698.09 us]`
- `sse_stream/parse/4096`: `[692.80 us 698.86 us 704.64 us]`

After:
- `sse_stream/parse/64`:   `[841.65 us 850.27 us 858.67 us]` (mean ~-4.6% time; p<0.05)
- `sse_stream/parse/1024`: `[676.31 us 689.18 us 700.43 us]` (within noise threshold)
- `sse_stream/parse/4096`: `[682.95 us 688.83 us 698.19 us]` (no change detected)

## Isomorphism Proof
- Ordering preserved: underlying byte stream order is unchanged; only an intermediate copy is removed.
- Delimiters preserved: UTF-8 validation still gates feeding; the same bytes are fed into `SseParser` in the same sequence.
- Error behavior preserved: invalid UTF-8 still returns `InvalidData`.

## Gates
- `cargo fmt --check` OK
- `cargo check --all-targets` OK
- `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` OK
- `cargo test` OK
close_reason: Completed (SseStream fast-path + bench improvement + gates green)

title: Phase 8: CI Integration and Continuous Conformance
description:
# Phase 8: CI Integration and Continuous Conformance

## Purpose
Conformance testing must run on EVERY PR to prevent regressions. A single missed comparison could break third-party extensions.

## CI Pipeline Design

### Fast Path (every PR, < 5min)
- Run Tier 1 (14 simple extensions) in differential mode
- Run Tier 2-3 (18 extensions) registration-only comparison
- Total: ~32 extensions, ~3 minutes

### Full Path (nightly, < 30min)
- All 60 official extensions, full differential
- All community extensions, full differential
- Performance benchmarks
- Total: ~200 extensions, ~20 minutes

### Weekly Path (weekend, < 2hr)
- Everything in Full Path
- 1-hour stress test
- Full npm/third-party corpus
- Conformance report generation and archival

## Implementation
- tests/ext_conformance_runner.rs with #[cfg] feature flags
- cargo test --features conformance-fast (fast path)
- cargo test --features conformance-full (full path)
- cargo test --features conformance-stress (weekly)

## Acceptance Criteria
- Fast path runs on every PR and passes
- Full path runs nightly and produces report
- Any conformance regression blocks PR merge
- Conformance report archived per run

title: Epic: Node.js Stdlib Shim Implementation — complete pi:node/* polyfill surface
description:
# Goal
Implement the full set of Node.js standard library shims (pi:node/*) so that existing npm extensions written for Node.js can run in the PiJS QuickJS runtime without modification.

# Background
The PiJS runtime (src/extensions_js.rs) runs extension JavaScript in QuickJS, which has NO Node.js stdlib. Extensions that import from "fs", "path", "url", "os", "crypto", "http", "buffer", "events", or "stream" fail immediately.

Current state:
- bd-1h06 covers node:child_process shim (the ONLY shim with a dedicated bead)
- bd-354t covers pi.* connector shims (different: PI-specific APIs, not Node compat)
- bd-1gbi covers MAPPING missing shims — but mapping is analysis, not implementation
- The compatibility scanner (src/extensions.rs) already DETECTS Node.js imports and reports them — it just cant fix them

Shim strategy per EXTENSIONS.md: each pi:node/* module routes through hostcalls to Rust implementations. For example, node:fs.readFile() calls pi.tool("read", ...) hostcall internally. This keeps the security model intact — all filesystem access goes through capability-gated dispatcher.

# Why This Matters
- The conformance corpus has 60+ extensions; many are npm packages that assume Node.js stdlib
- Without shims, compat scanner reports "unsupported import: fs" and extension fails
- THIS is the primary reason conformance tiers 3-5 are #[ignore] — multi-file extensions with npm deps need these shims
- Every major extension ecosystem (VSCode, Obsidian) has Node.js stdlib assumptions baked in

# Architecture
Each shim follows this pattern:
1. QuickJS module registered via Module::declare() in PiJsRuntime
2. Module exports match Node.js API surface (function signatures, return types)
3. Implementation delegates to hostcalls: pi.tool() for file ops, pi.exec() for process ops, pi.http() for network
4. Synchronous Node APIs (e.g., fs.readFileSync) shimmed via blocking hostcall bridge
5. Each shim has coverage matrix documenting which APIs are implemented vs stubbed

# Prioritization (by extension corpus usage frequency)
Tier 1 (blocks most extensions): node:fs, node:path, node:url
Tier 2 (blocks many extensions): node:os, node:crypto, node:buffer
Tier 3 (blocks some extensions): node:events, node:http/https, node:stream

# Dependencies
- Depends on bd-1gbi (Map missing shims) completing first to finalize exact API surface needed
- Relates to bd-xgo (extc pipeline) which handles import rewriting: import "fs" -> import "pi:node/fs"
- Relates to bd-29fu (compat scan on expanded corpus) which will validate shim coverage

# Children (8 shim subtasks)
One bead per stdlib module, each self-contained with its own API surface spec

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
ARCHITECTURAL CONTEXT: The shim strategy is: each pi:node/* module is registered in QuickJS via Module::declare() in src/extensions_js.rs. Pure-JS shims (path, url, events, buffer) are embedded as JS source strings. I/O shims (fs, crypto, http) route through hostcalls to Rust.

PRIORITIZATION RATIONALE: node:fs and node:path are Tier 1 because they appear in >80% of npm extensions. node:os and node:crypto are Tier 2 (30-50%). node:events and node:http are Tier 3 (10-30%). This is based on import frequency analysis from the conformance corpus.

CRITICAL DESIGN DECISION: Sync functions (readFileSync, etc.) MUST block the QuickJS event loop until the hostcall completes. This is intentional — Node.js sync functions block, and extensions expect this behavior. The blocking is contained to the QuickJS thread (doesn't block the main Rust event loop).

EXISTING PARTIAL WORK: Phase 5 community conformance (bd-2ru2) already added fragments: realpathSync, mkdirSync, promises namespace, hostname. This epic COMPLETES these partial implementations to full API surface.

DEPENDENCY NOTE: This epic depends on bd-1gbi (Map missing shims) to finalize the exact API surface needed. If bd-1gbi hasn't completed, individual shim tasks can still proceed based on the standard Node.js API — the mapping just helps prioritize which APIs to implement first.

ESTIMATED EFFORT: node:fs (12-16h), node:path (3-4h), node:crypto (6-8h), node:os (2-3h), node:url (3-4h), node:buffer (6-8h), node:events (3-4h), node:http (10-14h). Total: ~45-61 engineering hours.

title: Implement node:fs shim — filesystem operations via pi.tool hostcalls
description:
# Goal
Implement the node:fs (and node:fs/promises) shim module for PiJS QuickJS runtime, routing all filesystem operations through the capability-gated pi.tool("read"/"write") hostcalls.

# Background
node:fs is the MOST imported Node.js module in the extension corpus. Without it, any extension that reads config files, writes output, or checks file existence fails immediately. The existing PiJS runtime (src/extensions_js.rs) already has partial node:fs support added during Phase 5 community conformance (bd-2ru2): realpathSync, promises namespace, mkdirSync. This task completes the full surface.

# API Surface (prioritized by corpus usage)

## Tier 1 — Must Have (blocks 80%+ of extensions using fs)
- readFileSync(path, encoding?) → string | Buffer
- writeFileSync(path, data, encoding?)
- existsSync(path) → boolean
- readFile(path, encoding?, callback) — async version
- writeFile(path, data, encoding?, callback)
- statSync(path) → Stats object { isFile(), isDirectory(), size, mtime }
- stat(path, callback)
- readdirSync(path) → string[]
- readdir(path, callback)
- mkdirSync(path, { recursive }) — already exists, verify completeness
- unlinkSync(path) — delete file
- rmdirSync(path) — delete directory

## Tier 2 — Should Have (blocks 30%+ of extensions)
- promises.readFile / promises.writeFile / promises.stat / promises.readdir
- realpathSync(path) — already exists
- renameSync(oldPath, newPath)
- copyFileSync(src, dest)
- accessSync(path, mode) — check permissions
- createReadStream(path) — returns readable stream (depends on node:stream shim)
- createWriteStream(path)
- watchFile(path, callback) — polling file watcher

## Implementation Strategy
- Each sync function: blocking hostcall to Rust → pi.tool("read", { path }) or pi.tool("write", { path, content })
- Each async function: Promise-based hostcall (same as sync but non-blocking)
- Stats object: construct from tool result metadata (size, mtime from read tool details)
- existsSync: try-catch wrapper around statSync (return false on error)
- Encoding parameter: "utf8"→string, null/buffer→Buffer shim

# Files to Modify
- src/extensions_js.rs: Register node:fs module, implement shim functions
- May need to add new tool operations for stat/unlink/rename (currently tools.rs has read/write/edit but not stat-only or delete)

# Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All Tier 1 functions implemented and tested
- [ ] Tier 2 functions implemented where feasible
- [ ] Sync functions block the JS event loop correctly
- [ ] Async functions use Promises (no callback hell)
- [ ] Stats object matches Node.js shape (isFile, isDirectory, size, mtime)
- [ ] All operations go through capability-gated hostcalls (no direct filesystem access)
- [ ] At least 5 conformance corpus extensions that previously failed on fs now pass

title: Tests: Node.js shim integration suite — cross-shim interop and conformance validation
description:
# Goal
Comprehensive integration test suite that validates ALL Node.js shims work correctly both individually and in combination. This is the final validation gate before the Node.js shim epic can be considered complete.

# Background
Each individual shim bead (bd-1av0.1 through bd-1av0.9) includes its own unit tests. This bead adds INTEGRATION tests that verify cross-shim interop and real-world extension compatibility. Without this, individual shims might pass but break when used together.

# Test Categories

## 1. Cross-Shim Interop Tests (15+ tests)
These verify that shims work correctly TOGETHER:
- fs.readFile + path.resolve → read file at resolved path
- fs.writeFile + Buffer.from → write binary data
- crypto.createHash + fs.readFile → hash file contents
- http.get + url.parse → fetch from parsed URL
- events.EventEmitter + process.on → event chain works
- os.tmpdir + fs.writeFile + path.join → write to temp directory
- Buffer.from(fs.readFileSync(path)) → binary file round-trip
- process.env.HOME + path.join + fs.existsSync → check home dir file

## 2. Real Extension Replay Tests (10+ tests)
Take REAL code patterns from the conformance corpus and verify they work:
- Pattern: const configPath = path.join(process.env.HOME, '.config', 'ext.json')
           if (fs.existsSync(configPath)) { ... }
- Pattern: const hash = crypto.createHash('sha256').update(content).digest('hex')
- Pattern: const url = new URL(endpoint); url.searchParams.set('key', process.env.API_KEY)
- Pattern: const emitter = new EventEmitter(); emitter.on('data', (chunk) => { ... })

## 3. Error Path Tests (10+ tests)
- fs.readFileSync on nonexistent file → throws ENOENT
- crypto.createHash with unsupported algorithm → throws error
- process.exit during hostcall → clean shutdown, no crash
- Buffer.from with invalid encoding → throws TypeError
- http.get with invalid URL → error event fired
- path.resolve with no cwd hostcall available → fallback behavior

## 4. Performance Tests (5+ tests)
- 1000 sequential fs.readFileSync calls → complete within 5s
- 100 concurrent crypto.createHash operations → no deadlocks
- process.env access 10000 times → cached, sub-1ms per call
- Buffer.alloc(10MB) → completes without OOM
- EventEmitter with 1000 listeners → no performance cliff

## 5. Conformance Regression Tests (5+ tests)
- Re-run previously-failing extensions from conformance corpus
- Verify they now pass with shims enabled
- Track which tiers are unblocked by shim completion

# Logging Requirements (per bd-4u9 convention)
Every test MUST emit structured JSONL logs:
{
  "test": "cross_shim_fs_path_resolve",
  "timestamp": "2026-...",
  "inputs": { "relative_path": "./config.json", "cwd": "/project" },
  "expected": "/project/config.json",
  "actual": "/project/config.json",
  "pass": true,
  "duration_ms": 12,
  "shims_exercised": ["node:fs", "node:path"],
  "artifacts": ["test-config.json"]
}

# Test Infrastructure
- Use TestHarness from tests/common/ for JSONL logging
- Use tempdir for filesystem isolation
- Use VCR cassettes for HTTP shim tests
- No mock libraries (project convention)
- All tests deterministic (DeterministicClock for timers)

# Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] 45+ test cases covering all 5 categories
- [ ] All tests emit structured JSONL logs
- [ ] Cross-shim interop validated for all pairwise combinations
- [ ] At least 3 previously-failing conformance extensions now pass
- [ ] No mock libraries used
- [ ] All tests pass cargo test
- [ ] Performance baselines documented

title: Implement node:path shim — path manipulation utilities (pure JS)
description:
# Goal
Implement the node:path shim module. This is one of the simplest shims because path operations are pure string manipulation — no hostcalls needed.

# Background
node:path is the second most imported Node.js module. It provides cross-platform path manipulation utilities. Since these are pure functions with no I/O, the shim can be implemented entirely in JavaScript within QuickJS — no Rust bridge needed.

# API Surface (complete — all are pure functions)
- path.join(...segments) → string
- path.resolve(...segments) → string (needs cwd from hostcall)
- path.dirname(p) → string
- path.basename(p, ext?) → string
- path.extname(p) → string
- path.normalize(p) → string
- path.isAbsolute(p) → boolean
- path.relative(from, to) → string
- path.parse(p) → { root, dir, base, ext, name }
- path.format(pathObject) → string
- path.sep → "/" (Pi runs on Unix)
- path.delimiter → ":" (Pi runs on Unix)
- path.posix → self (Pi is always POSIX)
- path.win32 → stub that throws (Pi doesnt support Windows paths)

# Implementation Strategy
- Pure JavaScript implementation registered as QuickJS module
- Only path.resolve() needs a hostcall (to get cwd) — cache cwd at module load time
- All other functions are simple string operations
- Test against Node.js path module output for 50+ edge cases

# Files to Modify
- src/extensions_js.rs: Register node:path module with JS source

# Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All listed functions implemented
- [ ] Matches Node.js behavior for edge cases (empty strings, trailing slashes, .. traversal)
- [ ] path.resolve uses real cwd from runtime
- [ ] No hostcalls needed for non-resolve operations
- [ ] 20+ unit tests covering edge cases

title: Implement node:crypto shim — hashing, random UUID, and basic cryptographic primitives
description:
# Goal
Implement the node:crypto shim module, providing the most commonly used cryptographic functions that extensions rely on (hashing, UUID generation, random bytes).

# Background
Many extensions use crypto for content hashing (cache keys, dedup), UUID generation (unique IDs), and occasionally HMAC (webhook verification). QuickJS has no built-in crypto, so all operations must either be implemented in pure JS or routed through Rust hostcalls.

# API Surface (prioritized)

## Tier 1 — Must Have
- randomUUID() → string (v4 UUID)
- createHash(algorithm) → Hash object
  - Hash.update(data) → Hash (chainable)
  - Hash.digest(encoding) → string | Buffer
  - Algorithms: "sha256", "sha1", "md5"
- randomBytes(size) → Buffer
- randomInt(min?, max) → number

## Tier 2 — Should Have
- createHmac(algorithm, key) → Hmac object
  - Hmac.update(data) → Hmac
  - Hmac.digest(encoding) → string
- timingSafeEqual(a, b) → boolean
- getHashes() → string[] (list supported algorithms)

# Implementation Strategy
- randomUUID: Pure JS using Math.random() or delegate to Rust uuid crate via hostcall
- Hash/Hmac: Must delegate to Rust — QuickJS has no crypto primitives
  - Hostcall: pi.internal("crypto_hash", { algorithm, data, encoding })
  - Or: implement sha256/sha1/md5 in pure JS (slower but no hostcall overhead)
  - Recommendation: Rust hostcall for correctness + performance
- randomBytes: Delegate to Rust (OsRng) via hostcall
- timingSafeEqual: Must be Rust (constant-time comparison impossible in JS)

# Files to Modify
- src/extensions_js.rs: Register node:crypto module
- src/extension_dispatcher.rs: Add crypto hostcall handlers (if using Rust delegation)

# Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] randomUUID() returns valid v4 UUIDs
- [ ] createHash("sha256").update("hello").digest("hex") matches Node.js output
- [ ] randomBytes returns cryptographically secure random data
- [ ] At least sha256, sha1, md5 supported
- [ ] 10+ unit tests verifying output matches Node.js

title: Implement node:os shim — platform info and system utilities
description:
# Goal
Implement the node:os shim module, providing system information that extensions commonly use for platform detection and path defaults.

# Background
Extensions use node:os primarily for: platform detection (os.platform()), temp directory (os.tmpdir()), home directory (os.homedir()), and CPU info. The existing PiJS runtime (bd-2ru2) added partial os support (hostname, etc.) — this task completes the full surface.

# API Surface

## Must Have
- platform() → "linux" | "darwin" | "win32"
- arch() → "x64" | "arm64"
- tmpdir() → string
- homedir() → string
- hostname() → string (already implemented)
- EOL → "\n"
- type() → "Linux" | "Darwin" | "Windows_NT"
- release() → string (kernel version)
- cpus() → Array<{ model, speed, times }>
- totalmem() → number (bytes)
- freemem() → number (bytes)

## Nice to Have
- userInfo() → { username, homedir, shell, uid, gid }
- networkInterfaces() → object
- uptime() → number (seconds)
- loadavg() → [1min, 5min, 15min]

# Implementation Strategy
- Most functions return static system info → can be captured at runtime init and cached
- platform/arch/type: compile-time constants (cfg!(target_os), cfg!(target_arch))
- tmpdir/homedir: env vars or Rust std::env functions via hostcall
- cpus/totalmem/freemem: Rust sys-info via hostcall (or hardcode for sandboxed extensions)
- Hybrid: cache values at module load, no per-call hostcalls needed

# Files to Modify
- src/extensions_js.rs: Extend existing node:os module registration

# Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All "Must Have" functions return correct values for current platform
- [ ] platform() returns "linux" on Linux, "darwin" on macOS
- [ ] tmpdir() returns writable temp directory
- [ ] homedir() returns actual user home
- [ ] Values cached (no repeated hostcalls)

title: Implement node:url shim — URL and URLSearchParams constructors
description:
# Goal
Implement the node:url shim providing the WHATWG URL and URLSearchParams APIs that extensions use for URL parsing, construction, and query parameter manipulation.

# Background
The bd-2ru2 phase added a basic node:url module. This task verifies completeness and fills any remaining gaps. URL and URLSearchParams are WHATWG web standards — they can be implemented in pure JavaScript without hostcalls.

# API Surface

## URL class
- new URL(input, base?) → URL object
- url.href, url.origin, url.protocol, url.username, url.password
- url.host, url.hostname, url.port, url.pathname
- url.search, url.searchParams (returns URLSearchParams)
- url.hash
- url.toString() → string
- url.toJSON() → string
- URL.canParse(input, base?) → boolean (static)

## URLSearchParams class
- new URLSearchParams(init?) — string | object | iterable
- params.append(name, value)
- params.delete(name)
- params.get(name) → string | null
- params.getAll(name) → string[]
- params.has(name) → boolean
- params.set(name, value)
- params.sort()
- params.toString() → string
- params[Symbol.iterator]() → iterator

## Legacy API (node:url specific)
- url.parse(urlString) → Url object (legacy format)
- url.format(urlObject) → string
- url.resolve(from, to) → string

# Implementation Strategy
- Pure JavaScript: URL parsing is string manipulation, no I/O needed
- Use a well-tested URL parser implementation (port from a known JS polyfill)
- URLSearchParams: straightforward Map-like structure
- Legacy url.parse: regex-based parser matching Nodes output

# Files to Modify

# Acceptance Criteria

title: Implement node:buffer shim — Buffer class for binary data handling
description:
# Goal
Implement the node:buffer (Buffer) shim for binary data handling, which many extensions use for encoding/decoding, file I/O, and crypto operations.

# Background
Buffer is Node.js unique binary data type. Extensions use it for: base64 encoding/decoding, hex encoding, UTF-8 string conversion, and binary file handling. QuickJS has Uint8Array but not Buffer. The shim wraps Uint8Array with Buffers additional methods.

# API Surface

## Must Have
- Buffer.from(string, encoding) → Buffer
- Buffer.from(array) → Buffer
- Buffer.from(arrayBuffer) → Buffer
- Buffer.alloc(size, fill?, encoding?) → Buffer
- Buffer.allocUnsafe(size) → Buffer (alias for alloc in safe environment)
- Buffer.isBuffer(obj) → boolean
- Buffer.byteLength(string, encoding) → number
- Buffer.concat(list, totalLength?) → Buffer
- buf.toString(encoding?, start?, end?) → string
- buf.slice(start?, end?) → Buffer
- buf.length → number
- buf.write(string, offset?, length?, encoding?) → number
- buf[index] → number (Uint8Array behavior)
- Encodings: "utf8", "utf-8", "ascii", "base64", "hex", "binary", "latin1"

## Nice to Have
- buf.compare(other) → number
- buf.equals(other) → boolean
- buf.indexOf(value) → number
- buf.includes(value) → boolean
- buf.copy(target, targetStart?, sourceStart?, sourceEnd?)
- buf.fill(value, offset?, end?, encoding?)
- buf.toJSON() → { type: "Buffer", data: [...] }

# Implementation Strategy
- Extend Uint8Array prototype with Buffer methods (pure JS)
- Buffer.from with encoding: implement base64/hex decoders in JS
- buf.toString with encoding: implement base64/hex encoders in JS
- Keep internal storage as Uint8Array for interop with other APIs
- Performance: base64/hex encode/decode in pure JS is adequate for extension use cases (not crypto-grade throughput)

# Files to Modify
- src/extensions_js.js: Register node:buffer module, also make Buffer available as global

# Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Buffer.from("hello", "utf8").toString("base64") === "aGVsbG8="
- [ ] Buffer.from("aGVsbG8=", "base64").toString("utf8") === "hello"
- [ ] Buffer.from("68656c6c6f", "hex").toString("utf8") === "hello"
- [ ] Buffer.alloc(10) creates zero-filled buffer
- [ ] Buffer.isBuffer(Buffer.alloc(0)) === true
- [ ] Interop with Uint8Array (indexing, length)
- [ ] 15+ unit tests covering encodings + edge cases

title: Implement node:events shim — EventEmitter for pub/sub patterns
description:
# Goal
Implement the node:events (EventEmitter) shim, which many extensions use for internal pub/sub communication patterns.

# Background
EventEmitter is the foundation of Nodes event-driven architecture. Many npm packages (including popular extension dependencies) inherit from EventEmitter or use it directly for event-based APIs. Pure JS implementation — no hostcalls needed.

# API Surface

## Must Have
- new EventEmitter()
- emitter.on(event, listener) → this
- emitter.once(event, listener) → this
- emitter.off(event, listener) → this (alias: removeListener)
- emitter.emit(event, ...args) → boolean
- emitter.removeAllListeners(event?) → this
- emitter.listeners(event) → Function[]
- emitter.listenerCount(event) → number
- emitter.eventNames() → (string | symbol)[]
- emitter.setMaxListeners(n) → this
- emitter.getMaxListeners() → number
- EventEmitter.defaultMaxListeners (static, default 10)
- emitter.addListener(event, listener) → this (alias for on)
- emitter.prependListener(event, listener) → this
- emitter.prependOnceListener(event, listener) → this

## Nice to Have
- events.once(emitter, name) → Promise (static helper)
- events.on(emitter, name) → AsyncIterator (static helper)

# Implementation Strategy
- Pure JavaScript class
- Internal Map<string, Function[]> for listener storage
- once() wraps listener in auto-removing wrapper
- emit() calls all listeners synchronously (matching Node behavior)
- MaxListeners warning: console.warn if exceeded (not error)

# Files to Modify
- src/extensions_js.rs: Register node:events module

# Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] on/emit/off lifecycle works correctly
- [ ] once fires exactly once then auto-removes
- [ ] Multiple listeners on same event called in registration order
- [ ] removeAllListeners clears all or specific event
- [ ] MaxListeners warning at threshold

title: Implement node:http and node:https shims — HTTP client via pi.http hostcall
description:
# Goal
Implement node:http and node:https shims that route all HTTP requests through the capability-gated pi.http() hostcall, maintaining the security model while providing Node.js API compatibility.

# Background
Extensions that make HTTP requests (API calls, webhook delivery, data fetching) typically use either the native http/https modules or a library built on top of them (like node-fetch, axios, got). Providing http/https shims means these libraries MAY work without modification (if they only use the core request API).

Note: Many modern extensions use fetch() instead — global fetch is a separate concern (simpler to implement). This task covers the Node.js-specific http.request / https.request API.

# API Surface

## Must Have
- http.request(url | options, callback?) → ClientRequest
- http.get(url | options, callback?) → ClientRequest
- https.request(url | options, callback?) → ClientRequest
- https.get(url | options, callback?) → ClientRequest

## ClientRequest object
- req.write(chunk) — write request body
- req.end(chunk?) — finish request
- req.on("response", (res) => {}) — response event
- req.on("error", (err) => {}) — error event
- req.abort() / req.destroy() — cancel

## IncomingMessage (response) object
- res.statusCode → number
- res.headers → object
- res.on("data", (chunk) => {}) — body chunks
- res.on("end", () => {}) — body complete

## Options object
- hostname, port, path, method, headers, timeout

# Implementation Strategy
- ClientRequest accumulates body chunks via write()
- On end(): send pi.http() hostcall with accumulated body
- Response: parse hostcall result into IncomingMessage
- Streaming response: depends on streaming hostcall epic (bd-2tl1)
  - Without streaming: buffer full response, emit "data" + "end" immediately
  - With streaming: emit "data" events as StreamChunks arrive
- EventEmitter-based (depends on node:events shim)

# Dependencies
- Depends on node:events shim (for EventEmitter inheritance)
- Benefits from streaming hostcall (bd-2tl1) for true streaming responses
- Without streaming hostcall: still functional but buffers full response

# Files to Modify
- src/extensions_js.rs: Register node:http and node:https modules

# Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] http.get("http://example.com", (res) => { ... }) works
- [ ] https.request with POST body works
- [ ] Response headers and status code accessible
- [ ] Response body delivered via data/end events
- [ ] Error events on network failure
- [ ] Request timeout works
- [ ] All requests go through pi.http hostcall (capability-gated)

comments.text:
Fixed critical bug: node:http shim was referencing `globalThis.__pi_bridge.http` (doesn't exist) instead of `globalThis.pi.http`. All HTTP requests from extensions using node:http would always fail. Changed `_send()` to use the correct bridge object.

Added 21 new tests covering the full request→response flow with mocked pi.http: GET/POST body delivery, URL construction, header normalization, status codes/messages, error handling (rejection, invalid response), event ordering (data/end), abort/destroy events, timeout forwarding, https protocol enforcement, end-with-chunk. Total: 83 tests (62 existing + 21 new).

- POST with body: post_sends_body_via_hostcall, post_multiple_writes_joined
