title: Auth: Refresh expired OAuth tokens for extension providers (startup + deterministic logs)
description:
# Goal
Ensure extension-registered OAuth providers behave correctly in real runs by wiring automatic refresh for **expired extension OAuth tokens**.

# Background (Observed)
`src/auth.rs` implements `AuthStorage::refresh_expired_extension_oauth_tokens(...)` with unit tests, but there is no call site in the main runtime.

Current behavior risk:
- extension provider tokens can silently expire and never refresh unless the user re-auths
- conformance/E2E that rely on extension providers can become flaky or fail unexpectedly

# Scope
1) **Define refresh policy (spec-level)
- When to refresh:
  - on startup before running extensions
  - optionally just-in-time before first use of an extension provider
- What to refresh:
  - only expired tokens
  - skip built-in providers handled by `refresh_expired_oauth_tokens_with_client` (e.g. anthropic)
- Failure handling:
  - network failure: keep old token, emit actionable error/log event
  - invalid refresh token: mark token invalid and require re-login

2) **Wire call sites**
- Ensure extension configs (oauth provider configs) are available at the time refresh runs.
- Call refresh in all relevant entrypoints:
  - interactive mode
  - non-interactive (print)
  - RPC mode
- Ensure refresh respects:
  - timeouts
  - redaction policy (never log secrets)
  - deterministic structured logs for harness diffing

3) **Logging / Artifacts**
- Emit `pi.auth.refresh` events to the unified logging sink with:
  - provider id
  - token state transition (redacted)
  - timing
  - outcome classification
- Ensure bd-4u9 artifact index + redaction summary are used by any E2E script.

# Tests
- Unit tests: already exist for the refresh function; add any missing edge cases.
- Integration test:
  - execute a minimal runtime path that triggers the refresh call and asserts auth.json mutation
  - use VCR playback (no live network)
- E2E scenario:
  - drive a run where an extension provider token is expired and is refreshed automatically
  - capture deterministic JSONL logs + artifacts per bd-4u9

## Acceptance Criteria
- Expired extension OAuth tokens refresh automatically without manual user intervention.
- Refresh behavior is deterministic under test harness control.
- No secrets leak into logs/artifacts.
acceptance_criteria:
[ ] Refresh policy is explicitly defined (startup vs JIT) and implemented
[ ] Refresh is wired for all modes (interactive, print, RPC)
[ ] No secrets leak into logs; redaction summary present for E2E artifacts
[ ] Integration/E2E coverage proves the refresh call site executes (VCR playback; no live network)
[ ] JSONL logs + artifacts per bd-4u9 where applicable
[ ] Quality gates pass: cargo fmt --check, cargo check --all-targets, cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings, cargo test

title: Phase 0: Environment and Runtime Setup
description:
# Phase 0: Environment and Runtime Setup

## Purpose
Before we can do ANY differential testing, we need BOTH runtimes working and verified independently. This phase ensures:
1. The pi-mono TypeScript runtime can load and run extensions via Bun
2. The Rust QuickJS runtime can load and run extensions
3. A deterministic test environment exists (no randomness, fixed timestamps)

## Why This Is Phase 0
Everything else depends on this. If either runtime cannot load extensions, differential testing is impossible. We discovered Bun 1.3.8 is available at /home/ubuntu/.bun/bin/bun. The pi-mono source lives at legacy_pi_mono_code/pi-mono/. We need to verify it builds and its extension loader works.

## Acceptance Criteria
- pi-mono extension loader.ts can load the hello.ts extension and produce output
- Rust QuickJS runtime can load the hello.ts extension and produce output
- Both outputs can be captured as structured JSON
- Deterministic mode eliminates timestamps, random values, cwd-dependent paths
close_reason: Phase 0 complete: pi-mono loads extensions via Bun/jiti (tests/ext_conformance/ts_oracle/load_extension.ts), Rust QuickJS runtime loads extensions (tests/ext_conformance_diff.rs), both produce structured JSON, all 60 official extensions validated.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text: KEY DISCOVERY: Bun 1.3.8 is available at /home/ubuntu/.bun/bin/bun, which also provides a node shim. pi-mono uses jiti for extension loading (not native Bun module resolution). The virtualModules mechanism in loader.ts maps package names to bundled versions (@sinclair/typebox, @mariozechner/pi-agent-core, etc.). In development mode it uses aliases instead. For our harness, we need to run in development mode (not Bun binary mode) so that jiti resolves imports via filesystem.

A thorough gap analysis comparing every feature in pi-mono (legacy_pi_mono_code/pi-mono/packages/coding-agent/) against our Rust implementation revealed:

2. No programmatic SDK/library API (createAgentSession, RpcClient)

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## Structural Revision: PARITY↔DROPIN Decoupled

### What Changed
Removed hard dependencies from all PARITY sub-epics to DROPIN epics:
- PARITY-JSON no longer blocked by DROPIN-120
- PARITY-CLI no longer blocked by DROPIN-140
- PARITY-UX no longer blocked by DROPIN-140/160
- PARITY-SDK no longer blocked by DROPIN-130
- PARITY top epic no longer blocked by DROPIN-100

### Why
PARITY (implementation) and DROPIN (verification/certification) are complementary parallel workstreams, not sequential. Having implementation blocked on verification spec work is backwards. The critical path was 10+ links deep through DROPIN spec bottlenecks (112→113→114→...), preventing ANY parity sub-epic from closing until the full spec chain completed.

### New Architecture
- PARITY beads: implementation of specific gaps (add events, create API, add features)
- DROPIN beads: verification, certification, CI gating, documentation
- Cross-links: DROPIN implementation beads NOW depend on PARITY implementation beads (implement first, verify second)
  - DROPIN-122 ← PARITY-JSON.1 (need events before verifying schema)
  - DROPIN-141 ← PARITY-CLI.1 (flag pass-through is the key CLI gap)
  - DROPIN-132 ← PARITY-SDK.1 (need stable API before building SDK core)
- V beads (V1/V2/V3) linked as prerequisites for DROPIN-172/173/174 (smoke test before comprehensive suite)

### Result
Both workstreams can proceed in parallel. PARITY sub-epics close when implementation is done. DROPIN closes when verification is done. Both must complete for full drop-in status.

title: FUZZ-P1.8: Conformance Comparator — Proptest deep nesting, large arrays, type confusion
close_reason: Added 128-case proptests for deep nesting, large arrays, symmetry/reflexivity, and type confusion

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## FUZZ-P1.8: Conformance Comparator Proptest

### Background
src/conformance.rs (~136KB) contains the compare_conformance_output() function and helpers that perform semantic comparison of extension test outputs (JSON diff). This is used extensively in the extension conformance testing pipeline.

### Key Functions
1. **compare_conformance_output()** (line ~52-59): Entry point for semantic comparison
2. **compare_conformance_output_inner()** (line ~62-86): Recursive JSON traversal
3. Float comparison with epsilon (line ~12): Hardcoded 1e-10
4. Unordered array comparison: O(n^2) for large arrays
5. Missing vs null vs empty equivalence rules

### Specific Risks
1. **Stack overflow on deep nesting**: Recursive JSON traversal (lines 62-86) could overflow the stack on objects nested 100+ levels deep. Rust's default stack is 8MB, and each frame in the recursive function uses space for the Value, path String, etc.
2. **O(n^2) array comparison**: If unordered array comparison is used for arrays with 100K+ elements, this becomes a performance DoS
3. **Float comparison edge cases**:
   - NaN vs NaN (NaN != NaN in IEEE 754, but semantically they're 'the same')
   - Infinity vs Infinity
   - Very small numbers near epsilon (1e-10): 1e-11 vs 2e-11 — are they 'equal'?
   - Subnormal floats
4. **Mixed types in arrays**: [1, "1", true] — should comparison handle type coercion?
5. **Unicode string comparison**: Composed vs decomposed forms (e.g., cafe\u0301 vs café)
6. **Very large JSON objects**: Objects with 100K+ keys
7. **Null equivalence**: Is {"key": null} equivalent to {}? Is [null] equivalent to []?

### Implementation Approach
Create strategies:
- `nested_json(depth)`: Generates JSON nested to arbitrary depth
- `large_array_json(n)`: Arrays with n elements for performance testing
- `float_edge_cases()`: NaN, Inf, subnormals, epsilon-boundary values
- `equivalent_json_pairs()`: Two JSON values that should compare as equal
- `different_json_pairs()`: Two JSON values that should compare as different

### Invariants to Assert
- No stack overflow (or explicit recursion depth limit)
- compare(x, x) == Equal for any x (reflexivity)
- compare(x, y) == compare(y, x) for any x, y (symmetry)
- Performance: comparison of 10K-element arrays completes in <1 second
- NaN handling is explicitly documented and tested
- Float epsilon is applied consistently (not just for exact 0.0 comparison)

### Files to Modify
- src/conformance.rs (add proptest module)

### Acceptance Criteria
- At least 3 proptest functions
- Minimum 128 cases per property
- Stack overflow test with depth=200 nesting is mandatory
- Any panics/stack overflows found → add explicit recursion depth limit
- Float edge cases (NaN, Inf) have explicit documented behavior

# Background
After a large swarm closes all actionable work, agents still need a deterministic way to prove the queue is truly empty and distinguish no work from stale deferred epics, tombstones, broken bv output, or corrupt coordination tools. - Emit JSON and concise text; never mutate Beads, git, Agent Mail, RCH, or source files.

title: Design shared mock specification format (JSON schema)
description:
# Design shared mock specification format (JSON schema)

## Context
Both TS and Rust runtimes need identical mock behavior. The mock spec is a JSON file that defines exactly what each hostcall should return.

## Mock Spec Design

### HTTP Mocks
Match by method + URL pattern. Return deterministic status/headers/body.
Support: exact URL match, prefix match, regex match.

### Exec Mocks
Match by command + args pattern. Return deterministic stdout/stderr/exit_code.
Support: exact match, prefix match.

### Session State
Pre-defined: messages array, session name, current model, thinking level, active tools.
These are what getMessages(), getSessionName(), etc. return.

### UI Capture
Instead of rendering, capture all UI calls as structured events:
- showSpinner(text) -> {type: "spinner_show", text: "..."}
- updateSpinner(text) -> {type: "spinner_update", text: "..."}
- stopSpinner() -> {type: "spinner_stop"}
- showConfirm/showDialog -> auto-accept with configured response

### Event Payloads
Standard event payloads for: tool_call, tool_result, turn_start, turn_end, before_agent_start, input, context, resources_discover, user_bash, session_before_compact, session_before_tree.

## Output
- docs/schema/mock_spec.json (JSON Schema)
- tests/ext_conformance/fixtures/mock_spec_default.json (default mock spec)
- tests/ext_conformance/fixtures/mock_spec_with_http.json (example with HTTP mocks)

## Acceptance Criteria
- JSON Schema validates mock spec files
- Default mock spec covers all hostcall types
- Example specs demonstrate each mock category

title: Feature: Extension Tool Registration and Execution
description:
# Feature: Extension Tool Registration and Execution

## Overview

Extensions can register custom tools via pi.registerTool(). These tools must be:
1. Added to the agent's tool registry
2. Included in the tools array sent to the provider
3. Executable when the model invokes them

## Current State

The JS-side registration exists:
- `pi.registerTool(config)` registers a tool definition
- `__pi_execute_tool(name, callId, input)` exists in PI_BRIDGE_JS
- Tool definitions stored in extension's tools map

What's missing:
- Rust-side collection of registered tools
- Integration with agent's ToolRegistry
- Execution flow from model tool call → JS handler → result

## Architecture

```
Extension calls pi.registerTool()
            │
            ▼
JS runtime stores tool definition
            │
            ▼
Agent collects tools from all extensions ◄── [MISSING]
            │
            ▼
Tools added to ToolRegistry ◄── [MISSING]
            │
            ▼
Model receives tools in API call
            │
            ▼
Model invokes extension tool
            │
            ▼
Agent routes to extension handler ◄── [MISSING]
            │
            ▼
JS __pi_execute_tool() called ◄── [MISSING]
            │
            ▼
Result returned to model
```

## Implementation Requirements

### 1. Collect Registered Tools
After extension activation, query JS runtime for registered tools:
```rust
let ext_tools = runtime.get_registered_tools()?;
```

### 2. Create Tool Wrapper
Wrap each extension tool as an AgentTool:
```rust
struct ExtensionToolWrapper {
    name: String,
    label: String,
    description: String,
    parameters: serde_json::Value,
    runtime: Arc<PiJsRuntime>,
}

#[async_trait]
impl Tool for ExtensionToolWrapper {
    async fn execute(&self, call_id: &str, input: Value) -> Result<ToolOutput> {
        self.runtime.execute_extension_tool(&self.name, call_id, input).await
    }
}
```

### 3. Add to Registry
```rust
for tool_def in runtime.get_registered_tools()? {
    let wrapper = ExtensionToolWrapper::new(tool_def, runtime.clone());
    tool_registry.register(wrapper);
}
```

## Success Criteria

- [ ] Extension tools appear in provider's tools array
- [ ] Model can invoke extension tools
- [ ] Tool execution routes to JS handler
- [ ] Results return to model correctly
- [ ] Errors handled properly

title: Implement cancellation budgets for extension handlers
description:
Use asupersync cancellation budgets to bound cleanup time for extensions.

## Background
Cancellation budgets ensure:
- Cleanup completes in bounded time
- No indefinite waits during shutdown
- Predictable Ctrl+C behavior

## Current State
- Extensions use simple cancellation flags
- No guarantee cleanup completes quickly
- Long-running handlers may delay shutdown

## Implementation
1. Define cancellation budgets per operation type:
   - Extension event handler: 5s
   - Tool execution cleanup: 30s
   - UI dialog cancellation: 1s
2. Apply budgets via Cx::with_budget()
3. Force-cancel if budget exceeded

## Budget Configuration
Could be configurable in settings:
```json
{
  "extension_budgets": {
    "event_handler_ms": 5000,
    "tool_cleanup_ms": 30000
  }
}
```

## Test Plan
- Unit test: slow handler cancelled at budget
- Integration test: Ctrl+C cleanup completes quickly

## Files to Modify
- src/extensions.rs (apply budgets)
- src/config.rs (budget settings)

description:
# Goal
Make extension performance a *provable contract* by providing a repeatable benchmark harness for:
- extension startup (cold + warm)

title: Feature: Slash Command Handler for Extensions
description:
# Feature: Slash Command Handler for Extensions

## Overview

Extensions can register slash commands via pi.registerCommand(). When users type "/command", the agent must route to the extension's handler instead of built-in commands.

## Current State

### What Exists
- JS registration: pi.registerCommand() stores in __pi_registry.commands
- Command execution stub: __pi_execute_command() defined but not called from Rust
- Interactive module: Has slash command processing in src/interactive.rs

### What's Missing
- Rust querying registered commands from JS
- Integration with interactive command processor
- Command execution routing to JS
- Command completion/suggestions

## TypeScript Reference (extensions/src/runner.ts)

```typescript
class ExtensionRunner {
    executeCommand(name: string, args: string): Promise<CommandResult> {
        const cmd = this.registry.commands.get(name);
        if (!cmd) throw new Error(`Unknown command: ${name}`);
        return cmd.handler(args);
    }
    
    getCommands(): CommandDef[] {
        return Array.from(this.registry.commands.values());
    }
}
```

## Architecture

```
User types: /foo arg1 arg2
        │
        ▼
Interactive command processor
        │
        ├── Built-in command? → Execute directly
        │
        └── Extension command? → Route to JS handler
                │
                ▼
            __pi_execute_command("foo", "arg1 arg2")
                │
                ▼
            Extension handler runs
                │
                ▼
            CommandResult returned to user
```

## Command Definition

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Deserialize)]
pub struct ExtensionCommandDef {
```

title: Build differential test runner (orchestrates TS and Rust execution)
description:
# Build differential test runner (orchestrates TS and Rust execution)

## Context
This is the main conformance test binary/library. It orchestrates running each extension through both runtimes and comparing outputs.

## Implementation: Rust Integration Test
File: tests/ext_conformance_runner.rs

The runner:
1. Reads VALIDATED_MANIFEST.json to get list of extensions
2. For each extension:
   a. Selects appropriate mock spec (per-extension override or default)
   b. Spawns Bun subprocess: bun run tests/ext_conformance/ts_harness/run_extension.ts <ext_path> <mock_spec>
   c. Captures TS stdout as JSON
   d. Calls Rust conformance harness: load extension with ConformanceMockSession, capture output as JSON
   e. Compares the two JSON outputs
   f. Records result

## Dependencies
- bd-1l8n: TS mock layer (Bun harness)
- bd-1bje: Rust mock layer (ConformanceMockSession)

## Key Design Decisions
- Runner is a Rust integration test (#[test] functions) for CI integration
- Each extension can be a separate #[test] for parallelism and isolation
- Use macro to generate tests from manifest (similar to fixture_test! macro in conformance_fixtures.rs)
- Timeout per extension: 30s (some extensions are slow)
- Capture stderr from Bun for debugging failures

## Output Format (per extension)
{
  "extension_id": "hello",
  "ts_output": {...},
  "rust_output": {...},
  "comparison": {
    "status": "pass" | "fail" | "error",
    "registration_match": true,
    "event_match": true,
    "diffs": [
      {"category": "registration.tools", "ts": [...], "rust": [...], "diff": "..."}
    ]
  },
  "ts_time_ms": 42,
  "rust_time_ms": 38
}

## Acceptance Criteria
- Runner can execute hello.ts through both runtimes and compare
- Runner produces structured JSON report
- Runner supports --filter flag for running specific extensions
- Runner supports --tier flag for running specific tiers

title: [PERF-0] Refactor interactive.rs into logical modules
description:
## Problem

src/interactive.rs is 10,000+ lines — one of the largest single files in the codebase. All PERF track beads (PERF-1 through PERF-7) add new structs, fields, and logic to this file. Without modularization:
- Multiple agents working on PERF beads will have constant merge conflicts
- Code navigation is difficult (function references span thousands of lines)
- Testing isolated components requires importing the entire PiApp monolith

## Solution: Extract Logical Modules

Split interactive.rs into focused modules under src/interactive/:

```
src/interactive/
├── mod.rs           — PiApp struct, init(), main event dispatch
├── view.rs          — view(), build_conversation_content(), header/footer rendering
├── commands.rs      — Slash command handlers (/login, /share, /scoped-models, etc.)
├── keybindings.rs   — Key event dispatch (Ctrl+P cycling, navigation, etc.)
├── conversation.rs  — ConversationMessage rendering, tool output collapse logic
├── state.rs         — App state types (InputMode, AgentState, etc.)
└── perf.rs          — FrameTimingStats, FrameBudget, MemoryMonitor, RenderBuffers, MessageRenderCache
```

### Extraction Rules
1. **No behavior changes** — pure structural refactor, identical public API
2. **One module per commit** — allows bisection if something breaks
3. **Re-export from mod.rs** — existing test imports continue to work via `use crate::interactive::*`
4. **Move types first, then functions** — types are self-contained, functions have more dependencies

### Why Before PERF-1
- PERF-1 adds MessageRenderCache to PiApp and modifies build_conversation_content()
- PERF-3 adds FrameTimingStats and instruments view()
- PERF-4 adds FrameBudget state machine
- PERF-6 adds MemoryMonitor
- PERF-7 adds RenderBuffers
- All of these touch the same 10K-line file. Modularizing first means each PERF bead modifies a small, focused file.

## Files to Modify
- src/interactive.rs → split into src/interactive/mod.rs + submodules

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] src/interactive.rs split into 6+ focused modules
- [ ] All 263+ tui_state tests pass unchanged
- [ ] All imports via `use crate::interactive::*` continue to work
- [ ] No behavior changes (pure refactor)
- [ ] cargo check + clippy + fmt clean
- [ ] Each module < 2000 lines

title: [SEC-2.4] Quarantine-to-trust promotion workflow for unknown/high-risk extensions
description:
## Background
Not all extensions should execute immediately after install; trust must be staged.

## Scope
- Add quarantine state for unsigned/high-risk/unknown packages.
- Define explicit promotion workflow with user acknowledgment and policy constraints.
- Ensure quarantined extensions cannot bypass policy via indirect registration paths.

## Deliverables
- State machine for trust lifecycle: quarantined -> restricted -> trusted.
- UX + CLI hooks for promotion and rollback to quarantine.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Quarantined extensions cannot execute dangerous hostcalls.
- [ ] Promotion requires explicit operator action with audit trail.
- [ ] Demotion back to quarantine is supported and tested.
acceptance_criteria:
[ ] Scope in description is implemented fully with no feature loss
[ ] Unit tests added/updated for success, failure, edge cases, and determinism where applicable
[ ] E2E scripts added/updated for benign flow, adversarial flow, and rollback/recovery flow relevant to this bead
[ ] E2E runs emit structured JSONL logs with: timestamp, issue_id, extension_id, capability, policy_profile, score, reason_codes, action, latency_ms, correlation_id, and redaction_summary
[ ] Artifact manifest is deterministic and linked in bead comments (paths + checksums/identifiers)
[ ] Quality gates pass: cargo fmt --check, cargo check --all-targets, cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings, cargo test (plus targeted conformance/security suites)

title: Feature: Compatibility gap analysis for expanded corpus
description: Map expanded extensions to required shims/hostcalls; produce a prioritized gap matrix for unmodified compatibility.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
Purpose
Translate the expanded corpus into a concrete compatibility gap matrix. The goal is a prioritized, actionable list of shims/hostcalls required for unmodified compatibility.

Guiding Principles
- No per-extension exceptions: all compatibility gaps map to general-purpose shims or hostcalls.
- Prioritize Tier-1 coverage and high-frequency Node APIs (fs, path, child_process, process, Buffer, URL, crypto).
- Keep performance + determinism constraints from EXTENSIONS.md.

Outputs
- A gap matrix by extension + API.

title: Workstream: Theme System Implementation
description:
# Workstream: Theme System Implementation

## Goal
Implement theme loading and switching for the TUI, matching Pi Agent's theme system.

## Background
The TypeScript Pi Agent supports themes that control:
- Color palette (foreground, background, accent colors)
- Syntax highlighting colors
- Status line appearance
- Thinking block styling

Themes are stored as JSON files in:
- ~/.pi/agent/themes/ (global)
- .pi/themes/ (project)
- Package themes (installed via pi install)

## Scope

### In Scope
1. Theme file format definition (JSON schema)
2. Theme discovery from standard locations
3. Theme application to TUI components
4. Theme switching via /theme command
5. Default themes (dark, light, solarized)

### Out of Scope
1. Theme creation wizard
2. Real-time theme editing
3. Complex inheritance chains

## Theme Format
```json
{
  "name": "ocean-dark",
  "version": "1.0",
  "colors": {
    "foreground": "#d4d4d4",
    "background": "#1e1e1e",
    "accent": "#007acc",
    "success": "#4ec9b0",
    "warning": "#ce9178",
    "error": "#f44747",
    "muted": "#6a6a6a"
  },
  "syntax": {
    "keyword": "#569cd6",
    "string": "#ce9178",
    "number": "#b5cea8",
    "comment": "#6a9955",
    "function": "#dcdcaa"
  },
  "ui": {
    "border": "#3c3c3c",
    "selection": "#264f78",
    "cursor": "#aeafad"
  }
}
```

## Implementation Phases

### Phase 1: Theme Loading
- Parse theme JSON files
- Discover themes from standard locations
- Validate theme format
- Provide default themes

### Phase 2: Theme Application
- Apply colors to lipgloss styles
- Wire syntax colors to glamour
- Update all TUI components

### Phase 3: Theme Switching
- /theme command to list/switch
- Persist theme preference in settings
- Hot-reload on theme file change (optional)

## Success Criteria
- [ ] Theme files parsed correctly
- [ ] Default themes work
- [ ] /theme command works
- [ ] TUI renders with theme colors
- [ ] Settings remembers theme preference

## Files to Create
- src/theme.rs (theme loading/application)

- themes/light.json (default light theme)

## Files to Modify
- src/interactive.rs (apply theme to TUI)
- src/tui.rs (apply theme to console output)
- src/config.rs (theme preference setting)

title: [PERF-7] String allocation optimization: reuse buffers on rendering hot path
description:
## Problem

build_conversation_content() allocates a new String every frame. view() also allocates multiple Strings for header, footer, conversation visible lines. These allocations hit the allocator 60 times per second.

## Solution: Pre-allocated Reusable Internal Buffers

### CRITICAL CONSTRAINT: view() returns String

The charmed_bubbletea Model trait requires `fn view(&self) -> String`. This means:
1. The RETURN VALUE of view() must be a freshly-owned String -- we cannot return &str or reuse an external buffer
2. However, we CAN reuse INTERNAL buffers used to BUILD the content
3. The final String allocation is unavoidable but can be minimized to a single allocation with correct capacity

### What We CAN Optimize

**Internal buffers** -- rebuilt every frame but can reuse heap allocations:
```rust
struct RenderBuffers {
    /// Pre-allocated conversation content buffer. Cleared and reused each frame.
    conversation: String,
    /// Pre-allocated header buffer.
    header: String,
    /// Pre-allocated footer buffer.
    footer: String,
}
```

**Strategy:**
1. `build_conversation_content()` writes into `self.render_buffers.conversation` via clear() + push_str() -- reuses heap
2. Header/footer rendering writes into pre-allocated buffers
3. In view(), the final String is assembled with pre-allocated exact capacity:
   ```rust
   fn view(&self) -> String {
       // Build into internal buffers (reused heap)
       let buffers = self.render_buffers.borrow();
       let total_len = buffers.header.len()
                      + viewport_content.len()
                      + buffers.footer.len();
       let mut output = String::with_capacity(total_len);
       output.push_str(&buffers.header);
       output.push_str(viewport_content);
       output.push_str(&buffers.footer);
       output  // Single allocation with exact capacity
   }
   ```

**What We CANNOT Optimize:**
- The return value of view() -- must be a new String each frame (trait requirement)
- The viewport content extraction -- Viewport::view() also returns String (upstream library)

### view() &self Compatibility
Since RenderBuffers need &mut access but view() only has &self, use RefCell:
```rust
render_buffers: RefCell<RenderBuffers>,
```
Single-threaded TUI makes this safe. The borrow is short-lived (within view() only).

### Capacity Estimation
- On first frame, allocate with estimated capacity (terminal_width x terminal_height x 4 bytes -- accounts for UTF-8 and ANSI escapes)
- Subsequent frames: clear() preserves existing capacity, so heap is reused
- String::with_capacity(total_len) for final output uses exact size

### Why This Depends on PERF-1 AND PERF-2

Both PERF-1 (MessageRenderCache) and PERF-2 (incremental prefix) modify build_conversation_content(). PERF-7 must be implemented AFTER both to correctly integrate buffer reuse with:
- PERF-1's cache hit path (no rendering needed, just copy cached string into buffer)
- PERF-2's prefix path (cached_conversation_prefix is valid, just append streaming tail to buffer)

Without these dependencies, PERF-7 would optimize the unoptimized path, then need rework when PERF-1/PERF-2 change the function signature and flow.

### Measurement
- Use PERF-3 telemetry to compare frame allocation counts before/after
- Primary metric: allocation bytes per frame
- Expected improvement: reduce per-frame allocations from ~5 Strings to 1 (the return value)

## Files to Modify
- src/interactive.rs: Add RenderBuffers field (in RefCell), modify build_conversation_content() and view()

## Dependencies
- Depends on PERF-1 (cache hit path) and PERF-2 (incremental prefix path)

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] RenderBuffers struct with pre-allocated capacity in RefCell
- [ ] build_conversation_content() uses clear+push instead of new String
- [ ] Header/footer rendering uses pre-allocated buffers
- [ ] view() assembles final output with single String::with_capacity(exact)
- [ ] RefCell<RenderBuffers> for &self compatibility in view()
- [ ] All 263+ tui_state tests pass
- [ ] Benchmark shows per-frame allocation reduction (5 Strings to 1)

title: [REVIEW] CRITICAL: SSE parser buffer duplication in slow path
description:
**SEVERITY**: CRITICAL - Data corruption in streaming

**AFFECTED FILES**: src/sse.rs:344

**ISSUE**: Buffer duplication bug in SSE parser slow path causes data corruption:

Line 344: `self.buffer.push_str(&combined[consumed..]);`

**PROBLEM**: 
- `combined` buffer includes previous `self.buffer` content + new data
- After processing, unconsumed portion of `combined` is pushed back to `self.buffer`
- This causes duplication since `self.buffer` was already part of `combined`

**REPRO**: 
- SSE stream with incomplete lines that trigger slow path (line 327+)
- Subsequent feeds will duplicate previously buffered data
- Results in malformed SSE events and parsing failures

**ROOT CAUSE**: 
Line 330: `let mut combined = std::mem::take(&mut self.buffer);`
Line 344: `self.buffer.push_str(&combined[consumed..]);`
Should be: `self.buffer = combined[consumed..].to_string();`

**IMPACT**: Silent data corruption in SSE streaming, especially affecting tool call parsing and multi-chunk responses.

**PRIORITY**: P0 - Corrupts streaming data integrity
close_reason: Fixed SSE parser buffer duplication bug and added test

title: Implement pi.exec() for shell execution from extensions
description:
Allow extensions to execute shell commands.

## API Spec (from legacy)
```typescript
await pi.exec(
  command: string,
  args: string[],
  options?: {
    cwd?: string;
    env?: Record<string, string>;
    timeout?: number;
  }
): Promise<{
  code: number;
  stdout: string;
  stderr: string;
}>
```

## Use Cases
- Git operations from extensions
- Build/test automation
- File system operations beyond basic tools
- Custom tooling integration

1. Hostcall handler for 'exec'
2. Spawn subprocess with command, args, options
3. Capture stdout/stderr
4. Apply timeout if specified
5. Return result to JS

## Security Considerations
- Extensions execute with user's permissions
- Timeout prevents runaway processes
- Consider capability gating (strict policy might block)

## Implementation Notes
- Use asupersync::process or std::process::Command
- Stream output to rolling buffer
- Kill process tree on timeout

- Unit test: simple command executes and returns
- Unit test: timeout kills process
- Unit test: env vars passed correctly
- Integration test: extension can run git commands

title: PARITY-UX.4: Version update check on startup — query GitHub releases for newer version

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## PARITY-UX.4: Version Update Check on Startup

### The Gap
pi-mono checks npm registry for newer versions on startup (src/modes/interactive/interactive-mode.ts:528,585) and shows "New version X is available" in the footer.

Our Rust port has no version check.

### Implementation Plan
1. On startup (interactive mode only, non-blocking):
   - Spawn background task to check latest release version
   - For binary distribution: query GitHub releases API
   - For cargo: check crates.io (if published)
2. Compare against current version (from Cargo.toml)
3. If newer version available, show notification in footer or at startup
4. Cache check result for 24h to avoid repeated API calls
5. Respect offline mode / no-network scenarios (fail silently)

### API Endpoint
GitHub: `https://api.github.com/repos/Dicklesworthstone/pi_agent_rust/releases/latest`
Parse tag_name field for latest version.

### Config Option
Add `check_for_updates: bool` (default: true) to settings.json so users can disable.

### Acceptance Criteria
- Version check runs on startup (background, non-blocking)
- Shows notification if newer version available
- Fails silently if offline or API unavailable
- Configurable via settings.json
- Cache prevents repeated API calls within 24h

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone

### Unit Tests (tests/version_check.rs)
1. **Version comparison**: current=1.0.0, latest=1.1.0 → "update available"

3. **Ahead of release**: current=1.2.0-dev, latest=1.1.0 → no notification
4. **Network failure**: GitHub API unreachable → silently fails, no error shown to user
5. **Cache behavior**: Check once → cached for 24h → second check within 24h returns cached result without API call
6. **Cache expiry**: After 24h, new API call made
7. **Config disable**: check_for_updates=false → no API call made

### Integration Tests
8. **VCR cassette**: Mock GitHub releases API response, verify version comparison logic
9. **Notification display**: Verify "New version X.Y.Z available" appears in footer or startup message

### Structured Logging

title: FUZZ-P1.7: VCR Cassette — Proptest base64 decoding, header validation, version matching

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## FUZZ-P1.7: VCR Cassette Parser Proptest

### Background
src/vcr.rs (1985 lines) implements the VCR (Video Cassette Recorder) test infrastructure that records and replays HTTP interactions. Cassette files are JSON that store request/response pairs. While these are test infrastructure, corrupted cassettes should never crash the test harness.

### Key Structures
1. **Cassette** (line ~116-120):
   - version: String (expected: "1.0")
   - test_name: String
   - recorded_at: String (ISO 8601 timestamp)
   - interactions: Vec<Interaction>

2. **RecordedRequest** (line ~130-135):
   - method: String
   - url: String
   - headers: HashMap<String, String>
   - body: Option<String>

3. **RecordedResponse** (line ~140-147):
   - status: u16
   - headers: HashMap<String, String>
   - body_chunks: Option<Vec<String>>
   - body_chunks_base64: Option<Vec<String>>

4. **`into_byte_stream()`** (line ~149+): Converts response into streaming byte chunks
5. **`redact_json()`**: Redaction logic for API keys and sensitive fields
6. **`request_matches()`**: Exact body comparison after redaction

### Specific Risks
1. **Invalid base64 in body_chunks_base64**: Malformed base64 → should return error, not panic
2. **Mixed encoding**: Both body_chunks AND body_chunks_base64 present — which wins? Neither present?
3. **Version mismatch**: version: "2.0" or version: "" — how is this handled?
4. **Malformed URLs**: url: "not-a-url", url: "", url with special chars
5. **HTTP status codes**: status: 0, status: 999, status: 65535 (u16 max)
6. **Header injection**: Values containing \r\n (CRLF injection in HTTP headers)
7. **Non-ASCII headers**: Header names/values with Unicode
8. **Duplicate request signatures**: Two interactions with identical method+url+body — which is matched?
9. **Empty interactions array**: Cassette with no recorded interactions
10. **Timestamp format**: Non-ISO8601 strings in recorded_at

### Implementation Approach
Create strategies:
- `arbitrary_cassette()`: Generates valid/semi-valid cassette JSON
- `corrupted_response()`: Responses with invalid base64, bad status codes
- `edge_case_request()`: Requests with malformed URLs, injection headers

### Invariants to Assert
- No panic on any cassette JSON input
- Invalid base64 → error (not silent data corruption)
- into_byte_stream() on a response with no body → empty stream (not error)
- redact_json() is idempotent: redact(redact(x)) == redact(x)
- request_matches() is reflexive: request_matches(x, x) == true

### Files to Modify
- src/vcr.rs (add proptest module)

### Acceptance Criteria
- At least 3 proptest functions
- Minimum 128 cases per property
- Base64 edge cases are mandatory coverage
- Any panics found are fixed inline

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## FUZZ-V1: Phase 1 Validation Suite

### Purpose
After all P1 proptest tasks are complete, this validation suite runs ALL proptest targets together and generates a structured report verifying that:
1. All proptest functions pass
2. Total case count meets the >= 2000 target
3. No regressions from inline bug fixes
4. Detailed logging captures per-test timing and any shrunk failure cases

### What This Produces

A test binary (or script) that:
1. Runs `cargo test` with a filter matching all proptest functions
2. Captures output with --nocapture for detailed logging
3. Parses test results to count:
   - Total proptest functions executed
   - Total cases generated across all functions
   - Pass/fail per function
   - Time per function
4. Generates a JSON report:
```json
{
  "phase": "P1",
  "timestamp": "2026-02-15T...",
  "total_proptest_functions": 30,
  "total_cases_generated": 5120,
  "results": [
    {"module": "sse::tests", "function": "sse_chunking_invariant", "cases": 256, "status": "pass", "time_ms": 340},
    {"module": "sse::tests", "function": "sse_utf8_edge_cases", "cases": 256, "status": "pass", "time_ms": 890},
    ...
  ],
  "bugs_found_and_fixed": [
    {"module": "providers::anthropic", "description": "index OOB on content block delta", "fix": "bounds check added"}
  ]
}
```

### Implementation Options

**Option A: Shell script** (simplest):
```bash
#\!/bin/bash
# scripts/validate_fuzz_p1.sh
set -euo pipefail
echo '{"phase":"P1","timestamp":"'2026-02-14T11:18:35-06:00'","results":[' > report.json
cargo test --lib -- proptest 2>&1 | tee proptest_output.log
# Parse output for pass/fail counts...
```

**Option B: Rust test binary** (more robust):
Add a #[test] function in a dedicated file that:
- Calls each proptest function programmatically
- Measures timing
- Aggregates results
- Writes JSON report

**Option C: Criterion-style benchmark** (reusable):
Extend existing benchmark infrastructure to include proptest case count tracking.

### Recommendation
Option A (shell script) for initial validation. If this becomes part of CI, migrate to Option B.

### Logging Requirements (per user request)
- Each proptest function: name, case count, pass/fail, time_ms, any shrunk failures
- Summary: total functions, total cases, pass rate, total time
- Machine-readable: JSONL output per test, final JSON summary
- Human-readable: colored terminal output with pass/fail indicators

### Acceptance Criteria
- Script/test runs all P1 proptest functions
- Output includes per-function case counts and timing
- JSON report is generated at a known path
- Total case count >= 2000 verified programmatically
- Exit code 0 only if ALL functions pass and case count meets target
- Script is documented in fuzz/README.md

title: [SEC-WS3] Deterministic Runtime Anomaly Detection Engine
description:
## Purpose
Design and implement deterministic, explainable runtime anomaly detection over extension hostcall behavior.

## Why This Stream Exists
Even signed code can become risky at runtime (logic bombs, compromised updates, connector misuse). We need live detection that is mathematically principled and auditable.

## Deliverables
- Runtime telemetry schema and feature extraction
- Robust baseline modeling per extension
- Online risk scoring with reason codes
- Deterministic enforcement state machine
- Forensic ledger and threshold calibration loop

## Exit Criteria
- [ ] Same input trace always yields same score/action.
- [ ] Every enforcement decision is explainable from recorded features.

[ ] Security behavior changes are reflected in operator/user documentation and rollout guidance

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
Runtime detection stream design note:
- We explicitly avoid opaque ML in the online decision path.
- Preferred math stack: robust univariate stats (median/MAD/quantiles), Markov transition surprise, and bounded weighted scoring with reason codes.
- Threshold tuning occurs offline against labeled traces; production engine remains deterministic and explainable.

title: Validate + dedupe candidates (true Pi extension classifier)

comments.author: LavenderRobin
comments.text:
Problem
- Broad discovery turns up lots of “extension-adjacent” artifacts: prompt packs, MCP servers, templates, or plugins for other agents.
- We need a deterministic way to decide what counts as a Pi extension and to avoid double-counting duplicates.

Validation rules (deterministic)
- Candidate counts as a “true Pi extension” if:
  - It has an entrypoint file that matches Pi expectations (export default …)
  - AND it imports/uses Pi extension API (e.g., ExtensionAPI import from @mariozechner/pi-coding-agent) OR clearly uses Pi protocol calls.
- If it only *mentions* Pi but does not implement the protocol, it is tracked as “mention-only / out-of-scope”.

Dedup rules
- Canonical identity key should be based on: (upstream repo URL, path-to-entrypoint, entrypoint filename) OR npm package+version.
- When duplicates exist across sources (repo + npm, repo mirrored, forks), keep one canonical entry and record the aliases.

Output
- A validated, deduped candidate set with:
  - canonical_id
  - aliases (other URLs/names)
  - validation evidence (why it’s a true extension)
  - classification tags (single/multi-file, deps, exec/http/fs/ui/provider)

Acceptance criteria
- >= 95% of inventory entries have an explicit validation status: true-extension vs mention-only vs unknown.
- Dedup reduces double-counting without losing provenance.

Downstream
- This is a prerequisite input quality gate for bd-hhzv and bd-34io.

comments.author: LavenderRobin
comments.text:
TESTING + LOGGING REQUIREMENTS

This bead is the “truth filter”: it decides what counts as a Pi extension and prevents double-counting. It must be deterministic and heavily tested.

Unit tests
- Dedup key tests:
  - same extension via repo + npm -> merges correctly
  - forks/mirrors -> alias mapping preserved
  - different extensions with similar names -> do not merge
- Classifier tests:
  - true Pi extension signatures (import + export default + registrations)
  - mention-only repos (should be out-of-scope)
  - edge cases: re-exported entrypoints, multi-file bundles, generated code

Golden corpus regression
- Create a small “golden set” of known-valid extensions from our vendored artifacts and ensure:
  - classifier marks them true-extension
  - dedup produces stable canonical IDs

E2E script
- Offline E2E that:
  - takes mixed-source candidate inputs (repo/npm/marketplace)
  - runs validation + dedup
  - outputs stable JSON with expected counts

Logging
- JSONL must include per-candidate decision records:
  - canonical_id chosen
  - aliases recorded
  - validation evidence (which signature matched)
  - rejection reason for out-of-scope

User-facing benefit
- This makes “200+ extensions proven” credible: we can show exactly what was counted and why.

title: FUZZ-P2.1: Set up cargo-fuzz infrastructure — fuzz/ directory, Cargo.toml, arbitrary crate
close_reason: Infrastructure complete: fuzz/Cargo.toml, fuzz_targets/fuzz_smoke.rs, fuzzing feature, expanded fuzz_exports (Config, Model, Session, SSE types). Verified: cargo fuzz list, fuzz_smoke runs (3.9M exec in 6s), cargo check passes.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## FUZZ-P2.1: cargo-fuzz Infrastructure Setup

### What This Task Does
Set up the cargo-fuzz framework so we can write libFuzzer-based fuzz harnesses. This is a one-time infrastructure task that all other P2 harness tasks depend on.

### Steps

1. **Install cargo-fuzz** (if not already):
   ```bash
   cargo install cargo-fuzz
   ```

2. **Initialize fuzz directory**:
   ```bash
   cargo fuzz init
   ```
   This creates:
   - fuzz/Cargo.toml (workspace member with libfuzzer-sys dependency)
   - fuzz/fuzz_targets/ (directory for harness .rs files)

3. **Add arbitrary crate** to BOTH Cargo.toml files:
   - Main Cargo.toml dev-dependencies: `arbitrary = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }`
   - fuzz/Cargo.toml dependencies: `arbitrary = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }`

4. **Configure fuzz/Cargo.toml** to depend on pi_agent_rust as a library:
   ```toml
   [dependencies]
   pi_agent_rust = { path = ".." }
   libfuzzer-sys = "0.4"
   arbitrary = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
   ```

5. **IMPORTANT: Check lib.rs exposure**: cargo-fuzz harnesses can only access public APIs from the library crate. Verify that key parsing functions are accessible:
   - SSE parser: SseParser, SseStream (from src/sse.rs)
   - Session: decode_session_entries (from src/session.rs)
   - Config: Config struct (from src/config.rs)
   - Model: Message, ContentBlock (from src/model.rs)
   If functions are not public, consider adding pub(crate) → pub or creating a `#[cfg(fuzzing)]` feature flag to expose internals.

6. **Create a trivial test harness** to verify the setup works:
   ```rust
   // fuzz/fuzz_targets/fuzz_smoke.rs
   #\![no_main]
   use libfuzzer_sys::fuzz_target;
   
   fuzz_target\!(|data: &[u8]| {
       let _ = std::str::from_utf8(data);
   });
   ```

7. **Verify**: `cargo fuzz run fuzz_smoke -- -max_total_time=10` should run for 10 seconds and exit cleanly.

### Architectural Decision: Feature Flag vs Public API
Option A: Make parsing functions pub (simpler, but exposes internals)
Option B: Add `#[cfg(feature = "fuzzing")]` feature flag that opens up internal APIs for fuzzing only
Recommendation: Option B is cleaner — add `fuzzing` feature to Cargo.toml `[features]` section and gate pub exports on it. The fuzz/Cargo.toml would then use `pi_agent_rust = { path = "..", features = ["fuzzing"] }`.

### Important: #\![forbid(unsafe_code)] Compatibility
libfuzzer-sys uses unsafe internally (it's a C FFI binding). The fuzz/ crate is a SEPARATE crate (not part of the main pi_agent_rust crate), so it does NOT inherit #\![forbid(unsafe_code)]. This is fine — the fuzzer binary can use unsafe, while the code under test remains safe.

### Files to Create
- fuzz/Cargo.toml
- fuzz/fuzz_targets/fuzz_smoke.rs (smoke test)

### Files to Modify
- Cargo.toml (add arbitrary to dev-deps, add fuzzing feature)
- src/lib.rs (conditionally expose internals under fuzzing feature)

### Acceptance Criteria
- cargo fuzz list shows fuzz_smoke target
- cargo fuzz run fuzz_smoke -- -max_total_time=10 completes successfully
- cargo test still passes (fuzzing feature doesn't break normal builds)
- cargo clippy still passes

title: Implement pi.registerCommand() for extension slash commands
description:
Allow extensions to register custom slash commands that integrate with the TUI.

## API Spec (from legacy)
```typescript
pi.registerCommand(name, {
  description: string,
  handler: (args, ctx) => Promise<void>,
  getArgumentCompletions?: (prefix) => CompletionItem[]
});
```

## Implementation Requirements
1. CommandRegistry in extension runtime to store registered commands
2. Hostcall handler for 'registerCommand' that validates and stores
3. Integration with autocomplete system (src/autocomplete.rs)
4. Integration with slash command processor (src/interactive.rs)
5. Command execution via extension runtime (JS handler)

## Data Flow
1. Extension calls pi.registerCommand('mycommand', {...})
2. Hostcall stores in CommandRegistry
3. /mycommand shows in autocomplete suggestions
4. User types /mycommand args
5. Interactive processor detects extension command
6. Invokes JS handler with args and ExtensionCommandContext

## Test Plan
- Unit test: registerCommand stores command metadata
- Integration test: registered command appears in autocomplete
- E2E test: /mycommand executes JS handler

## Files to Modify
- src/extensions.rs (CommandRegistry)
- src/extensions_js.rs (hostcall handler)
- src/autocomplete.rs (include extension commands)
- src/interactive.rs (dispatch to extension handler)

title: PARITY-CLI.1: Extension CLI flag pass-through — two-pass arg parsing for extension-registered flags
close_reason: Completed: two-pass CLI parsing and extension flag pass-through are implemented (src/cli.rs parse_with_extension_flags + extracted extension flags), and extension runtime flag propagation is wired via ExtensionManager::set_flag_value/list_flags paths in src/extensions.rs with parser-level coverage tests.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## PARITY-CLI.1: Extension CLI Flag Pass-Through

### The Gap (IMPORTANT)
pi-mono uses two-pass arg parsing:
1. First pass: discovers extensions and collects their registered flags
2. Second pass: parses CLI args including extension-registered flags

This means extensions can register flags like --plan, --verbose-ext, etc. and users can pass them on the command line: `pi --plan "implement feature X"`

Reference: legacy_pi_mono_code/pi-mono/packages/coding-agent/src/main.ts:463-516
And: legacy_pi_mono_code/pi-mono/packages/coding-agent/src/cli/args.ts:156-167

Our Rust CLI uses clap (src/cli.rs), which rejects unknown flags. The test at src/cli.rs:554 (unknown_flag_rejected) explicitly verifies this behavior. Extensions CAN register flags internally, but there is NO mechanism for users to pass those flags on the command line.

### Why This Matters
Extensions like claude-code-style planning tools register --plan as a flag. Users expect to type `pi --plan "task"` and have the flag forwarded to the extension. This is a core extension ecosystem feature.

### Implementation Plan

**Approach: Two-pass parsing with clap**
1. First pass with clap using `allow_external_subcommands` or `ignore_errors`:
   - Parse known flags normally
   - Collect unknown flags into a HashMap<String, String>
2. Load extensions (using parsed known flags like -e, --no-extensions)
3. Collect extension-registered flags
4. Second pass: validate unknown flags against extension registry
   - Known extension flag → store in extension flag values map
   - Unknown extension flag → error (reject truly unknown flags)
5. Pass flag values to extensions via ExtensionManager

**Alternative: TrailingVarArg approach**
Use claps trailing_var_arg to capture everything after `--` as extension args:
`pi --model gpt-4 -- --plan "implement feature X"`
This is simpler but changes the CLI ergonomics. NOT recommended.

**Recommended: First approach (two-pass)**

### Key Technical Challenges
1. clap v4 does not natively support unknown flag collection
   - May need `Arg::allow_hyphen_values` or custom parser
   - Or use clap_lex for first pass
2. Extension loading needs config/paths from first pass
3. Extension flags need to be typed (string, bool, number per RegisterPayload)
4. Must not break existing tests

### Pi-Mono Reference
- Two-pass: legacy_pi_mono_code/pi-mono/packages/coding-agent/src/main.ts:463-516
- Flag collection: src/cli/args.ts:156-167
- Flag values to extensions: search for flagValues in src/core/extensions/runner.ts

### Acceptance Criteria
- Extensions can register flags via RegisterPayload
- Users can pass those flags on the command line
- Flag values are forwarded to extensions
- Unknown flags still produce errors
- Existing CLI behavior unchanged for known flags
- Tests cover flag pass-through end-to-end

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## Testing Requirements

### Unit Tests (tests/cli_extension_flags.rs)
1. **Known flags accepted**: pi --model gpt-4 still works as before
2. **Unknown flags rejected (no extensions)**: pi --bogus-flag errors with "unknown flag" (when no extension registers it)
3. **Extension flag registration**: Test extension registers --plan flag with type=string, verify it appears in extension flag registry
4. **Extension flag pass-through**: pi --plan "task" with test extension → extension receives flagValues.plan = "task"
5. **Extension boolean flag**: Extension registers --verbose-ext (boolean), pi --verbose-ext → flagValues.verbose_ext = true
6. **Extension number flag**: Extension registers --depth (number), pi --depth 5 → flagValues.depth = 5
7. **Multiple extension flags**: Two extensions each register different flags, both receive correct values
8. **Flag conflict**: Two extensions register same flag name → deterministic error or first-wins with warning

### E2E Tests (tests/e2e_cli_flags.rs)
9. **Full CLI round-trip**: Build pi binary, load test extension that registers --plan, run `pi --plan "hello" --no-tools --print` with VCR, verify extension receives flag value
10. **Help text**: pi --help includes dynamically registered extension flags in output
11. **Error message quality**: pi --unknown-flag shows helpful error mentioning available flags

### Structured Logging
- Each test logs: flags registered, argv used, flags parsed, flags delivered to extension, test verdict
- Extension flag registry snapshot logged before and after extension loading

title: Phase 1: Extension Corpus Validation and Inventory
description:
# Phase 1: Extension Corpus Validation and Inventory

## Purpose
Before testing ANY extension, we must VALIDATE it is actually a real pi extension. Our corpus of 1,167+ TS files includes:
- Genuine extensions (export default function with ExtensionAPI)
- Broken/incomplete extensions
- Non-extension TypeScript files (utilities, configs, tests)
- Files that import ExtensionAPI but are not entry points

We must build a VALIDATED MANIFEST that definitively says: these N extensions are real, loadable, and should be tested. Everything else is excluded.

## Validation Approach
1. Static analysis: scan for required patterns (export default, ExtensionAPI usage)
2. Dynamic validation: actually try loading each in pi-mono TS runtime
3. Classification: tag each by capability (tools, events, commands, UI, providers, etc.)
4. Manifest generation: JSON file mapping extension-id -> entry point, capabilities, tier

## Why Both Static AND Dynamic
Static analysis catches obvious non-extensions (no export default). But some extensions may have correct syntax yet fail to load (missing deps, runtime errors). Dynamic validation catches those. The TS runtime IS the validator -- if pi-mono can load it, it is a valid extension.

## Current Corpus Stats
- tests/ext_conformance/artifacts/ contains 1,167 TS files
- official-pi-mono: 60 dirs (76 TS files)
- community: 58 dirs
- npm: 63 dirs (67 packages)
- third-party: 23 dirs
- agents: 7 dirs

## Output
- tests/ext_conformance/VALIDATED_MANIFEST.json
- Includes: extension_id, entry_path, capabilities, tier, ts_load_status, error_if_any

title: Phase 6: Fix Runtime Bugs Discovered by Conformance Testing
description:
# Phase 6: Fix Runtime Bugs Discovered by Conformance Testing

## Purpose
Conformance testing WILL find bugs. This phase is dedicated to fixing them. Each bug discovered gets its own sub-task with the extension(s) that exposed it and a clear reproduction path.

## Expected Bug Categories

### Registration Mismatches
- Missing fields in tool/command/flag registration
- Type coercion differences (string vs number)
- Default value handling differences
- Array vs single value normalization

### Event Handler Differences
- Different event payload shapes
- Missing event types in Rust
- Handler return value interpretation differences
- Async handler timing differences

### Hostcall Implementation Gaps
- Missing hostcall methods
- Different error messages
- Different error types (string vs Error object)
- Missing capability checks

### Module Resolution Issues
- Import path resolution differences between swc/QuickJS and Bun/jiti
- Relative import handling
- node_modules resolution
- Package.json main/exports field handling

### TypeScript Compilation Issues
- swc vs jiti compilation differences
- Decorator handling
- Type-only imports
- Re-export patterns

## Bug Tracking
Each bug gets a child task with:
- Extension(s) that exposed it
- Expected output (from TS runtime)
- Actual output (from Rust runtime)
- Root cause analysis
- Fix description
- Regression test

## Acceptance Criteria
- All P0 bugs (from official extensions) fixed
- All P1 bugs (from community extensions) triaged
- Each fix has a regression test
- Conformance pass rate improves with each fix

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
IMPORTANT: Bug tasks will be created AS conformance testing discovers issues. This phase is intentionally left with no child tasks -- they will be added dynamically as Phase 4 and Phase 5 execute. Each bug task should include:
1. Extension(s) that exposed the bug
2. Expected output (TS runtime JSON)
3. Actual output (Rust runtime JSON)
4. Minimal diff showing the discrepancy
5. Root cause analysis
6. Fix description
7. Regression test (add to the extension's conformance test)

title: Random unproven extension trials (seeded): run N/A pool in Rust harness + gap intake
description:
# Goal
Take extensions that are currently **N/A (not yet tested in Rust)** and prove (or disprove) that they “just work” by running them **sight unseen** in the Rust conformance harness.

The key user requirement here is *randomness*: we should not cherry-pick. We want an unbiased sample that quickly surfaces systemic gaps (missing shims/hostcalls, resolver bugs, UI/session plumbing gaps, etc.).

# Background / Where “N/A” Comes From
- `tests/ext_conformance/VALIDATED_MANIFEST.json` contains the corpus.
- `tests/conformance_report.rs` generates:
  - `tests/ext_conformance/reports/CONFORMANCE_REPORT.md`
  - `tests/ext_conformance/reports/conformance_summary.json`
- An extension is “PASS” only when there is Rust evidence (fixtures, smoke logs, parity logs, load benchmarks).
- Many corpus entries are currently “N/A” in Rust, even though the TS oracle harness can load them.

# Scope
## 1. Deterministic randomness (so results are reproducible)
- Selection must be random but reproducible:
  - seed: `PI_EXT_RANDOM_SEED` (default fixed seed if unset)
  - sample size: `PI_EXT_RANDOM_N` (global or per-tier)
  - pool filter: default to Rust-“N/A” extensions, optionally restricted by tier/category.
- The exact selected list must be written to the run JSONL log as the first event.

## 2. Run strategy (minimal proof first)
We want the cheapest “does it load and register correctly?” proof before we invest in full per-extension fixtures.

Minimum per-extension run should capture:
- load time
- registration snapshot (tools/commands/flags/providers/hooks)
- capability manifest (declared + inferred)
- structured logs (`pi.ext.log.v1`)

## 3. Evidence + artifacts
Every run must write:
- JSONL log: `target/ext_conformance/logs/random_trials/<run_id>.jsonl`
- Deterministic artifact manifest (paths + checksums)
- Summary JSON for machine consumption:
  - pass/fail
  - failure reason classification
  - extracted missing shim/module names (when possible)

## 4. Gap intake (no duplicate beads)
For each failure, immediately do:
1. `br search` for the missing shim/hostcall/module name.
2. If an existing bead already covers it:
   - add a comment to the existing bead with:
     - extension id
     - failing import/hostcall

Completed bd-2fps.1.1: Deterministic extension selector for N/A pool.

## Implementation: tests/ext_conformance_selector.rs

### Core Components
- **SplitMix64 PRNG**: Self-contained deterministic 64-bit generator with rejection-sampled bounded values (no modulo bias)
- **ExtensionSelector**: Loads manifest + conformance events, identifies N/A pool
  - from_files(manifest_path, events_path) — loads real data
  - from_entries(entries, passed_ids) — for unit testing without filesystem
  - select(seed, sample_size, filter) — deterministic Fisher-Yates partial shuffle
- **SelectionFilter**: tier_range (inclusive min/max) + source_category
- **format_selection_log()**: JSON logging with schema pi.ext.trial_selection.v1

### Data Flow
1. Load VALIDATED_MANIFEST.json → 218 extensions
2. Load conformance_events.jsonl → partition by overall_status
3. N/A pool = entries where overall_status == 'N/A' (158 extensions)
4. Sort eligible by ID for determinism
5. Apply tier/source filters
6. Fisher-Yates partial shuffle with SplitMix64(seed)
7. Return first sample_size IDs

### Test Suite (12 tests)
- selector_deterministic_stability: same seed → identical results across runs
- selector_different_seeds: different seeds → different selections (sanity)
- selector_filter_by_tier: tier_range (1,2) selects only tiers 1-2
- selector_filter_by_source: source_category restricts to matching tier
- selector_combined_filter: tier + source together
- selector_sample_capped: sample_size > pool → returns full pool
- selector_empty_pool: all passed → empty selection
- selector_no_match_filter: nonexistent category → empty
- selector_no_duplicates: 50/100 selection has no duplicate IDs
- selector_log_format: JSON log has required schema fields
- selector_from_real_files: integration test with actual conformance data
- prng_distribution_sanity: 10K samples uniform across 10 buckets (< 30% deviation)

title: [AUTH-SPIKE] Research OAuth CLI feasibility for OpenAI and Google providers
description:
## Problem

AUTH-1 and AUTH-2 assume OpenAI and Google have publicly documented CLI OAuth flows, but this has not been verified. This research spike must complete BEFORE any implementation begins.

## Research Questions

### OpenAI
1. Does OpenAI expose a public OAuth2 authorization endpoint for CLI tools?
2. What is the client_id? Is there a registered public CLI client?
3. Does OpenAI support PKCE flow? Or only device_code?
4. Are the endpoints at auth0.openai.com still valid?
5. What scopes are needed for API access?
6. **Key question**: Or does OpenAI only support API key auth for CLI tools (no OAuth)?

### Google (Gemini)
1. Does Google AI Studio / Gemini require OAuth, or is API key sufficient?
2. If OAuth: what scopes grant generative-language API access?
3. Is there a public CLI client_id, or must each project register its own?
4. Does gcloud auth application-default login suffice instead of custom OAuth?
5. Is the generative-language scope available without Google Cloud project setup?

## Expected Outcomes

One of:
- **Feasible**: Document exact endpoints, client_id, scopes, flow type for each provider. Unblock AUTH-1/AUTH-2.
- **Partially feasible**: Only one provider supports CLI OAuth. Adjust scope of AUTH track.
- **Not feasible**: Both providers use API keys only. Pivot AUTH-1/AUTH-2 to API key setup UX instead of OAuth, or remove them.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Written summary of findings for OpenAI OAuth feasibility
- [ ] Written summary of findings for Google/Gemini OAuth feasibility
- [ ] Decision: proceed with OAuth, pivot to API keys, or remove beads
- [ ] Update AUTH-1 and AUTH-2 descriptions based on findings

## Files
- No code changes -- research only
notes:
2026-02-13 research findings (primary-source docs):

OpenAI:
- OpenAI API auth docs state API requests use API keys via `Authorization: Bearer OPENAI_API_KEY`.
- Quickstart/docs/libraries pages consistently instruct API-key setup (`OPENAI_API_KEY`), with no public OpenAI API OAuth client registration flow for CLI tools.
- OAuth docs found are for GPT Actions (connecting ChatGPT actions to third-party APIs), where the developer supplies OAuth client_id/secret + auth/token URLs for their own external API. This is not an OAuth flow for authenticating to OpenAI API itself.

Google/Gemini:
- Gemini API reference states API requests use `x-goog-api-key` and positions API key as the standard auth path.
- Gemini OAuth quickstart explicitly says API key is the easiest method; OAuth is optional for stricter controls.
- OAuth quickstart requires user/project setup in Google Cloud: enable API, OAuth consent screen, create Desktop OAuth client, and run `gcloud auth application-default login --client-id-file ...` (or equivalent credential management in-app).
- This implies there is no single public built-in Gemini CLI client_id suitable for hardcoding in pi_agent_rust.

Decision for AUTH track:
- Pivot AUTH-1 and AUTH-2 away from built-in OpenAI/Google OAuth constants.
- Make `/login openai` and `/login google|gemini` API-key-first UX tasks.
- If OAuth is pursued later for Google, it should be BYO client credentials/ADC guidance, not hardcoded shared secrets in repo.

Sources:
- OpenAI API reference (Authentication): https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference
- OpenAI quickstart auth: https://platform.openai.com/docs/quickstart/authentication
- OpenAI production best practices (API keys): https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/production-best-practices/setting-up-your-organization
- OpenAI GPT Actions auth (OAuth is for actions to third-party APIs): https://platform.openai.com/docs/actions/authentication
- Gemini API reference (Authentication): https://ai.google.dev/api
- Gemini OAuth quickstart: https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/oauth
- Gemini API key setup/security: https://ai.google.dev/tutorials/setup

title: [MOCK-CODE-FINDER] Replace hostcall io_uring delegated-fast-path placeholder with real executor or disable lane
description:
# Finding
A production mock-code-finder pass found that src/hostcall_io_uring_lane.rs can select HostcallDispatchLane::IoUring, but src/extension_dispatcher.rs dispatch_hostcall_io_uring still delegates to dispatch_hostcall_fast and emits fallback_reason io_uring_bridge_delegated_fast_path. The code comment says submission/completion wiring is introduced incrementally until the ring executor lands. br search found no existing bead for io_uring, iouring, hostcall io, or ring executor.

# Why this matters
README and runtime docs discuss io_uring lane policy and hostcall dispatch optimization. A policy-only lane that can select io_uring while execution stays on the fast path risks misleading telemetry and operator tuning under large swarm workloads. If the real ring executor is not ready, the lane should fail closed or remain explicitly advisory rather than appearing as an executed io_uring path.

# Desired outcome
Pick one truth-preserving path and complete it end to end:
- Implement a real io_uring-backed execution bridge for the bounded hostcall classes the policy allows, with cancellation, queue-depth enforcement, telemetry, and deterministic fallback to fast or compat lanes when the ring is unavailable.
- Or, if real ring execution is not ready, change the policy/config/telemetry so HostcallDispatchLane::IoUring cannot be selected as an execution lane and the output clearly reports advisory-only or unavailable status.

# Test obligations
Add regression coverage that proves enabled+ring_available+io-heavy filesystem/network hostcalls either use a real executor path with non-placeholder telemetry or fail closed to a non-io_uring lane with an explicit reason. Include negative controls for forced compat kill switch, ring unavailable, queue-depth budget exceeded, cancellation before dispatch/completion, and unsupported capabilities.

# Validation
Use rch for any cargo-heavy work. Minimum expected proof: cargo fmt --check, focused tests for hostcall_io_uring_lane and extension_dispatcher telemetry, cargo check --all-targets and clippy via rch if Rust code changes, staged UBS or staged-delta gate, and ./scripts/reconcile_beads_ledger.sh.

# Claim boundary
Do not use this bead to make release-facing performance or capacity claims. Any new telemetry is advisory until backed by benchmark evidence and claim-integrity gates.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## FUZZ-P3: Phase 3 — Continuous Fuzzing CI Integration

### Strategy
Phase 3 turns fuzzing from a manual activity into an automated, continuous process. The goal is that every push to main gets 60 seconds of fuzz testing per target, and nightly runs provide deep 30-minute sessions for the highest-priority targets.

### Components
1. **P3.1: GitHub Actions Workflow** — Runs fuzz targets in CI with matrix parallelism
2. **P3.2: Crash Corpus Management** — Systematic triage, minimization, and storage of crash inputs
3. **P3.3: Coverage Dashboard** — Track which code paths fuzzing exercises (nice-to-have)
4. **P3.4: Regression Test Generation** — Convert fixed crashes into permanent regression tests

### Dependency Chain
P3.1 (CI workflow) → P3.2 (crash management) → P3.4 (regression tests)
P3.1 (CI workflow) → P3.3 (coverage dashboard)

### Key Design Principles
1. **Fast feedback on PRs**: Quick fuzz runs (60s) should not block PR merges
2. **Deep exploration nightly**: Extended runs find deeper bugs
3. **Corpus persistence**: GitHub Actions cache preserves fuzzing progress across runs
4. **Crash-to-test pipeline**: Every crash becomes a permanent regression test
5. **Coverage awareness**: Know which code paths are NOT being fuzzed

### Prerequisites
- All Phase 2 harnesses must be complete and passing
- Seed corpora must be committed
- fuzz/ directory must be fully set up

### Definition of Done
- GitHub Actions workflow running on every push + nightly schedule
- At least one crash has been walked through the full triage-to-regression pipeline
- Coverage report available for at least one target
- Documentation in fuzz/README.md covers the full workflow

title: Spec: Unified JS+WASM capability model
description:
# Goal
Define a **single, coherent capability model** that applies equally to JS (PiJS) and WASM extensions, so security policy, logs, and tooling are identical across runtimes.

# Why
- Avoid divergent permission semantics between JS and WASM.
- Enable shared tooling (manifests, scanners, audit logs) and a consistent user mental model.
- JS-tier may execute wasm via PiWasm bridge (bd-1ry); capability semantics must remain identical.

# Scope / Deliverables
- Capability taxonomy: common names, scopes, and semantics across JS/WASM.
- Hostcall mapping: how JS `pi.*` calls and WASM hostcalls map to the same capabilities.
- Manifest alignment: how a single manifest expresses capabilities for both runtimes.
- Logging schema alignment: identical fields and redaction rules.

# Constraints
- Must compose with `bd-37z` ABI.
- Must be compatible with WASM host (`bd-nom`) and JS runtime (`bd-123`).

# Tests This Enables
- Cross-runtime capability conformance tests.
- E2E security suite verifying identical enforcement paths.

title: Extension UI protocol integration (interactive + RPC)
description:
# Background
- Legacy spec defines `extension_ui_request` / `extension_ui_response` covering: `confirm`, `select`, `input`, `editor`, plus fire-and-forget notifications.
- `src/extensions.rs` already has:
  - `ExtensionUiRequest` + `ExtensionUiResponse` types
  - `ExtensionManager::{request_ui, respond_ui}` with timeout support
- `src/interactive.rs` already has an extension UI queue and an interactive handler (`handle_extension_ui_request`).

# Gap (Observed)
- RPC mode is not end-to-end:
  - `src/rpc.rs` accepts a command `extension_ui_response` but **does not route** the response to the extension runtime.
  - RPC mode **never emits** `extension_ui_request` events, so headless controllers cannot respond.
- Runtime dispatch is not guaranteed to be expressed via the unified Hostcall ABI taxonomy/logging. The UI surface must converge on the `host_call` / `host_result` contract (bd-1uy.1.*), not grow its own ad-hoc error mapping.

# Goal
Make extension UI requests work end-to-end in **both**:
- interactive TUI mode
- RPC mode (stdin/stdout protocol)

and ensure the behavior is:
- deterministic (queueing + ordering)
- capability/policy compatible
- taxonomy-correct (`timeout|denied|io|invalid_request|internal`)
- observable (structured logs, redaction rules)

# Scope / Deliverables
1) **Contract + normalization**
- Enumerate the supported UI methods and their payload shapes (defaults, required fields, cancel semantics).
- Define response normalization rules so JS + WASM + protocol adapter behave identically.

2) **Interactive integration**
- Ensure each UI method renders with clear provenance:
  - show extension id/name
  - show requested method
  - show timeout/cancel affordance
- Ensure queue semantics are sane:
  - one active request at a time
  - bounded queue
  - cancellation does not deadlock

3) **RPC integration**
- Emit `extension_ui_request` events on stdout.
- Accept `extension_ui_response` commands on stdin.
- Enforce request/response id matching, timeouts, and cancellation.

4) **Conformance + E2E**
- Add conformance fixtures for each method + edge cases (timeout, cancel, invalid payloads).
- Add E2E scenarios that exercise UI via:
  - interactive tmux capture
  - RPC controller script
- All scenarios emit detailed JSONL logs + deterministic artifact indexes per bd-4u9.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] A sample extension can invoke confirm/select/input/editor and receive responses in both interactive + RPC modes.
- [ ] RPC emits `extension_ui_request` and routes `extension_ui_response` back into the runtime.
- [ ] Timeouts and cancellation propagate correctly without deadlocks.
- [ ] Error mapping uses only hostcall taxonomy codes.
- [ ] Fixtures pass and logs are deterministic.
- [ ] Quality gates pass: cargo fmt --check, cargo check --all-targets, cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings, cargo test.

[ ] Scope in description implemented fully with no feature loss

title: Spec: Extension UI API contract (methods, payloads, defaults, errors)
description:
# Goal
Define the *exact* extension UI contract, spec-first, so both interactive + RPC implementations can be correct and deterministic.

# Background
- The runtime uses `ExtensionUiRequest` / `ExtensionUiResponse` (host <-> UI surface).
- Legacy extensions expect stable method names + payload shapes.
- If we get payload defaults/cancel semantics wrong, extensions will subtly break.

# Scope
- Enumerate supported `method` values (minimum):
  - `confirm`
  - `select`
  - `input`
  - `editor`
  - `notify` (fire-and-forget)
- For each method, define:
  - required fields
  - optional fields + default values
  - validation rules and `invalid_request` mapping
  - response shape (`value` vs `cancelled`)
  - timeout semantics (`payload.timeout` vs hostcall timeout vs global budget)
  - cancellation semantics (user cancel, timeout cancel, shutdown)
  - deterministic redaction rules (never log raw secrets)

# Deliverables
- A written spec in this bead that is detailed enough to implement without re-reading legacy markdown.
- A mapping table:
  - `ExtensionUiRequest` <-> RPC `extension_ui_request` event shape
  - RPC `extension_ui_response` command <-> `ExtensionUiResponse`

# Implementation Notes
- Prefer a single normalized payload per method so interactive and RPC share the same validation/normalization code.
- IDs:
  - `request.id` MUST be stable and round-tripped; it is the correlation key for queueing, logs, and timeouts.

# Tests
- Add unit tests for request validation + normalization once the contract is finalized (implementation lives in follow-up beads; this bead is spec-only).
acceptance_criteria:
[ ] Spec is complete enough to implement without consulting legacy docs
[ ] Every method has explicit required/optional fields + defaults + validation rules
[ ] Response shapes and cancellation semantics are fully specified
[ ] RPC mapping is explicitly defined and unambiguous
