## Implementation Details: Missing Asset File Fallback

### The Problem
Some extensions call `readFileSync()` on asset files (HTML templates, CSS themes,
config files) that are bundled alongside the extension source. When we load the
extension from the conformance corpus, these files may not exist because we only
have the .ts/.js source files.

### Affected Extensions
- nicobailon-interview-tool: reads form/index.html, form/styles.css, form/script.js,
  form/themes/*.css (7 files total)
- Any extension that bundles static assets alongside source

### Current Manual Fix
Created all 7 files under `tests/ext_conformance/artifacts/community/nicobailon-interview-tool/form/`
with minimal stub content (empty HTML, empty CSS, empty JS).

### Auto-Repair Implementation

Location: `__pi_host_read_file_sync` in `src/extensions_js.rs`

When a read fails with ENOENT AND the requested path is within the extension's
own directory tree:
```rust
// In __pi_host_read_file_sync, after file open fails:
if error.kind() == io::ErrorKind::NotFound {
    if let Some(repair_config) = &repair_config {
        if repair_config.missing_asset && is_within_extension_dir(path, extension_root) {
            emit_repair_event(RepairPattern::MissingAsset, path, "<empty>");
            return Ok(String::new()); // Return empty string
        }
    }
}
```

### Content Heuristics (Optional Enhancement)
For known file types, return type-appropriate empty content:
- `.html` → `<!DOCTYPE html><html><body></body></html>`
- `.css` → (empty string)
- `.js` → `// auto-generated stub`
- `.json` → `{}`
- `.toml`/`.yaml`/`.yml` → (empty string)
- Everything else → (empty string)

Start with plain empty string for all types. Add type-specific content only if
test failures reveal that extensions check for valid HTML structure, etc.

### Security Constraints
- CRITICAL: Only return empty content for paths WITHIN the extension's own directory
- Never apply this fallback for paths outside the extension root
- Never apply for system paths (`/etc/`, `/usr/`, `/home/`, etc.)
- The `is_within_extension_dir()` check must canonicalize to prevent traversal attacks
  (`../../etc/passwd` must NOT get empty-string treatment)

### Testing
- Unit: read missing file inside extension dir → returns empty string
- Unit: read missing file OUTSIDE extension dir → returns original error
- Unit: read file that EXISTS → returns real content (repair does NOT activate)
- Unit: path traversal attempt → returns error, NOT empty string
- Unit: repair_config.missing_asset = false → returns original error
- Integration: load nicobailon-interview-tool WITHOUT manual form/ stubs → succeeds

title: Pattern 3: stub generation for monorepo sibling module imports
description:
## Problem

Extensions from monorepos import shared modules via relative paths that escape
the extension's own directory:

    import { foo, bar } from "../../shared";

In the original monorepo, this resolves to a sibling package.  In our flat
artifact layout, it resolves to a path outside the extension directory, and
no file exists there.

### Real examples
- community/qualisero-background-notify: \`import { ... 17 items } from "../../shared"\`
- community/qualisero-safe-git: \`import { ... 12 items } from "../../shared"\`
- npm/aliou-pi-processes: \`import { ProcessesComponent } from "../components/processes-component"\`

We manually created stub files at the resolved locations, but this is fragile
and doesn't scale to new extensions.

## Solution

This is the most complex pattern because we need to:
1. Detect that a relative import escapes the extension root
2. Determine what named exports the importing module needs
3. Generate a stub module with those exports

### Phase A: Detect escape

In \`PiJsResolver::resolve()\`, after \`resolve_module_path()\` returns None
for a relative specifier:

```rust
if specifier.starts_with("..") {
    let resolved = base_dir.join(specifier);
    let canonical = resolved.canonicalize().ok()
        .or_else(|| resolved.parent()?.canonicalize().ok());
    if let Some(canon) = canonical {
        if !canon.starts_with(&extension_root) {
            // Monorepo escape detected
        }
    }
}
```

### Phase B: Extract needed exports

Read the importing file's source, scan for the import statement, and extract
the named imports.  We already have TypeScript transpilation — we can parse
the import declaration to get the list.

A simpler approach: use a regex on the raw source to extract names from:
    import { name1, name2, type Name3 } from "../../shared"

Type-only imports can be ignored (they're erased at transpile time).
Value imports get stub implementations.

### Phase C: Generate stub module

Create an in-memory virtual module (no filesystem write) that exports:
- Functions → \`export function name() {}\`
- Constants → \`export const NAME = undefined;\`  (or smart defaults based on name)
- Classes → \`export class Name {}\`

The stub is registered as a virtual module keyed by the resolved absolute path.

```rust
// In the resolver, when escape is detected:
let stub_source = generate_import_stub(base_file_path, specifier);
self.state.borrow_mut().virtual_modules.insert(
    resolved_path.to_string_lossy().to_string(),
    stub_source,
);
return Ok(resolved_path.to_string_lossy().to_string());
```

## Security Analysis

- SAFE: No filesystem access is granted.  The stub module is generated
  in-memory from the importing file's source (which we already read).
- Stub exports are no-op functions/empty values — they can't perform
  any privileged operations.
- The resolved path is never read from disk — only the virtual module
  is loaded.

## Heuristics for smart stubs

Based on analysis of the actual qualisero shared module:
- Names starting with \`is\` → \`export function isX() { return false; }\`
- Names starting with \`check\`/\`has\` → \`export function checkX() { return false; }\`
- Names starting with \`get\` → \`export function getX() { return {}; }\`
- Names starting with \`detect\` → \`export function detectX() { return {}; }\`
- Names in ALL_CAPS → \`export const NAME = [];\`
- Names starting with uppercase → \`export class Name {}\` or type (skip)
- Everything else → \`export function name() {}\`

## Testing

1. Unit test: detect monorepo escape (path resolves outside extension root)
2. Unit test: extract import names from TS import statement
3. Unit test: generate stub with correct exports for function-like names
4. Unit test: generate stub with correct exports for CONSTANT names
5. Unit test: type-only imports are excluded from stub
6. Unit test: repair event emitted with MonorepoEscape pattern
7. Integration: qualisero-background-notify loads without manual shared/ stub
8. Integration: qualisero-safe-git loads without manual shared/ stub
9. Regression: all 223 extensions still pass

## Complexity Note

This is the most complex pattern because it requires source analysis.  However,
the regex approach is sufficient — we don't need a full TypeScript parser.  The
import syntax is regular enough that a well-crafted regex handles 99%+ of cases.

## Estimated Effort: 3-4 hours

## Files to Modify
- src/extensions_js.rs (PiJsResolver::resolve, new generate_import_stub fn)

## Dependencies
- Requires bd-k5q5.8.1 (logging infrastructure) for repair event emission
- Should come after bd-k5q5.8.2 (dist→src) and bd-k5q5.8.3 (missing assets)
  because those are simpler and can be shipped independently

comments.text:
## Implementation Details: Monorepo Sibling Module Stubs

### The Problem
Extensions authored in monorepos import shared modules using relative paths that
escape their own directory: `../../shared/index.ts`, `../common/utils.ts`, etc.
When loaded standalone, these paths resolve to nonexistent locations outside the
extension's artifact directory.

### Affected Extensions
- qualisero-background-notify: imports from `../../shared` (17 exports)
- qualisero-safe-git: imports from `../../shared`
- aliou-pi-processes: imports from sibling `./constants`, `./utils` (within same package,
  but the package was missing these files)

### Current Manual Fix
Created `tests/ext_conformance/artifacts/shared/index.ts` with 17 stub exports
matching what the qualisero extensions expect (getBackgroundNotifyConfig, playBeep,
detectTerminalInfo, isTerminalInBackground, BEEP_SOUNDS, etc.).

### Auto-Repair Implementation

This is the most complex pattern. The approach is a TWO-PHASE strategy:

**Phase A: Import Analysis** (at load time, before execution)
1. When `resolve()` encounters a relative path that escapes the extension root:
   - `path.starts_with("..")` or resolved path is outside extension_root
2. Analyze the importing file to find what names are imported:
   - Quick regex scan for `import { X, Y, Z } from '../../shared'`
   - Or `const { X, Y } = require('../../shared')`
3. Generate a synthetic module that exports no-op stubs for each name

**Phase B: Synthetic Module Generation**
```javascript
// Auto-generated stub for monorepo escape: ../../shared
export const getBackgroundNotifyConfig = () => ({});
export const playBeep = () => {};
export const detectTerminalInfo = () => ({ isBackground: false });
// ... one export per imported name
```

For unknown exports, generate:
- `const` exports → empty object `{}`
- Function-looking names (verbs: get, set, play, detect, is, has, create) → `() => {}`
- UPPER_CASE names → empty object (likely constants)
- Type-only imports → skip (TypeScript strips them at compile time)

### Implementation Location
`PiJsResolver::resolve()` in `src/extensions_js.rs`:
```rust
if repair_config.monorepo_escape {
    if let Some(escape_info) = detect_monorepo_escape(specifier, referrer, extension_root) {
        let imports = analyze_imports(referrer_source, specifier);
        let stub_source = generate_monorepo_stub(&imports);
        let virtual_path = format!("pijs-repair://{}/{}", extension_id, specifier);
        register_dynamic_virtual_module(virtual_path, stub_source);
        emit_repair_event(RepairPattern::MonorepoEscape, specifier, &virtual_path);
        return Ok(virtual_path);
    }
}
```

### Why This Depends on Patterns 1 and 2
Pattern 3 can trigger AFTER Pattern 1 (the src/ fallback might reveal new imports
that escape the monorepo). It also shares the fallback-within-extension-dir logic
with Pattern 2. Building on those foundations avoids duplication.

### Security Notes
- Generated stubs contain ONLY no-op values — no code execution
- Stubs are registered as virtual modules, never written to disk
- The import analysis is read-only regex matching on already-loaded source
- No network access, no arbitrary file reads

### Testing
- Unit: detect escape path `../../shared` → recognized as monorepo escape
- Unit: analyze_imports extracts correct names from import statement
- Unit: generate_monorepo_stub creates valid JS for function/const/type exports
- Unit: normal relative import `./utils` NOT treated as monorepo escape
- Integration: load qualisero-background-notify WITHOUT shared/ stub → succeeds via repair

Removed dependencies on bd-k5q5.8.2 (dist→src) and bd-k5q5.8.3 (missing asset).

Rationale: The monorepo escape pattern is conceptually independent. It detects when

No shared utility functions, no shared state. The only valid dependency is .8.1

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## Import Analysis Regex Patterns (Detailed Specification)

The import analysis needs to handle all common import syntaxes. Here are the exact
regex patterns to implement and test:

### ESM Import Patterns

**1. Named imports**: `import { X, Y, Z } from '../../shared'`
```regex
import\s*\{([^}]+)\}\s*from\s*['"]SPECIFIER['"]
```
Capture group 1 contains comma-separated names. Split by comma, trim whitespace.
Skip names prefixed with `type ` (TypeScript type-only imports).

**2. Default import**: `import X from '../../shared'`
```regex
import\s+(\w+)\s+from\s*['"]SPECIFIER['"]
```
Generate: `export default function() {}` (if name is lowercase) or `export default class Name {}` (if uppercase).

**3. Namespace import**: `import * as X from '../../shared'`
```regex
import\s*\*\s*as\s+(\w+)\s+from\s*['"]SPECIFIER['"]
```
Generate: `const X = {}; export default X; export { X };`

**4. Side-effect import**: `import '../../shared'`
```regex
import\s+['"]SPECIFIER['"]
```
Generate: empty module (`// auto-repair stub`).

**5. Mixed**: `import X, { Y, Z } from '../../shared'`
```regex
import\s+(\w+)\s*,\s*\{([^}]+)\}\s*from\s*['"]SPECIFIER['"]
```
Handle both default and named.

### CJS Require Patterns

**6. Destructured require**: `const { X, Y } = require('../../shared')`
```regex
(?:const|let|var)\s*\{([^}]+)\}\s*=\s*require\s*\(['"]SPECIFIER['"]\)
```

**7. Default require**: `const X = require('../../shared')`
```regex
(?:const|let|var)\s+(\w+)\s*=\s*require\s*\(['"]SPECIFIER['"]\)
```

### TypeScript Type-Only Import Filtering

In named imports, skip entries that start with `type `:
`import { type Foo, bar, type Baz } from '../../shared'`
→ Only generate stubs for `bar`, skip `Foo` and `Baz`.

Also skip entire type-only imports:
`import type { Foo } from '../../shared'`
→ Generate empty module (types are erased at compile time).

### Specifier Matching

The SPECIFIER in all patterns must be escaped for regex matching. Since specifiers
often contain `..`, use `regex::escape(specifier)` when building the pattern.

### Multi-Line Imports

Some extensions split imports across lines:
```typescript
import {
    foo,
    bar,
    baz,
} from '../../shared';
```

Use `(?s)` (DOTALL) mode or match `[^}]+` which captures newlines.

### Implementation

```rust
fn analyze_imports(source: &str, specifier: &str) -> Vec<ImportedName> {
    let escaped = regex::escape(specifier);
    let mut names = Vec::new();

    // Pattern 1: named imports
    let re = Regex::new(&format\!(
        r#"import\s*\{{([^}}]+)\}}\s*from\s*['"]{}['"]"#,
        escaped
    )).unwrap();
    if let Some(caps) = re.captures(source) {
        for name in caps[1].split(',') {
            let name = name.trim();
            if name.starts_with("type ") { continue; }  // skip type imports
            if let Some(alias) = name.split(" as ").next() {
                names.push(classify_import(alias.trim()));
            }
        }
    }

    // Pattern 2: default import
    // ... similar for each pattern

    names
}

enum ImportedName {
    Function(String),   // lowercase starting names
    Constant(String),   // UPPER_CASE names
    Class(String),      // PascalCase names
    Default(String),    // default import
    Namespace(String),  // namespace import
}
```

title: Pattern 4: proxy-based universal stubs for missing npm dependencies
description:
## Problem

Extensions import npm packages that aren't in our virtual module registry.
Currently we have ~30 hand-written virtual module stubs (openai, adm-zip,
linkedom, p-limit, etc.) but new extensions will always bring new dependencies.

### Real examples of packages we had to stub
- openai, adm-zip, linkedom, p-limit, unpdf
- @sourcegraph/scip-typescript, @sourcegraph/scip-python
- @marckrenn/pi-sub-shared
- @aliou/pi-utils-settings, @aliou/sh
- node-pty, chokidar, jsdom, @mozilla/readability, beautiful-mermaid, turndown

Each required a hand-written stub.  The Proxy approach can cover the long tail
of packages that don't need functional behavior — just need to not crash.

## Solution

When a bare package specifier fails resolution (not in virtual_modules, not a
node: builtin), instead of immediately throwing, generate a Proxy-based stub
that silently absorbs all property accesses and function calls:

```javascript
// Generated universal stub module:
const _noop = () => {};
const handler = {
    get(target, prop) {
        if (typeof prop === 'symbol') return undefined;
        if (prop === '__esModule') return true;
        if (prop === 'default') return target;
        return new Proxy(_noop, handler);
    },
    apply() { return new Proxy({}, handler); },
    construct() { return new Proxy({}, handler); },
};
const stub = new Proxy(_noop, handler);
export default stub;
// Re-export as both default and named 'default'
export { stub as __pijs_proxy_stub };
```

### Allowlist approach

NOT all packages should get proxy stubs.  We need an allowlist strategy:

**Always allow** (safe — these are utility/UI packages):
- @sourcegraph/*, @marckrenn/*, @aliou/*
- Packages matching extension author's scope (e.g., if extension is from
  @foo, allow @foo/* packages)

**Never allow** (dangerous — could mask security-critical failures):
- node:*, fs, child_process, net, http, https, crypto (already handled)
- Any package that provides system access

**Conditional allow** (based on extension tier):
- Tier 1-2 (official): Never use proxy stubs — these should always work
- Tier 3-5 (community/npm): Allow proxy stubs with logging

### Implementation

In \`PiJsResolver::resolve()\`:

```rust
// After checking virtual_modules and resolve_module_path:
if is_bare_specifier(spec) && !is_node_builtin(spec) {
    if should_auto_stub_package(spec, extension_tier) {
        let stub = generate_proxy_stub_module(spec);
        self.state.borrow_mut().virtual_modules.insert(
            spec.to_string(),
            stub,
        );
        // TODO: emit RepairEvent(MissingNpmDep)
        return Ok(spec.to_string());
    }
}
```

## Security Analysis

- SAFE for utility packages: Proxy stubs return no-op values, granting
  no system access.
- RISKY for system packages: That's why we have the allowlist.  System
  packages (fs, net, child_process) are NEVER auto-stubbed.
- The proxy can't perform I/O, spawn processes, or access the filesystem.
  It can only return empty/no-op values.
- All proxy activations are logged, so we can audit what fired.

## Key Trade-off

Proxy stubs make extensions "load" but their functionality may be degraded.
This is acceptable for conformance testing (we just need the extension to
register its commands/tools/hooks).  For production use, we'd want the
real packages installed.  The repair event logging makes this transparent.

## Testing

1. Unit test: proxy stub absorbs property access chains
2. Unit test: proxy stub absorbs function calls
3. Unit test: proxy stub absorbs constructor calls
4. Unit test: allowlist blocks system packages

comments.text:
## Implementation Details: Proxy-Based Universal npm Stubs

### The Problem
Extensions import npm packages that aren't in our virtual module registry. Unlike
system modules (node:fs, node:path) which we shim carefully, these are third-party
packages that the extension uses for non-critical functionality (UI components,
utility libraries, optional integrations).

### Affected Extensions
- marckrenn-pi-sub-core: imports `@marckrenn/pi-sub-shared` (custom package)
- scip-python extensions: import `@sourcegraph/scip-python`
- Various npm-registry extensions importing uncommon packages

### Current Manual Fix
Added 16+ entries in `default_virtual_modules()` HashMap, each with hand-written
stub implementations. Examples:
- `@marckrenn/pi-sub-shared`: PROVIDERS array, MODEL_MULTIPLIERS, PROVIDER_METADATA
- `@sourcegraph/scip-python`: empty class exports
- `node-pty`, `chokidar`, `jsdom`, etc.

### Auto-Repair Implementation

Instead of hand-writing stubs for every possible package, use JavaScript Proxy
objects to create universal no-op modules that respond to any property access:

```javascript
// Universal proxy stub template
const handler = {
    get(target, prop) {
        if (prop === Symbol.toPrimitive) return () => '';
        if (prop === 'default') return target;
        if (prop === '__esModule') return true;
        // Return a callable proxy for any property access
        return new Proxy(function(){}, handler);
    },
    apply() { return new Proxy({}, handler); },
    construct() { return new Proxy({}, handler); },
};
export default new Proxy({}, handler);
export const __esModule = true;
```

This proxy auto-responds to:
- `import { anything } from 'unknown-pkg'` → returns a proxy
- `anything()` → returns a proxy (callable)
- `new anything()` → returns a proxy (constructable)
- `anything.nested.deep.access` → returns a proxy
- `String(anything)` → returns ''

### Allowlist Strategy
NOT all missing packages get proxy treatment. Only packages matching:
1. Scoped packages from known authors: `@aliou/*`, `@marckrenn/*`, `@sourcegraph/*`
2. Known utility packages: `node-pty`, `chokidar`, `jsdom`, `turndown`
3. Generic pattern: any `@*/pi-*` scoped package (Pi extension ecosystem)

NEVER proxy:
- `node:*` built-in modules (these need real shims)
- `fs`, `path`, `child_process` etc. (bare node built-ins)
- Packages known to have security-sensitive APIs

### Implementation Location
`PiJsResolver::resolve()` in `src/extensions_js.rs`:
```rust
if repair_config.npm_proxy {
    if is_bare_specifier(specifier) && !is_virtual_module(specifier) {
        if matches_npm_proxy_allowlist(specifier) {
            let stub = generate_proxy_stub(specifier);
            let virtual_path = format!("pijs-npm-proxy://{}", specifier);
            register_dynamic_virtual_module(virtual_path, stub);
            emit_repair_event(RepairPattern::NpmProxy, specifier, &virtual_path);
            return Ok(virtual_path);
        }
    }
}
```

### Interaction with Existing Virtual Modules
The proxy only activates AFTER checking `default_virtual_modules()`. If a hand-written
stub exists, it takes priority. This means:
1. We keep the well-tested hand-written stubs for important packages
2. Proxy handles the long tail of rare/unknown packages
3. Over time, if a proxy stub proves insufficient, we promote it to a real stub

### Security Notes
- Proxy stubs execute NO code — they just return proxy objects
- The allowlist prevents abuse (can't proxy `fs` or `child_process`)
- Proxies don't have access to the host runtime — they're pure JS objects
- All proxy activations are logged as repair events

### Testing
- Unit: bare import of allowlisted package → gets proxy stub
- Unit: bare import of blocked package → returns error
- Unit: proxy.anything() → returns proxy (callable)
- Unit: proxy.anything.deep.nested → returns proxy (nestable)
- Unit: String(proxy) → returns '' (toPrimitive works)
- Unit: existing virtual module NOT replaced by proxy
- Integration: load extension with rare npm dep → succeeds via proxy

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## QuickJS Proxy Edge Cases (Critical for Testing)

JavaScript Proxy in QuickJS has subtle behaviors that MUST be tested:

1. **typeof proxy** — If the Proxy target is a function, `typeof` returns 'function'.
   This is important because extensions may do `typeof dep.someMethod === 'function'`
   before calling it. Our proxy stub uses a function target so this works, but VERIFY.

2. **JSON.stringify(proxy)** — Can throw TypeError if the proxy handler doesn't implement
   `ownKeys` and `getOwnPropertyDescriptor`. We need to either:
   - Add these traps to the handler, OR
   - Accept that JSON.stringify on a proxy throws (and document it)
   Best approach: add `ownKeys` returning `[]` and `getOwnPropertyDescriptor` returning
   `undefined` so that `JSON.stringify` returns `{}`.

3. **Spread operator** — `{...proxy}` calls `ownKeys` + `getOwnPropertyDescriptor`.
   Same fix as JSON.stringify.

4. **Array.isArray(proxy)** — Always returns `false` for Proxy objects (spec behavior).
   Extensions checking `Array.isArray(dep.someList)` will get `false`. This is acceptable
   but should be documented.

5. **for..of iteration** — `for (const x of proxy)` tries `Symbol.iterator`. Our handler's
   `get` trap returns a proxy for all property access including symbols. Need to ensure:
   - `Symbol.iterator` returns something that doesn't infinite-loop
   - Best: return a function that returns `{ next: () => ({ done: true }) }`
   - Or catch and return empty iterator

6. **Promise.resolve(proxy)** — QuickJS may treat this differently than V8. Test it.

7. **Equality checks** — `proxy === proxy` is `true` (same ref), but
   `proxy.foo === proxy.foo` is `false` (new proxy each time). Extensions
   doing identity checks on imports will fail. Acceptable trade-off.

### Recommended Handler (Revised)

```javascript
const handler = {
    get(target, prop) {
        if (typeof prop === 'symbol') {
            if (prop === Symbol.toPrimitive) return () => '';
            if (prop === Symbol.iterator) return function*() {};
            if (prop === Symbol.toStringTag) return 'ProxyStub';
            return undefined;
        }
        if (prop === '__esModule') return true;
        if (prop === 'default') return target;
        if (prop === 'then') return undefined; // prevent Promise unwrapping
        return new Proxy(function(){}, handler);
    },
    apply() { return new Proxy(function(){}, handler); },
    construct() { return new Proxy(function(){}, handler); },
    ownKeys() { return []; },
    getOwnPropertyDescriptor() { return undefined; },
    has() { return false; },
};
```

Key additions from original:
- **Symbol.iterator** → generator that yields nothing (prevents infinite loops)
- **Symbol.toStringTag** → 'ProxyStub' (for debugging)
- **then: undefined** → prevents Promise.resolve from treating proxy as thenable
- **ownKeys/getOwnPropertyDescriptor** → makes JSON.stringify and spread safe
- **has** → makes `'prop' in proxy` return false (clean behavior)

comments.text:
## Allowlist Design: Configurable, Not Just Hardcoded

The allowlist should be implemented as a layered system:

### Layer 1: Hardcoded Denylist (never overridable)
```rust
const NEVER_PROXY: &[&str] = &[
    "fs", "path", "os", "child_process", "net", "http", "https",
    "crypto", "tls", "dns", "dgram", "cluster", "worker_threads",
    "vm", "v8", "inspector",
];
const NEVER_PROXY_PREFIX: &[&str] = &["node:"];
```

### Layer 2: Default Allowlist (in RepairConfig)
```rust
pub struct NpmProxyConfig {
    pub enabled: bool,
    pub allow_scoped: Vec<String>,       // e.g., ["@aliou/*", "@marckrenn/*"]
    pub allow_patterns: Vec<String>,     // e.g., ["@*/pi-*"]
    pub allow_packages: Vec<String>,     // e.g., ["node-pty", "chokidar"]
    pub deny_packages: Vec<String>,      // operator additions to denylist
}

impl Default for NpmProxyConfig {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Self {
            enabled: true,
            allow_scoped: vec![
                "@aliou/*".into(), "@marckrenn/*".into(),
                "@sourcegraph/*".into(), "@juanibiapina/*".into(),
            ],
            allow_patterns: vec!["@*/pi-*".into()],
            allow_packages: vec![
                "node-pty".into(), "chokidar".into(), "jsdom".into(),
                "turndown".into(), "linkedom".into(), "adm-zip".into(),
            ],
            deny_packages: vec![],
        }
    }
}
```

### Layer 3: Environment Variable Override
`PI_AUTO_REPAIR_PROXY_ALLOW=@foo/*,bar-pkg` — add to allowlist
`PI_AUTO_REPAIR_PROXY_DENY=dangerous-pkg` — add to denylist

### Resolution Order
1. Check NEVER_PROXY denylist → if match, deny (not overridable)
2. Check deny_packages + env deny → if match, deny
3. Check allow_scoped + allow_patterns + allow_packages + env allow → if match, allow
4. Default: deny (conservative)

### Logging When Denied
When a package is denied proxy treatment, log it at WARN level:
`[auto-repair:warn] Package 'some-pkg' not proxied (not in allowlist). Extension may fail.`

This helps operators diagnose failures and decide whether to add to the allowlist.

title: [LISR] Dynamic Secure Extension Repair Program (Intent-Legible Self-Healing)
description:
This program introduces a secure, deterministic, and auditable mechanism to dynamically repair broken extensions when intent is legible and risk can be bounded. Current extension breakage often comes from schema drift, API renames, and minor structural issues; we want a first-class self-healing path that reduces operator toil without compromising safety.

This epic exists to coordinate all required workstreams: policy and threat boundaries, legibility scoring, deterministic rewrites, constrained model assistance, behavior proofs, controlled rollout, and operational observability.
design:
Architecture is phase-gated and fail-closed:
1) Security contract and policy modes define what is allowed.
2) Intent legibility pipeline decides whether auto-repair is even eligible.
3) Deterministic rule engine performs known-safe rewrites first.
4) Optional model-assisted proposal stage is constrained by a primitive whitelist.
5) Proof pipeline verifies behavioral and capability invariants.
6) Overlay canary rollout validates production safety before promotion.
7) Full audit and telemetry enable forensic confidence and operator trust.
acceptance_criteria:
- End-to-end repair path exists from broken extension input to safe promoted output.
- Repair never increases privilege without explicit human approval.
- Validation/proof pipeline blocks unsafe or ambiguous repairs.
- Canary/rollback controls are automated and deterministic.
- Audit trail is complete enough for security review and incident forensics.
notes:
Strategic justification:
- Improves reliability and user trust in extension ecosystem.
- Reduces mean-time-to-recovery for breakages caused by upstream/API drift.
- Preserves project principle: safety and determinism over convenience.

Non-goals:
- No unconstrained AI patching.
- No silent privilege expansion.
- No executing untrusted broken code to infer intent.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
Execution map and dependency rationale:

Phase A (Policy foundation): LISR-1 defines mode semantics, static-only boundaries, and privilege monotonicity. Every downstream epic depends on this because no repair behavior is acceptable without enforceable safety policy.

Phase B (Eligibility and deterministic repair): LISR-2 determines whether intent is legible enough to repair. LISR-3 performs deterministic rewrites for known breakage classes. These two epics establish the safe default path and reduce reliance on model assistance.

Phase C (Constrained AI path): LISR-4 is explicitly downstream of LISR-2 and LISR-3. We only allow model proposals after deterministic options and confidence gating are available, and only through strict primitive schemas.

Phase D (Proof before activation): LISR-5 blocks production rollout. Structural checks, capability monotonicity, hostcall parity, and conformance replay/golden checksums are the hard activation gate.

Phase E (Runtime rollout safety): LISR-6 adds overlay artifacts, canary routing, and deterministic rollback. This assumes proof pipeline outputs are trustworthy and machine-readable.

Phase F (Operational trust): LISR-7 captures append-only ledger, telemetry, operator inspection, and forensic bundles to support incident response and governance.

Phase G (Institutional memory): LISR-8 codifies ADRs, playbooks, developer guidance, and release governance so system intent survives team turnover.

Phase A - Policy Foundation:
LISR-1 is upstream of all work because no repair automation is acceptable without mode semantics, static-only boundaries, and privilege monotonicity controls.

Phase B - Legibility + Deterministic Repair:
LISR-2 determines eligibility (is intent legible enough?) and LISR-3 provides deterministic, auditable repair behavior for common breakage classes.

Phase C - Constrained AI Assist:
LISR-4 is intentionally downstream of LISR-2 and LISR-3 so model usage remains bounded, policy-governed, and secondary to deterministic fixes.

Phase D - Proof Gate:
LISR-5 is the hard activation barrier. Candidates must pass structural checks, security invariants, semantic parity checks, and conformance replay.

Phase E - Runtime Safety:
LISR-6 delivers canary and rollback controls to handle real-world runtime regressions even after offline proof passes.

Phase F - Trust and Operations:
LISR-7 ensures every decision is observable, explainable, and reconstructable for incidents.

Phase G - Long-Term Maintainability:
LISR-8 captures rationale, operator procedures, and governance so future teams can evolve the system safely.

title: Research: GitHub repo search (broad net)

comments.author: LavenderRobin
comments.text:
Goal
- Use GitHub repo discovery to find extension repos/bundles that may not show up in the initial community lists.

Repeatable repo-search queries (start broad, then tighten)
- Keywords:
  - "buildwithpi" extension
  - "pi-mono" extension
  - "Pi Agent" extension
  - "pi agent" registerTool
  - "pi extension" (expect noise; use language/topic filters)
- Topics (if present): topic:pi-agent, topic:pi-extension, topic:buildwithpi
- Language focus: TypeScript/JavaScript first; then Python/Rust for wrappers that ship TS entrypoints.

Process
1) Run each query and export the top results (at least: name, URL, stars, last update).
2) For each promising repo, validate “true Pi extension” via a quick code signature check (see bd-?? GitHub code search task) before adding to the inventory.
3) Record popularity signals (stars, forks, recent commits) and *why* the repo is in-scope.

Output
- A list of candidate repos (with metadata) that can be merged into docs/EXTENSION_CANDIDATES.md and the machine-readable enumerations.
- Each entry must include a “discovered_via” field (query + timestamp) so this can be repeated.

Acceptance criteria
- >= 10 distinct queries executed and recorded.
- >= 200 repos reviewed at triage level.
- >= 50 new validated “true Pi extension” candidates surfaced (or a written explanation of why the ecosystem is smaller than expected).

comments.author: LavenderRobin
comments.text:
TESTING + LOGGING REQUIREMENTS

Treat GitHub discovery as an ingest pipeline (even if executed manually at first).

Deliverables must be machine-usable
- Candidate repo list must be exportable as JSON (not just notes), including discovered_via (query + timestamp).

Unit tests
- If we build any helper tooling (query runner, scorer, parser), add unit tests using saved GitHub API/HTML fixtures:
  - query result parsing
  - repo metadata normalization
  - dedup key generation

E2E script
- Offline E2E that replays fixture responses and produces the same normalized candidate output.

Logging
- JSONL log per run:
  - query string + filters
  - number of repos returned/triaged/accepted
  - reasons for accept/reject (e.g., “true Pi extension signature present”, “mention-only”)
  - timing per stage

CI posture
- CI should run in offline/fixture mode; live GitHub queries should be opt-in (rate limits, nondeterminism).

# Goal

- bd-kh2.1: extension UI request/response roundtrip
- bd-kh2.2: extension session connector scenarios

title: Eliminate remaining cargo-audit warning-only dependency inventory
description: Release v0.2.0 removes all known cargo-audit vulnerabilities, but RustSec still reports warning-only inventory: lru 0.12.5 unsound IterMut through charmed-glamour 0.2.0 (upstream constraint; verify the vulnerable LruCache::iter_mut API remains unreachable), plus unmaintained bincode/yaml-rust via syntect/rich_rust, paste via image/rav1e, proc-macro-error2 via charmed-bubbletea, and rustls-pemfile via asupersync. Upgrade or coordinate upstream replacements without unsafe overrides; retain cargo audit exit-0 verification.
notes:
INVENTORY DISPOSITION (2026-08-16). cargo audit exit-0 retained throughout; 8 warning-only advisories triaged:

REPO-SIDE FIXED:
- paste (RUSTSEC-2024-0436) via image→ravif→rav1e: image dep trimmed to default-features=false + [jpeg,png,gif,webp,rayon] — exactly what the read tool decodes/encodes (2f6c227b). rav1e/exr/tiff/qoi/bmp decoders no longer compiled into ANY build (verified cargo tree --all-features --target all: unreachable). NOTE: Cargo.lock retains rav1e/paste/ravif rows (cargo keeps optional-dep entries; fresh generate-lockfile probe reproduces this), so cargo-audit still LISTS paste — the exposure is gone even though the inventory line remains until upstream cargo prunes differently. Bonus: helps bd-2ohw2 size budget.

VERIFIED-UNREACHABLE (upstream bumps still recommended):
- lru 0.12.5 IterMut (RUSTSEC-2026-0002): charmed-glamour 0.2.0 syntax.rs uses only new/get_or_insert-family/cap/len/clear — iter_mut NEVER called. Confirmed per the bead's explicit ask.
- lru 0.12.5 + 0.16.4 pop() panic-safety (RUSTSEC-2026-0253): neither glamour nor rich_rust (style/cells/color caches) calls pop(); exposure requires panicking Drop/Hash on cached types — theirs are String/Style/Arc tuples (no panicking impls). No patched 0.12.x/0.16.x exists (fix is 0.17+, verified against the sparse index) — REQUIRES upstream: bump lru to >=0.17 in charmed_rust (glamour) and rich_rust.

UPSTREAM-ONLY (sibling repos, coordinate there):
- rustls-pemfile unmaintained via asupersync: real runtime use (TLS PEM parsing); migrate asupersync to rustls-pki-types' pem API.
- proc-macro-error2 unmaintained via charmed-bubbletea: compile-time proc-macro only, zero runtime exposure; swap to syn::Error-based diagnostics upstream.
- bincode + yaml-rust unmaintained via syntect (rich_rust): syntect dump-load/yaml-load features; rich_rust can disable yaml-load (use plain defs) and rely on syntect's bincode2 migration when released.

No unsafe overrides, no audit.toml suppressions added. Follow-up = 3 upstream PRs (charmed_rust lru, rich_rust lru+syntect features, asupersync pemfile); repo re-verifies with cargo audit after each upstream release lands in the lock.

title: [TUI-2] Scoped-models UI polish: pattern validation and dry-run preview (bd-27a8)
description:
## Problem

/scoped-models accepts patterns but provides minimal feedback about what they match. Users cannot preview matches before committing.

## Solution

### Enhanced Pattern Feedback
1. **Validation**: Check if pattern is valid glob syntax. If not, show error with example:
   ```
   /scoped-models [invalid
   → Error: Invalid glob pattern "[invalid" — unclosed bracket
     Example: /scoped-models gpt-4*,claude-3*
   ```

2. **Preview**: After parsing patterns, show what they match BEFORE saving:
   ```
   /scoped-models gpt-4*,claude-3*
   → Matching 7 models:
     claude-3-haiku-20240307
     claude-3-opus-20240229
     claude-3-sonnet-20240229
     gpt-4
     gpt-4-turbo
     gpt-4o
     gpt-4o-mini
   Patterns saved. Press Ctrl+P to cycle through matched models.
   ```

3. **Deduplication**: If patterns overlap (e.g., "gpt-4*" and "gpt-4o"), show unique matches only.

4. **Clear feedback**: `/scoped-models clear` shows what was cleared: "Cleared 2 patterns (was: gpt-4*,claude-3*)"

### UX Design: Two-Phase Confirmation

**IMPORTANT COMPLEXITY NOTE**: The original design proposed "Enter to confirm, Esc to cancel" after preview. This is HARD in the bubbletea TUI architecture because:
- /scoped-models is processed as a slash command in the input handler
- The command handler runs synchronously in update()
- Adding a "waiting for confirmation" state requires a new app mode (like InputMode::ScopedModelsConfirm)
- This mode would need to intercept Enter/Esc in the key handler

**Decision: Skip confirmation, apply immediately.** The preview is informational only — patterns are saved immediately after showing the match list. This is simpler and matches how other slash commands work (/theme, /model, etc.). If the user made a mistake, they can run `/scoped-models clear` or `/scoped-models <new-pattern>`.

**Rationale**: Adding a confirmation mode for one slash command creates inconsistency and complexity. The current slash command UX is "type command, see result, adjust if needed." Keep that pattern.

## Files to Modify
- src/interactive.rs: /scoped-models handler (handle_scoped_models() function)

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Invalid glob syntax shows clear error with example
- [ ] Preview shows matched model list immediately (no confirmation prompt)
- [ ] Deduplication of overlapping patterns
- [ ] Clear command shows what was removed with previous pattern text
- [ ] No-match warning when patterns match zero models
- [ ] Unit tests for validation, preview, deduplication
- [ ] No regression in existing scoped-model tests

## Dependencies
- Depends on TUI-1 (scoped cycling must work before polishing UI)
close_reason: Already fully implemented: pattern validation with error messages, match preview, deduplication, clear feedback, no-match warnings. All 5 unit tests pass. Verified no regressions.

title: [PERF-TRACK] TUI performance: content caching, frame budgets, adaptive rendering, memory bounds
description:
## Overview

This track transforms the TUI from a naive full-redraw architecture into a high-performance rendering pipeline with:

1. **Content memoization** — Cache rendered markdown per message; only re-render when content changes (PERF-1)
2. **Incremental viewport updates** — Append-only updates during streaming instead of full rebuild (PERF-2)
3. **Frame timing telemetry** — Instrument view()/update() with microsecond-precision timing (PERF-3)
4. **Frame budget enforcement + CPU pressure** — Degrade gracefully when frame render exceeds 16ms budget; detect CPU pressure from /proc/loadavg and floor rendering fidelity accordingly (PERF-4, absorbs former PERF-5)
5. **Memory pressure detection** — Monitor RSS, progressive collapse of old messages when exceeding thresholds (PERF-6)
6. **String allocation optimization** — Reuse buffers, minimize allocations on hot path (PERF-7)
7. **Benchmark suite** — Criterion benchmarks for all critical rendering paths (PERF-8)
8. **CI regression gates** — Fail CI if performance regresses >20% (PERF-9)

## Current Architecture (problems)

- `build_conversation_content()` re-renders ALL messages (including markdown) every single frame
- New String allocation per frame for the entire conversation content
- No frame timing measurement — framerate target is "N/A"
- No memory monitoring — idle memory target is "Not measured"
- No adaptive behavior under load — renders at full 60fps regardless of system pressure
- bubbletea already has differential rendering (skip terminal I/O if view unchanged) — we need to leverage this

## Target Architecture

- MessageRenderCache: per-message cache keyed on (content_hash, collapsed, thinking_visible)
- Incremental append buffer for streaming deltas (avoid full content rebuild)
- Frame budget state machine: Normal→Degraded→Emergency with hysteresis, plus CPU pressure floor
- Memory watcher: VmRSS sampling via /proc/self/status at 1Hz with progressive collapse
- Pre-allocated conversation buffer: clear+push_str instead of new String per frame

## Dependencies

- This track blocks DOC (must measure before documenting)
- Independent of AUTH and TUI tracks

## Sub-beads (8 items)

| # | Bead | Name | Priority |
|---|------|------|----------|
| 1 | PERF-1 | MessageRenderCache | P0 |
| 2 | PERF-2 | Incremental viewport | P0 |
| 3 | PERF-3 | Frame timing telemetry | P0 |
| 4 | PERF-4 | Frame budget + CPU pressure | P0 |
| 5 | PERF-6 | Memory pressure detection | P1 |
| 6 | PERF-7 | String allocation optimization | P1 |
| 7 | PERF-8 | Criterion benchmark suite | P1 |
| 8 | PERF-9 | CI regression gates | P2 |

Note: PERF-5 (Adaptive FPS / CPU pressure) was merged into PERF-4 as they share the same FrameBudget state machine.

## Files Involved
- src/interactive.rs (primary — view(), build_conversation_content(), update handlers)
- benches/tui_perf.rs (new benchmark file)
- tests/tui_state.rs (new performance unit tests)
- tests/e2e_tui_perf.rs (new E2E perf tests)

Full TUI performance pipeline implemented: MessageRenderCache, incremental viewport, frame timing telemetry, frame budget enforcement, memory pressure detection, string allocation optimization, Criterion benchmarks, CI regression gates, cross-platform fallbacks, and comprehensive E2E test scripts.

title: Make fs chmod/chown stubs fail on missing paths
description:
Source-only mock/stub pass found that node:fs chmodSync/chownSync and node:fs/promises chmod/chown currently return success without checking whether the target path exists. That differs from Node.js and can let extensions record false success for permission changes.

Evidence:
- src/extensions_js.rs exports chmodSync(_path, _mode) and chownSync(_path, _uid, _gid) as unconditional no-ops.
- node:fs/promises re-exports chmod/chown as unconditional returns.
- tests/ext_conformance/api_usage_matrix.json records chmodSync and fs/promises chmod/chown calls as stubbed API usage.

Acceptance:
- chmodSync/chownSync and async wrappers must at least resolve the path through existing fs access checks and throw ENOENT for missing paths while preserving the sandbox/no-permission-model boundary for existing paths.
- Add focused node_fs_shim coverage for existing-path no-op success and missing-path failure.
- Update extension compatibility docs if the claim boundary changes.
- Validate with low-write checks and RCH when available; do not run local heavy cargo under disk pressure.
notes: Claimed by Codex on 2026-05-18. Agent Mail remains unavailable, so Beads is the soft lock. Scope: patch existing fs shim functions and focused tests only; avoid local heavy cargo while disk/RCH are unhealthy.

title: EPIC: Close G06 SDK contract shape — decide keep-or-retire, then deliver
description:
# Background
Hard gate G06 (SDK parity) FAILS with reason: "SDK contract-shape critical gap remains open for strict drop-in embedding compatibility." Named critical gap: gap-sdk-contract-shape.

docs/sdk.md documents a Rust SDK cookbook for embedding Pi programmatically. pi-mono ships a TypeScript SDK surface. Strict drop-in at the SDK level would require Rust types/traits/functions to be semantically interchangeable with pi-mono's TS SDK types from the caller's perspective (not literally identical — ecosystems differ — but contract-shape equivalent).

# Goal
First decide: is strict drop-in SDK parity *worth* delivering? If yes, implement it and pass G06. If no, officially retire the SDK-drop-in claim and update docs to position the Rust SDK as an independent, idiomatic companion.

# Scope (decision branch)
Option A (keep + deliver):
1. Audit pi-mono SDK surface against docs/sdk.md and src/lib.rs Rust exports.
2. Close gap-sdk-contract-shape with concrete implementations.
3. Parity-tested via tests/dropin_sdk_differential/ exercising identical flows.

Option B (retire):
1. Update docs/dropin-certification-contract.json to remove SDK gate (or downgrade to informational).
2. Update README "Execution surfaces" language: remove SDK drop-in claim; frame Rust SDK as companion, not replacement.
3. Update AGENTS.md guardrail wording if needed.

# Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Explicit go/no-go decision documented in the bead close comment with rationale
- [ ] If kept: G06 status=pass in verdict.json + differential suite in CI
- [ ] If retired: contract.json updated, README + FAQ updated, gap-ledger entry moved to "retired" state with closure reason
- [ ] docs/dropin-certification-verdict.json regenerated reflecting chosen path

# Considerations / Risks
- SDK drop-in is the hardest and least-valuable of the three failing gates (most consumers use CLI/RPC, not programmatic embedding). Retirement may be the right call.
- If retired, README "programmatically control" claim needs a careful rewrite that still accurately describes the Rust SDK as useful.
- If kept, watch for over-engineering — contract-shape parity ≠ type-literal parity.

# Refs
- docs/sdk.md
- docs/dropin-sdk-contract.json
- src/lib.rs
- README "Execution surfaces" table

title: Fix node:buffer utf16le and ucs2 encoding semantics
description: Node Buffer supports utf16le/utf-16le/ucs2/ucs-2 aliases across Buffer.from(string, encoding), buf.toString(encoding), buf.write(..., encoding), Buffer.byteLength, and Buffer.isEncoding. The node:buffer module shim currently lacks these aliases, while the global Buffer fallback recognizes them but still falls through to UTF-8 encode/decode/length behavior. Add Node reference vectors and implement UTF-16LE code-unit encode/decode in both shims.

title: [AUTH-1] /login openai API-key auth flow (replace built-in OAuth assumption)
description:
## Problem

`/login` does not provide an OpenAI-specific first-party auth UX. Earlier assumptions about built-in OpenAI OAuth constants are not supported by current OpenAI API docs.

## Verified Constraint (from bd-2gdoo)

OpenAI API documentation uses API-key authentication (`OPENAI_API_KEY`) for API access. Public OAuth docs found are for GPT Actions connecting to third-party APIs, not for authenticating a CLI to OpenAI API.

## Solution

Implement an API-key-first `/login openai` flow:

1. `/login openai` prompts for an OpenAI API key (or accepts pasted key input).
2. Key is stored in `auth.json` under `openai` as an API-key credential.
3. UX provides actionable guidance: where to create keys and how to rotate/revoke.
4. Optional lightweight verification call can be used to fail fast on invalid keys.
5. `/logout openai` removes stored credentials.

No built-in OpenAI OAuth constants, client secrets, or PKCE flow should be added for this task.
acceptance_criteria: 1) `/login openai` stores API-key credentials in `auth.json` and OpenAI requests resolve auth from storage. 2) `/logout openai` removes stored credentials cleanly. 3) User-facing messaging clearly identifies API-key flow (not OAuth), including setup guidance. 4) Unit tests cover key storage/load/overwrite and provider key resolution precedence.
notes: Implemented /login openai API-key flow in src/interactive.rs using pending login kind ApiKey, input normalization, and provider-specific prompt text. /logout messaging now reflects generic stored-credential removal. Added helper/tests for API-key normalization and slash help wording. Prompt now includes key-creation plus rotation/revocation guidance. Verification: cargo fmt --check, cargo check --all-targets, cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings all pass (using isolated CARGO_TARGET_DIR/TMPDIR).

title: Implement pi.session metadata APIs (setSessionName, getSessionName, setLabel)
description:
Allow extensions to manage session metadata.

## API Spec (from legacy)
```typescript
pi.setSessionName(name: string): void
pi.getSessionName(): string | undefined
pi.setLabel(entryId: string, label: string | undefined): void
```

## Use Cases
- Auto-naming sessions based on content
- Bookmarking important conversation points
- Extension-managed session organization

## Implementation Requirements
1. Hostcall handlers for setSessionName, getSessionName, setLabel
2. SessionInfoEntry for name changes
3. LabelEntry for entry labels
4. Integration with session picker (show names)

## Session Entry Formats
```json
// SessionInfoEntry
{"type": "session_info", "id": "...", "name": "My Feature Work"}

// LabelEntry
{"type": "label", "id": "...", "target_id": "abc123", "label": "important"}
```

## Test Plan
- Unit test: setSessionName creates SessionInfoEntry
- Unit test: getSessionName returns current name
- Unit test: setLabel creates LabelEntry
- Integration test: session picker shows custom name

## Files to Modify
- src/extensions.rs (hostcall handlers)
- src/session.rs (entry types if needed)
- src/session_picker.rs (display names)
close_reason: All three session metadata APIs implemented: (1) pi.getSessionName() - JS bridge __pi_get_session_name (extensions_js.rs:2980) calls pi.session('get_name') Rust handler (extensions.rs:5494). (2) pi.setSessionName(name) - JS bridge __pi_set_session_name (extensions_js.rs:2984) calls pi.session('set_name') Rust handler (extensions.rs:5503). title: fsqlite 0.3.4 'native' force-enables ALL extension vtabs + serde_json preserve_order (breaks JSON key-order goldens; explains size bloat)
description:
Discovered 2026-08-16 while landing bd-cv653.5.1, immediately after the bd-oc1wu fsqlite cutover (432c90cc).

FACTS (verified via cargo tree + fsqlite-core 0.3.4 Cargo.toml):
- pi declares fsqlite = { default-features = false, features = ["native"] } with a comment claiming json/fts5/rtree vtabs are excluded for the size budget.
- fsqlite-core's `native` feature itself pulls `extensions` = ext-json + ext-fts5 + ext-icu + ext-misc + ext-rtree, AND `diagnostic-pragmas` whose serde_json dep hard-enables `preserve_order`.
- Effect 1: serde_json Maps switch from BTreeMap (sorted keys) to IndexMap (insertion order) ACROSS THE WHOLE LIB — every JSON we serialize changes byte order. First casualty: tools_conformance::e2e_read::e2e_read_diagnostic_artifact_matches_golden_contract (insta golden 'tool_diagnostic_read_success' expects sorted keys). Semantically JSON order is meaningless, but goldens/hashes/diff-based tests are affected; full blast radius being measured.
- Effect 2: all extension vtabs compiled in → very likely the 24.5 MiB binary (bd-2ohw2) vs the old 22 MiB budget.

FIX OPTIONS:
a) Upstream (preferred, sibling project /data projects frankensqlite): decouple `extensions` from `native`, and drop `preserve_order` from diagnostic-pragmas' serde_json (or feature-gate it). Then pi returns to native-only.
b) Repo-side stopgap: accept insertion-order JSON (update the broken goldens, comment why); document that preserve_order is active.

Related: bd-2ohw2 (size reclaim), bd-oc1wu (cutover, closed).
notes: STOPGAP LANDED (14a57a4e): tool-diagnostic golden normalizer now sorts keys recursively, immune to preserve_order either way; tools_conformance 264/264. REMAINING: upstream fsqlite fix (decouple extensions from native; drop/gate preserve_order in diagnostic-pragmas serde_json) — then pi gets its size budget back (links bd-2ohw2). Verified worker-side that session/rpc/store suites (480) pass under preserve_order; no other goldens broken in the suites run so far. Full-matrix confirmation deferred to CI.
close_reason: fsqlite 0.3.5 decouples native from ext vtabs + preserve_order; bump landed b9c459e8, goldens verified green

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text: Upstream fix LANDED: frankensqlite 76d07fba (main+master) decouples 'extensions' from core's 'native' (default keeps extensions; facade ext features now forward to core registration features, icu+misc added to facade default so default capability is unchanged) AND scopes serde_json preserve_order to fsqlite-ext-json only — ext-json-less embedders like pi get sorted maps back. Verified upstream: ext-less native build compiles; minimal facade shape resolves core=diagnostic-pragmas,native with serde_json default,std; ext-json 191/191. REMAINING for pi: wait for the next fsqlite crates.io publish (0.3.5), bump, then (a) pi's existing default-features=false features=[native] actually takes effect, (b) preserve_order leaves pi's graph — the 14a57a4e golden normalizer stopgap can stay (it is order-agnostic), (c) re-measure binary size for bd-2ohw2 and consider tightening the 26 MiB budget.

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text: RESOLVED by fsqlite 0.3.5 bump (commit b9c459e8). 0.3.5 decouples 'native' from both 'extensions' and diagnostic-pragmas' preserve_order. Verified: (1) cargo tree -e features,normal -i serde_json => zero preserve_order refs in artifact graph — JSON maps back to sorted keys, goldens green (worker session 820/820 + tools_conformance 264/264). (2) All five fsqlite-ext-* crates dropped from Cargo.lock. One prediction in this bug was WRONG: the ext vtabs were NOT the size bloat — measured darwin-arm64 release 24.59 MiB on 0.3.5 vs 24.48 on 0.3.4 (delta ≈ concurrent failover/ask code growth). lto=true had already dead-stripped the unreferenced vtab code; the 18.85→24.5 growth is fsqlite engine core (matches the cargo-bloat attribution on bd-2ohw2).

title: Thirteenth-wave completion-audit closeout enforcement
description:
## Background
The project now has `scripts/build_completion_audit.py`, closeout gates, operator handoff summaries, runpacks, Beads ledger reconciliation, and Agent Mail coordination, but completion admission is still mostly a human convention. Future agents need a self-contained track that turns the completion-audit generator into a standard closeout proof layer: every claimed deliverable should map to direct command, artifact, commit, push, Beads, and handoff evidence, while proxy-only evidence and stale or missing proof fail closed.

## Goals
- Operationalize `pi.completion_audit.v1` as advisory closeout-admission evidence for Beads work.
- Add real Beads/git-backed and fixture Agent Mail/RCH coverage so closeout proof is not just a synthetic unit test.
- Project completion audit status into runpacks/operator summaries without replacing Beads, git, Agent Mail, RCH, UBS, CI, or source artifacts.
- Create CI/runbook guidance for lightweight audit gates that do not invoke heavy cargo unless explicitly routed through RCH.

## Non-goals and boundaries
- Do not mutate Beads except through explicit `br` workflow.
- Do not send live Agent Mail or launch RCH from the audit generator.
- Do not authorize file deletion, release/performance/capacity claims, or strict drop-in claims.
- Completion audit evidence remains advisory and fail-closed; it never replaces source systems.

## Idea-wizard rationale
Phase 2/3 ideas were screened against the current closed/open queue. Closeout freshness and proof-memory registry ideas already exist under closed children of `bd-63x3v.6.13`, so this track focuses on the adjacent uncovered gap: prompt-to-artifact completion admission from direct evidence.

## Acceptance
- Child beads define contract/inventory, adapters, no-mock tests, runpack/operator projection, CI/runbook wiring, and closeout evidence.
- Each child includes unit or fixture coverage plus at least one negative control.
- `bv` robot checks show an acyclic graph and at least one ready child.
- Heavy validation, if introduced by a child, is RCH-only with agent-specific target/tmp guidance.
notes: Idea-wizard tracking epic only. Do not claim this parent for implementation unless the child graph needs restructuring; claim ready child beads, starting with bd-nji8x.1. Parent remains open so the child graph is visible in br/bv until CA-6 closeout.
close_reason: Completed completion-audit closeout enforcement track after children bd-nji8x.1 through bd-nji8x.6 closed and closeout evidence commit dda994870 was pushed to origin/main and origin/master; final evidence is docs/evidence/completion-audit-enforcement-closeout-gate.json.

title: CA-1: Inventory completion-audit closeout admission contract
description:
## Background
`scripts/build_completion_audit.py` can evaluate prompt-to-artifact requirements against direct evidence, but the closeout-admission contract is not documented as a first-class artifact for agents. This child makes the expected schema, required evidence classes, source boundaries, and negative controls explicit before implementation expands.

## Scope
- Inventory current inputs: Beads issue details/close reasons, git commits and pushed refs, command results, artifacts, Agent Mail thread/reservation summaries, RCH posture/proof-memory status, UBS and ledger gates, and existing runpack/operator summary surfaces.
- Define a proposed contract for completion-audit closeout admission, including direct evidence classes, proxy-only blockers, stale proof blockers, and forbidden claim/deletion boundaries.
- Identify exact implementation surfaces for later children, especially `scripts/build_completion_audit.py`, `scripts/build_swarm_operator_runpack.py`, `scripts/summarize_operator_handoff.py`, docs/contracts, docs/evidence, and tests/golden_corpus/completion_audit.

## Tests and evidence
- JSON or Markdown inventory must be machine-readable enough for downstream beads.
- Validate touched JSON with `python3 -m json.tool`; validate Markdown/docs with `git diff --check`.
- Run `./scripts/reconcile_beads_ledger.sh` before commit.

## Negative controls
- Completion audit cannot mark work complete from proxy-only evidence.
- Missing pushed ref or failed command evidence blocks closeout.
- No live Agent Mail/RCH mutation, file deletion, release claim, performance claim, capacity claim, or strict drop-in claim is authorized.

## Acceptance
A future agent can implement CA-2 through CA-6 from the inventory without consulting the original planning conversation.
close_reason: Added docs/evidence/completion-audit-closeout-admission-inventory.json with source inventory, proposed closeout-admission contract, direct evidence classes, negative controls, and follow-on requirements; validated with json.tool, git diff --check, and reconcile_beads_ledger.

title: CA-2: Add Beads/git evidence adapter for completion audit
description:
## Background
The current completion audit accepts explicit evidence JSON and can capture basic git state, but agents still have to hand-build the evidence bundle. To make the audit useful at closeout time, it needs a deterministic adapter that converts Beads and git state into direct evidence without mutating source systems.

## Scope
- Extend `scripts/build_completion_audit.py` or add a narrow wrapper to ingest Beads issue IDs, `br show`-style JSON, close reasons, commit IDs, pushed-ref checks, and optional Agent Mail/RCH fixture summaries.
- Keep the adapter read-only: it may run `git`/`br` read commands or read fixture JSON, but it must not close beads, reserve files, send mail, launch RCH, run cargo, or delete files.
- Emit evidence entries with stable refs for commands, artifacts, commits, pushes, source files, unresolved gaps, and proxy-only markers.
- Preserve existing self-test/golden behavior and add deterministic projections for the adapter.

## Tests and evidence
- Unit/self-test coverage for successful direct evidence assembly.
- Negative fixtures for missing pushed ref, failed command, proxy-only command, missing artifact, stale close reason, and dirty worktree mismatch when the objective requires clean state.
- Validate with `python3 -m py_compile scripts/build_completion_audit.py` and `python3 scripts/build_completion_audit.py --self-test`.

## Acceptance
A future closeout can build an audit evidence bundle from real Beads/git state plus fixture coordination summaries without writing any live source-system state.
close_reason: Added read-only Beads/git closeout admission adapter to scripts/build_completion_audit.py with fixture-backed Agent Mail/RCH summaries, stable closeout evidence refs, CLI flags, and golden self-test coverage for success plus missing push, failed/proxy command, missing artifact, stale close reason, and dirty worktree blockers; validated with py_compile, self-test, json.tool, git diff --check, and reconcile_beads_ledger.

title: CA-3: Add no-mock completion-audit closeout integration coverage
description:
## Background
Completion admission must prove real workflow edges, not only synthetic in-memory fixtures. This child adds no-mock-style coverage using temporary git and Beads state while keeping Agent Mail/RCH inputs as fixture summaries to avoid live mutation.

## Scope
- Build deterministic temp workspaces with real git commits, branches, pushed-ref simulations or local remote refs, and minimal Beads JSONL/DB state.
- Feed those workspaces through the completion-audit adapter from CA-2.
- Cover successful closeout, missing push, command failure, proxy-only evidence, artifact missing, stale Beads status, unresolved follow-up gap, and forbidden file-deletion authority.
- Emit detailed JSON/JSONL logs with redacted command text, artifact paths, statuses, and timing.

## Tests and evidence
- Add fixture/golden artifacts under the existing completion-audit test area or a clearly named adjacent directory.
- `python3 scripts/build_completion_audit.py --self-test` must cover the no-mock scenarios or call a focused no-mock subtest.
- The test must not call live providers, live Agent Mail, live RCH, or heavyweight Cargo.

## Acceptance
The audit fails closed for every negative control and only allows completion when direct evidence covers every extracted requirement with no unresolved gaps.
close_reason: Added no-mock completion-audit self-test coverage that initializes real temporary git repositories and Beads state with br, captures pushed and unpushed git evidence, and verifies pass plus missing push, failed command, proxy-only command, missing artifact, stale Beads status, unresolved follow-up, and forbidden file-deletion authority cases with stable JSON projection logs; validated with py_compile, self-test, json.tool, git diff --check, and reconcile_beads_ledger.

title: CA-4: Project completion-audit status into runpacks and handoff summaries
description:
## Background
Operators need completion-audit state in the same handoff surface they already use for validation routing, proof-memory, stale evidence, and next actions. This child projects completion-audit status into runpacks and operator summaries while preserving source-system authority boundaries.

## Scope
- Add optional completion-audit JSON input to `scripts/build_swarm_operator_runpack.py` and/or `scripts/summarize_operator_handoff.py`.
- Surface concise status, blocked requirements, unresolved gaps, proxy-only evidence, missing pushes, required next actions, and claim boundaries.
- Keep the projection read-only; it must not run the audit, mutate Beads, reserve files, send mail, launch RCH, or edit artifacts.
- Add contract fields and golden fixtures for pass, block, degraded/missing-source, and proxy-only scenarios.

## Tests and evidence
- Update focused Python self-tests/goldens for runpack or handoff projection.
- Validate JSON contracts/goldens and run `python3 -m py_compile` on touched scripts.
- Include detailed fixture output showing redaction posture and operator next-action text.

## Acceptance
A runpack/handoff consumer can see whether completion is allowed and exactly which direct-evidence requirements block closure, without treating the projection as Beads/git/CI authority.
close_reason: Added read-only completion-audit projection to operator handoff summaries, including normalized completion_audit output, invariant, safe next actions, claim-boundary must-not-touch guidance, markdown section, contract updates, and fixture/golden coverage for pass, blocked, missing-source, and proxy-only states; validated with py_compile, handoff self-test, json.tool, git diff --check, and reconcile_beads_ledger.

title: CA-5: Wire lightweight completion-audit gate into CI and runbooks
description:
## Background
After the adapter and projections exist, the project needs clear operator and CI guidance so completion audits become a standard lightweight closeout gate without turning into another heavyweight cargo path.

## Scope
- Add documentation and/or script wiring that explains when to run completion audit, what inputs are authoritative, and what output blocks closeout.
- Integrate a lightweight gate into an existing script or CI path only if it can run without heavy cargo, live providers, live Agent Mail mutation, or live RCH mutation.
- Ensure failure output includes concise remediation for missing commands, missing artifacts, proxy-only evidence, failed commands, missing pushes, and unresolved follow-up beads.
- Preserve RCH-only language for any future heavy validation referenced by the audit.

## Tests and evidence
- Run focused Python self-tests and docs/JSON validation appropriate to touched files.
- Add at least one fixture proving CI/remediation output is stable and machine-readable.
- Run `./scripts/reconcile_beads_ledger.sh` and `ubs --staged --only=rust .` before commit.

## Acceptance
Agents have an executable, documented closeout-audit gate that is cheap enough for routine use and explicit enough to prevent completion illusion.
close_reason: Added lightweight read-only completion-audit closeout gate script with fixture/golden remediation output, wired CI to run its self-test, and documented operator replay/remediation in docs/ci-operator-runbook.md; validated with py_compile, gate self-test, pass and expected-block CLI fixture checks, json.tool, YAML parse, git diff --check, and reconcile_beads_ledger.

title: CA-6: Close out completion-audit enforcement with advisory evidence gate
description:
## Background

title: Hostcall ABI: WASM host.call Uses Shared Dispatcher (Parity Refactor)
description:
# Goal
Refactor the WASM component hostcall path (`host.call(name, input_json)` in `src/extensions.rs` `mod wasm_host`) so it uses the shared hostcall dispatcher:

`HostCallPayload (from JSON) -> dispatch_host_call_shared() -> HostResultPayload -> WIT return string`

# Current State (Observed)
- WASM hostcalls are implemented in `src/extensions.rs` under `mod wasm_host`, in `impl host::Host for HostState { async fn call(...) }`.
- The current implementation:
  - parses JSON into `HostCallPayload`
  - validates capability mismatch
  - performs policy + logging + timeout
  - dispatches by method with bespoke logic
- A shared dispatcher already exists (`dispatch_host_call_shared()`), but WASM hostcalls do not yet call it.

# Scope
1. Keep input validation that is specific to the WIT contract:
   - `name` must match `payload.method` (or explicitly document any tolerated mismatch).
   - JSON parse errors are `invalid_request`.

2. Replace the bespoke WASM dispatch path with:
   - Build `HostCallContext`:
     - `runtime = "wasm"`
     - `extension_id` (from registration state)
     - `policy`, `tools`, `http`, `fs`, `env_allowlist`, `manager`
   - Call `dispatch_host_call_shared()`.

3. Convert `HostResultPayload` to the WIT return type:
   - On success: return `Ok(<serialized output JSON>)`.
   - On error: return `Err(<serialized HostCallError JSON>)`.
   - Ensure error codes are taxonomy-only (shared dispatcher guarantees this).

4. Ensure logging is not duplicated:
   - `dispatch_host_call_shared()` already emits `host_call.start/end` and `policy.decision`.
   - Remove duplicate logging from the WASM entrypoint so we don’t double-count or drift.

# Tests
- `--features wasm-host` unit/integration tests:
  - capability mismatch -> `invalid_request`
  - denied -> `denied`
  - timeout -> `timeout` with retryable
  - session/ui/events with manager absent -> deterministic taxonomy
  - params_hash parity vs JS for canonical calls (tie into `bd-1uy.1.4`)

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] No duplicated policy/timeout/logging logic remains in the WASM hostcall entrypoint.
- [ ] WASM hostcall errors and success outputs match the shared dispatcher’s semantics.
- [ ] `cargo test --all-targets --features wasm-host` is green.
close_reason: Completed: WASM host.call uses shared dispatcher; wasm-host gates green

title: Mock-code-finder explicit placeholder remediation backlog
description:

Three production-adjacent placeholders remain worth explicit tracking so future agents do not rediscover them as transient TODO noise.

- `tests/franken_node_compat_harness.rs:6` states the harness captures Node/Bun baseline data, but FrankenNode parity execution is not yet implemented.

- `br search` for ACP permission, FrankenNode compatibility, and MissingRuntimeApi returned no existing open tracker.

## Non-findings
Heredoc labels named STUB in release/installer scripts, dummy API keys in local mock legacy capture setup, docs examples containing TODO strings, fuzz corpus bytes, and tests that deliberately simulate failures are intentional fixtures or examples and are not production placeholders.

## Acceptance

- Each child includes concrete source paths, expected real implementation shape, tests/evidence, and blocker boundaries.
- Heavy Rust validation remains RCH-only per AGENTS.md.

## Validation for this planning pass

title: Implement ACP request-permission callback flow
description:
## Background
`src/acp.rs:165` documents that permission callback support is not yet implemented and `tool_approval` is advertised as false until the ACP request-permission flow is implemented. This is a real production-adjacent placeholder because ACP clients cannot delegate tool approval through the protocol today.

## Scope
- Re-read the current ACP protocol expectations used by this repo and inspect `src/acp.rs`, `src/agent.rs`, `src/interactive.rs`, `src/permissions.rs`, and relevant ACP tests before patching.
- Design the request/response flow so tool approval remains fail-closed when the client does not support callbacks, disconnects, times out, or returns malformed approval data.
- Wire the advertised capability only when the callback path is implemented and tested.
- Preserve existing non-ACP permission behavior and do not weaken extension capability or filesystem safety checks.

## Tests and evidence
- Add focused ACP tests for approve, deny, timeout/disconnect, malformed response, and capability advertisement.
- Add at least one end-to-end or stdin/RPC-style fixture that proves the protocol message ordering around a tool request.
- Heavy Rust validation must use `rch exec -- cargo ...` with agent-specific `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` and `TMPDIR`; if a narrow non-cargo proof is sufficient for planning, state that explicitly.

## Acceptance
ACP tool approval is no longer a source-code placeholder: supported clients get a real request-permission flow, unsupported clients remain fail-closed or explicitly not-capable, and docs/comments no longer claim the feature is not implemented.
close_reason: Implemented ACP request-permission callback flow with fail-closed approval handling

title: Inventory and prioritize MissingRuntimeApi conformance gaps
description:
## Background
`src/conformance_shapes.rs` defines `RemediationBucket::MissingRuntimeApi` for extensions requiring a QuickJS virtual-module stub or host API that is not yet implemented. The bucket is useful, but without a current inventory and priority order, missing runtime APIs can persist as a classification rather than an implementation backlog.

## Scope
- Trace where `MissingRuntimeApi` is assigned and emitted in conformance reports.
- Build or refresh a machine-readable inventory of current MissingRuntimeApi cases, grouped by missing module/hostcall, affected extensions, frequency, and likely implementation surface in `src/extensions_js.rs`, `src/extensions.rs`, or harness policy.
- Cross-check existing Beads before creating implementation children so this does not duplicate tracked runtime API work.
- Create follow-up child Beads only for confirmed production runtime or conformance gaps, not intentionally unsupported fixtures.

## Tests and evidence
- Add a focused report/golden or script self-test that proves MissingRuntimeApi cases are surfaced with enough detail for remediation.
- Include at least one negative control showing intentionally unsupported extensions remain separated from missing runtime APIs.
- Heavy conformance or cargo validation must use `rch exec -- cargo ...`; source-only JSON/script validation may run locally when no Rust build is invoked.

## Acceptance
The MissingRuntimeApi placeholder bucket becomes an actionable, deduplicated remediation inventory with concrete next Beads or a documented empty result, so future agents are not blocked by an opaque not-yet-implemented class.

title: [AUTH-4] Refresh failure recovery UX: actionable /login suggestion
description:
## Problem

When token refresh fails, the token is silently discarded. The user has no idea what happened or how to fix it.

## Solution

### User-Facing Recovery Flow
When refresh fails:
1. Log error via tracing::warn with redacted details
2. Show system message in TUI: "OAuth token for {provider} has expired. Run /login {provider} to re-authenticate."
3. If in RPC mode: emit error event with recovery suggestion
4. Set agent_state to Idle (do not attempt API call with expired token)

### Implementation
- In refresh_expired_oauth_tokens(), return a Vec<RefreshFailure> for each failed refresh
- In main.rs startup: if any RefreshFailure, queue system message
- In interactive.rs: if mid-session refresh fails, show recovery message in conversation

### Edge Cases
- Multiple providers with expired tokens: show one message per provider
- Token expired during streaming: gracefully end stream, show recovery message
- Network error vs auth error: different messages ("Network issue" vs "Re-authenticate")

## Files to Modify
- src/auth.rs: Return RefreshFailure structs instead of silently discarding
- src/main.rs: Handle refresh failures at startup
- src/interactive.rs: Handle mid-session refresh failures

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] RefreshFailure struct with provider, error type, recovery action
- [ ] System message shown in TUI on refresh failure
- [ ] RPC event emitted on refresh failure
- [ ] Different messages for network vs auth errors
- [ ] Unit test for RefreshFailure generation
- [ ] TUI state test for recovery message display
close_reason: Completed AUTH-4 implementation: refresh failure model + TUI/RPC recovery UX + tests
